meta.method: deep-entry form: senses+context synthesized ONLY from LC/Hopkins comparanda (hgm_evidence and corpus English withheld); POS deterministic only (SOAS / tense evidence); see_also restricted to a computed candidate list of real headwords; INSUFFICIENT allowed

ka 'khor ba.gloss: cycling from the beginning (from the letter ka)

senses.gloss: cycling from the beginning (from the letter ka)
senses.context: Formed on ka, the first letter of the Tibetan alphabet, plus 'khor ba 'to cycle, revolve'; literally the turning or cycling of the alphabet-series from its first letter. The etymological image is of a cycle running from the very start.

By extension the phrase is glossed as cyclic existence (saṃsāra) that has been revolving from the beginning, i.e., without any first point. Here ka, as the first letter, stands for 'the very beginning'.

ka cog zhang.gloss: Ka, Chok, and Zhang (the three translators)

senses.gloss: Ka, Chok, and Zhang (the three translators)
senses.context: An abbreviation compounding the first syllables of three names: Ka-wa Pel-tsek (ka ba dpal brtsegs), Chok-ro Lü'i-gyel-tsen (cog ro klu'i rgyal mtshan), and Zhang Na-nam Ye-she-de (zhang sna nam ye shes sde). Used as a set designation for these three figures taken together.

ka dag.gloss: primordial purity; pure from the beginning

senses.gloss: primordial purity; pure from the beginning
senses.context: A contraction of ka nas dag pa, 'pure from ka', ka being the first letter of the Tibetan alphabet and hence standing for the very beginning. Rendered as primordially pure, essentially pure, or essential purity.

ka nas dag pa.gloss: pure from the beginning; essential purity

senses.gloss: pure from the beginning; essential purity
senses.context: Literally 'pure from ka', the first letter of the Tibetan alphabet, hence pure from the very start. The full form of which ka dag is the contraction; also rendered essential purity.
Tibetan phonetic transcription of the Sanskrit name Kamalaśīla.

ka tsan dbyangs gsum.gloss: the three [grammatical treatises/authors]: Kalāpa, Candra, and Sarasvatī (dbyangs can)

senses.gloss: the three [grammatical treatises/authors]: Kalāpa, Candra, and Sarasvatī (dbyangs can)
senses.context: An enumerative abbreviation formed from the first syllables of three names, referring to the three core Sanskrit grammatical traditions: Kālāpa (attributed to Śarvavarman), Candragomin's Cāndra system, and the system associated with Anubhūti (dbyangs). Used as a set phrase for the standard trio of Sanskrit grammars studied in Tibet.
Tibetan transliteration of the Sanskrit kāya, "body." It appears where the Sanskrit word is retained rather than translated by the usual Tibetan equivalent sku/lus.
Transliteration of Sanskrit kālacakra, rendered in Tibetan translation as dus kyi 'khor lo, "wheel of time." It designates the Kālacakra tantric system and its associated deity and cycle of texts.
A term of Tibetan medical diagnosis for a pulse position, specified as the one felt with or under the middle finger. The gloss is provisional (marked as a proposed rendering).

Rendering Sanskrit upakleśa, the derivative or branch afflictions that arise in dependence on the root afflictive emotions (nyon mongs). Commonly abbreviated nye nyon, and traditionally enumerated as a set of twenty (nye nyon nyi shu).

karṇa pa.gloss: a person of Karṇāṭa; the Karṇāṭa people

senses.gloss: a person of Karṇāṭa; the Karṇāṭa people
senses.context: A transcription-based term designating an inhabitant of Karṇāṭa (Karṇa-), used collectively for the people of that region. The comparanda give only this ethnic/geographical identification.
Tibetan transcription of Sanskrit kārṣapaṇa, a unit of coined money. Variant spellings of the same transcription occur, and the term appears in compounds specifying sums of money.

see_also: kar sha pa na mgron ('gron) bu stong drug brgya'i rin

senses.context: Renders Sanskrit chattra, an umbrella or overhead covering, hence also 'canopy'. In one attested usage it is glossed 'parachute', i.e. an umbrella-like device.
Corresponds to Sanskrit samantatamas, darkness extending everywhere; kun khyab renders samanta ('all-encompassing') and mun pa renders tamas ('darkness').
A paired epithet combining omniscience (kun mkhyen) with all-seeing vision (kun gzigs). The comparanda support only this descriptive sense of complete knowledge and complete vision.

see_also: kun mkhyen bu ram shing pa

senses.context: Epithet rendering Sanskrit ikṣvāku, literally 'sugar-cane (one)', here prefixed with kun mkhyen 'omniscient'. Used as a title/name applied to a personage of the Sugar-Cane (Ikṣvāku) lineage.
Renders Sanskrit sarvārtha-siddhi (attested in the Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra), i.e. achieving or establishing the aims/welfare of all beings. Also rendered 'achieving/establishing the welfare of all'.
Renders Sanskrit ārāma-sampad / ārāmasaṃpanna, a pleasure-garden (kun dga' ra ba) that is complete or excellent (phun sum tshogs pa). Attested in Conze's materials simply as 'gardens'.
Glossed by Hopkins as 'personal altar'. The illustrative Tibetan phrase given has someone searching even behind the kun dga' rwa ba and inside the rubbish bin, indicating a fixture within a room.

kun dga' rwa ba.sanskrit: tha na kun dga' rwa ba'i rgyab log dang; gad snyigs tshud chad kyi nang du zhib 'tshol byas

senses.context: Renders Sanskrit ānanda-śabda (attested in the Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra), the sound or cry expressing joy (kun dga', ānanda).

Renders ādeśanā-prātihārya, a marvel or miraculous display (cho 'phrul) consisting in reading and announcing what others are thinking. Attested in Prajñāpāramitā (C) and Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra (MSA) contexts, where it figures among the miraculous powers of a buddha or advanced practitioner.

kun nyon dang rnam byang tha dad med pa.gloss: non-difference of the thoroughly afflicted and the purified

senses.gloss: non-difference of the thoroughly afflicted and the purified
senses.context: Renders saṃkleśa-vyavadāna-abheda, i.e., the absence of any difference (tha dad med pa) between thoroughly afflicted phenomena (kun nyon, saṃkleśa) and purified phenomena (rnam byang, vyavadāna). Used in doctrinal discussions where the two classes of phenomena are said not to differ.
Renders the paired term saṃkleśa-vyavadāna as found in the Madhyāntavibhāga (MV), where the afflicted class of phenomena and the purified class are treated together as a topical pair.
Hopkins also glosses the compound verbally, as the purifying (rnam par byang) of thorough afflictions (kun nyon mongs).

Renders the causative saṃvardhayati (saṃ √vṛdh) in Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra contexts; the prefix kun tu conveys the sense of 'thoroughly, fully'. Glossed as thoroughly producing, generating, or engendering something.
Renders saṃvega (MV) and udvega, the state of thorough sadness, dejection, or disquiet; by extension also 'thoroughly disgusted' or 'pathetic'.
Also given for ākṣepa, saṃkopa, and prahasana, terms suggesting agitation or being stirred up; the exact nuance depends on the source text.

Rendering Sanskrit forms of saṃ-√tras, 'to be terrified, tremble with fear.' The Tibetan combines the intensifying kun tu ('thoroughly, completely') with skrag ('fear, be afraid'), hence a fear that is total or overwhelming. The Sanskrit causative saṃtrāsayati given in the comparanda indicates that contexts may also involve terrifying or frightening another.

Given as an equivalent of samutpāda, 'arising, production, origination.' The Tibetan uses the causative/transitive bskyed pa ('to generate, engender') with kun tu, so the term may be rendered as generating or engendering as well as arising.

kun tu bskyod.gloss: to shake thoroughly, set completely in motion

senses.gloss: to shake thoroughly, set completely in motion
senses.context: Corresponds to forms of saṃ-√kamp, 'to tremble, quake,' in its causative sense of making something shake or quiver. With kun tu ('thoroughly, completely') the sense is of moving or agitating something entirely, as when a realm is said to be caused to quake.

A gerundive form (nas, 'having...') corresponding to Sanskrit saṃchādya, 'having covered over.' The intensifier kun tu indicates complete or total covering, and mdzad nas marks the honorific/agentive construction.

A continuative form (ste) corresponding to saṃdhāvati, 'runs together, runs about.' The comparanda give both a neutral sense of moving, going, or wandering and, in Conze's usage, the pejorative nuance of erring or straying about.
Renders Sanskrit parivrājaka, a religious wanderer who has left home and roams as a mendicant. Used as a designation of such ascetics generally, including non-Buddhist ones.
In its verbal/general sense the term corresponds to āgama, āgamuka, i.e. going or moving about in all directions, with kun tu conveying 'thoroughly, everywhere'.
Feminine form of kun tu rgyu ba, designating a woman who lives as a wandering mendicant or ascetic.
Corresponds to saṃtrāsam āpadyante, 'they fall into terror'. kun tu marks the thoroughgoing or complete character of the fright.

Renders samudghātita-śukla-dharma, where dkar po'i chos are the white, i.e. virtuous, doctrines or qualities, and kun tu bcom indicates their being thoroughly vanquished or done away with. Hopkins glosses the compound rather as 'all-conquering wholesome doctrines/practices', so both a destroying and a destroyed reading are attested in the comparanda.
Corresponds to samucchinna-kuśala-mūla: the roots of virtue (dge ba'i rtsa ba) have been entirely cut off or annihilated, kun tu indicating the completeness of the severance.

kun tu 'jug.gloss: engagement in all; entering into everything

senses.gloss: engagement in all; entering into everything
senses.context: Formed with kun tu ("in all, thoroughly") plus 'jug ("enter, engage"), rendered by Hopkins as "engagement in all." No Sanskrit equivalent is supplied in the comparanda, so the range of the term beyond this general sense cannot be specified.

Corresponds to Sanskrit samudghāta / samuddhāta and uccheda, terms of complete extirpation or cutting off. Hopkins gives "thoroughly conquered; thoroughly destroyed; thoroughly wrecked," the intensive force coming from kun tu ("utterly, thoroughly").

Renders Sanskrit parikalpa / parikalpana and saṃkalpa, the mental activity of constructing or imagining an object. Hopkins gives "conceptuality; thorough conceptualization; ideation; comprehensive imagination."

In the past-participial sense of parikalpita the term qualifies what is merely posited by thought: "imputed; imputational; imaginary; thoroughly [mentally] constructed; imagined" (Hopkins). Attested in Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra and Madhyāntavibhāga contexts per the comparanda.

Renders Sanskrit parikalpa-mātra, with tsam corresponding to -mātra ("mere, only"). Hopkins glosses "imputation-only; conceptualization-only," i.e. something that is nothing more than a construction of thought.

A phrase built on kun tu rtog pa (conceptuality, imputation) with las byung ("arisen from"). Hopkins renders it "arisen from conceptuality; arisen from conceptualization; arisen from imputation," i.e. produced by mental construction rather than existing in its own right.
Verbal noun in the sense of fully comprehending or realizing something; Hopkins renders it both as the act ("thoroughly realize") and as the result ("thorough realization").

In Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra contexts the term corresponds to Sanskrit saṃkalpa, i.e. a thoroughgoing act of conceiving or imagining. Here the Tibetan rtogs pa covers the mind's constructive activity rather than veridical understanding.

kun tu rtogs par bya ba.gloss: to be thoroughly realized; that which is to be thoroughly realized

senses.gloss: to be thoroughly realized; that which is to be thoroughly realized
senses.context: Gerundive/future form of kun tu rtogs pa, marking what is to be fully comprehended, and by extension the object of such realization. Conze's materials associate it with āvedhyate, a passive form.

Corresponds to Sanskrit darśana, saṃdarśana, ādarśita, nirdeśa: the act of fully displaying, demonstrating, or expounding something to others. Hopkins gives "thoroughly teach, show, demonstrate, reveal, disclose."

senses.gloss: appearing, showing up (as in a mirror); perceiving
senses.context: Rendering ādarśana / avadarśika, the term can denote something's becoming visible or being reflected, hence Conze's "perceive" and "show up [in a mirror]."
Where it renders ākhyāna, the emphasis falls on verbal telling or announcing — a narration or piece of counsel imparted to another.

Perfect/past-stem counterpart of kun tu ston pa, rendering ādarśayati and saṃdarśana: to have fully displayed, demonstrated, or disclosed something. Hopkins glosses "thoroughly teach, show, demonstrate, reveal, disclose."

senses.gloss: shown up, reflected (as in a mirror)
senses.context: Following Conze's rendering of ādarśayati, the term can describe something being made to appear or be reflected.
Rendering Sanskrit ākarṣaṇa (drawing, attracting), the term denotes fully leading or drawing something or someone along. Hopkins gives "thoroughly lead."

Renders Sanskrit sarva-gātmika, describing something whose very nature (bdag nyid) is to pervade or extend to all (kun 'gro). Used of a nature that is present everywhere rather than confined to particular instances.

Renders Sanskrit sarvatraga-hetu, a cause (rgyu) characterized as going everywhere or operating in all cases (kun 'gro). Designates a causal factor whose scope is not restricted to a particular locus or occasion.

kun 'gro'i tshul.gloss: manner of applying to everything; universal mode

senses.gloss: manner of applying to everything; universal mode
senses.context: Literally the mode or way (tshul) of that which goes everywhere (kun 'gro); glossed as 'applicable to everything'. Used of a manner or formulation whose application is not restricted to particular cases.

rgyal kun yab gcig.gloss: sole father of all the Conquerors

senses.gloss: sole father of all the Conquerors
senses.context: An epithet: the one (gcig) father (yab) of all (kun) the Conquerors or Buddhas (rgyal), glossed as 'the only father of all the Buddhas'. Used honorifically of a figure presented as the single source from which all Buddhas arise.

Renders Sanskrit paryavāpnoti; the phrase indicates bringing everything (kun) within one's competence or understanding (chub par bya ba). Glossed variously as understanding all, realizing all, and mastering.
In some attestations the same verbal phrase is rendered 'study', i.e. to take up a subject so as to master it completely.
Renders Sanskrit ākīrṇa, indicating that things are completely intermingled or run together. Used where distinct items are conflated or blended so as to be indistinguishable.
Renders Sanskrit saṃgraha in the sense of gathering many items under one head — being combined, comprised, or summed up in something. Hence also 'collection, combination, summary'.
Used of the act of collecting or drawing things together, and by extension of withdrawing (drawing in) what has been extended.
In the sense recorded by Conze as 'means of conversion', saṃgraha designates the ways in which others are attracted and gathered to the teaching.
Corresponds to saṃdṛśyate, 'is seen, comes into view'; said of what manifests or is beheld.
With the intensive kun tu, the verb also carries the sense of appearing bright or illuminating on all sides.
Renders samanta-avabhāsa / samanta-āloka, light or illumination extending in every direction.
Attested as the name of a samādhi and as the name of a bodhisattva, so translated as a title rather than a common noun in such contexts.

kun tu snang bar byas nas.gloss: having illuminated everywhere; having appeared everywhere

senses.gloss: having illuminated everywhere; having appeared everywhere
senses.context: Gerundive form corresponding to ābhāya-avabhāsya, i.e. after shining forth and lighting up all around. Conze's rendering 'illuminate with their lustre' reflects the same image of rays pervading in every direction.

Renders Sanskrit āgraha in the sense of seizing upon or insisting on something; Hopkins glosses it as thorough grasping or thorough apprehension, with the Conze rendering 'acquisitiveness'. In this sense it names a mental holding-on to an object.
Also corresponds to Sanskrit dhāraṇa, i.e. holding or keeping (in mind). Here the emphasis is on retention rather than on afflicted clinging.

Equivalent to Sanskrit avalīyate / saṃlīyate, of the mind shrinking back or sinking; Hopkins glosses 'become thoroughly slack/weak/timid/cowardly', 'become cowed', 'be cast down', 'hide despondently (in)'. Attested in the phrase cittaṃ nāvalīyate na saṃlīyate, i.e. the mind is neither cowed nor shrinks back.
The nominal/participial form corresponding to the verb kun tu zhum; Hopkins glosses 'become thoroughly slack/weak/timid/cowardly', i.e. a state of despondency or faint-heartedness.
Renders Sanskrit ālīna, literally 'settled/stuck upon', which Conze glosses as 'clinging to, hanging on to'. The same Sanskrit root underlies both the sense of shrinking back and that of adhering.

Verbal form with 'gyur, rendering Sanskrit saṃlīyate: the mind shrinks back, becomes stolid or despondent. Hopkins glosses 'become thoroughly slack/weak/timid/cowardly', with Conze's 'become stolid; despond; is cowed'.
Corresponds to Sanskrit parimaṇḍala, 'entirely circular/spherical'; rab tu intensifies zlum po 'round'. Used to describe a shape as fully or perfectly rounded.
Rendering of Sanskrit samantabhadrā/samantabhadrī, the feminine counterpart of Samantabhadra; Lokesh Chandra also records it as the name of a ḍākinī.
As an adjectival form it renders samantabhadra- in compounds such as samantabhadracaryā ('the conduct of Samantabhadra/the all-good conduct'), where the sense is 'wholly good, good in every respect.'

kun tu bzod.gloss: patient in all situations, thoroughly forbearing

senses.gloss: patient in all situations, thoroughly forbearing
senses.context: Renders Sanskrit kṣāntiḥ sarvatra, patience or forbearance exercised everywhere, i.e., toward all circumstances without exception. Also translatable as tolerance or endurance in all [situations].
Renders jānāti and saṃjānāti in the sense of knowing, cognizing, perceiving or fully understanding something.
Corresponding to saṃjñāta (glossed as equivalent to saṃkhyāta) in Conze's material, with the senses 'reckoned as, be called,' i.e., identified or held to be such.
The nominal/verbal form: to know, perceive, or comprehend thoroughly.
Conze's material aligns the term with ajñā, which is glossed both as 'non-knowledge' and as 'to know, perceive'; the reference works thus record contrary readings, so context must decide.
Future passive participle form rendering ājñeyā: that which is to be fully known, understood or comprehended.
Rendering Sanskrit saṃjānāti, of complete or thorough knowing and understanding of something. Hopkins also records the weaker senses 'perceive' and 'can cognize'.

senses.gloss: hold to be true, apprehend as such
senses.context: In some contexts the term is glossed as taking or holding something to be true, i.e. apprehending it in a definite way rather than merely knowing it.

Verb of complete accumulation or gathering together, as glossed by Hopkins ('thoroughly accumulate/collect'). One of a set of verb-form spellings (kun tu gsog / gsogs / bsag / bsags) sharing the same meaning.

Verb of complete accumulation or gathering together, glossed by Hopkins as 'thoroughly accumulate/collect'. It is a spelling variant within the set kun tu gsog / gsogs / bsag / bsags, all given the same gloss.
Verb of complete accumulation or gathering, glossed by Hopkins as 'thoroughly accumulate/collect'. It belongs to the same verb-form set as kun tu gsog, kun tu gsogs, and kun tu bsags.
Verb of complete accumulation or gathering, glossed by Hopkins as 'thoroughly accumulate/collect'. It is one of the spellings of this verb alongside kun tu gsog, kun tu gsogs, and kun tu bsag.

Past/perfect form describing what has been completely gathered or amassed, corresponding to Sanskrit ācita. Rendered by Hopkins as 'thoroughly accumulated/collected' and, in the Conze-based material, as 'piled up', suggesting a mass built up by accumulation.
Verbal expression corresponding to Sanskrit ārakṣa, denoting complete protection or guarding. Hopkins extends the range to keeping, maintaining, and preserving — as in safeguarding vows and pledges.

kun gtong.gloss: to give away all; complete renunciation

senses.gloss: to give away all; complete renunciation
senses.context: Corresponds to Sanskrit saṃtyāga (also given as agrahaṇatā, 'non-grasping'), i.e. total relinquishment. Hopkins glosses it as giving away everything, with the Conze-based rendering 'complete renunciation'.
Nominalized form corresponding to Sanskrit sarvāsti-dāna, the giving of all that one possesses. Hopkins glosses simply 'giving away all', i.e. an act of total generosity.
Corresponds to Sanskrit parikalpita-svabhāva, the nature that is merely imputed or imagined. Hopkins gives both 'imputational nature' and 'imaginary nature' as renderings of this term.

Tibetan rendering of Sanskrit parikalpitalakṣaṇa, the character or defining feature that is merely imputed. In the threefold analysis of characters it designates that which is imaginary rather than established by way of its own nature.
Tibetan for Sanskrit parikalpitasvabhāva, the first of the natures (svabhāva), that which is merely imputed or imagined. It is contrasted with natures that are not established by imputation alone.

kun btags bden med yin pas de 'dra'i dog.gloss: no sensible way for such a qualm to occur regarding imputational natures, since they are not truly established

senses.gloss: no sensible way for such a qualm to occur regarding imputational natures, since they are not truly established
senses.context: A phrase asserting that, because imputational natures (kun btags) lack true establishment (bden med), a doubt or qualm of the sort under discussion has no basis for arising with respect to them.
Tibetan for parikalpita-dharma, a phenomenon that is merely imputed or imagined rather than established in its own right. It applies the category of the imputational (kun btags) to phenomena (chos).

Tibetan for parikalpitāvidyā, ignorance that is acquired or artificially adopted—i.e., imputed through learning or speculation—rather than innate. Rendered variously as artificial, acquired, or imputed ignorance.

Renders Sanskrit parikalpita-lakṣaṇa, the character or defining feature of what is merely imputed or imagined. Used of the first of the characters/natures in threefold classifications, contrasted with characters that are not merely superimposed by conceptual designation.

Equivalent to Sanskrit parikalpitasvabhāva, the nature of phenomena insofar as they are merely imputed or imagined. It is the first member of the threefold division of natures (svabhāva), designating what exists only through conceptual imputation.

An object to be abandoned that is artificial or acquired (kun btags) rather than innate, i.e., produced through imputation and conditioning such as adherence to tenets. Hopkins glosses it as 'artificial object of abandonment'; no Sanskrit equivalent is supplied in the comparanda.
Verbal expression for complete or comprehensive realization, understanding everything or realizing something thoroughly.
In Conze's material the term is aligned with Sanskrit āvidhyate, glossed tentatively as 'is pierced'. The equivalence is marked as uncertain in the comparanda.

kun brtags kyi mig ngos 'dzin skabs.gloss: occasion of identifying the imputational eye

senses.gloss: occasion of identifying the imputational eye
senses.context: A contextual heading marking the point in a discussion where the eye (mig) as an imputational (kun brtags) phenomenon is being identified or pointed out. The term belongs to expositions of the imputational nature applied to particular sense faculties.

kun brtags pa la sogs pa'i ngo bo nyid g.gloss: the three natures, beginning with the imputational

senses.gloss: the three natures, beginning with the imputational
senses.context: Sanskrit parikalpita-ādi-svabhāva(tri-): the triad of natures (svabhāva) of which the imputational (parikalpita) is named first, the remaining two being understood as the other-powered and the thoroughly established. Used where a text cites the set by naming only its first member followed by 'and so forth'.

Sanskrit parikalpita-pudgala-abhāva: the absence (abhāva) of a person (pudgala) as it is imputed or imagined (parikalpita). The phrase denies the imputed status of the person, not a person conventionally posited.
Sanskrit sarva-dharmāṇāṃ parikalpitānāṃ: the totality of phenomena (dharma) insofar as they are imputational or imaginary (parikalpita), i.e., taken as belonging to the first of the natures.
Sanskrit parikalpita-dharma-abhāva: the absence (abhāva) of phenomena (dharma) as they are imputed or imagined (parikalpita). Parallel in form to the denial of the imputed person.

kun brtags pa'i bdag med.gloss: non-existence of the imputed self; selflessness of the imputational

senses.gloss: non-existence of the imputed self; selflessness of the imputational
senses.context: Sanskrit parikalpita ātma nāsti, 'an imputed self does not exist': the self (ātman) as imputed or imagined (parikalpita) has no existence. Rendered in Tibetan with bdag med, the standard term for absence of self.
A form (gzugs) that is merely imputed or conceptually designated, rendering Sanskrit parikalpita-rūpa. The term applies the category 'imputational' (kun brtags pa, parikalpita) to form.
Glossed as a compendium, i.e. something in which all (kun) is gathered together ('dus pa). The Hopkins gloss is marked as a provisional rendering.
Corresponds to Sanskrit sampraśna, the act of asking or interrogation. Used for a question put to another.
A tentatively recorded equivalent paripṛcchaka suggests the agent who asks or inquires; this identification is marked as uncertain in the sources.
To put all (kun) together, reconcile or make agree. Used of harmonizing or bringing parties or points into accord.
Renders Sanskrit saṃgraha, a gathering together of all (kun) into a condensed presentation. Used of a text or exposition that summarizes a subject.

kun nas nyon mongs kyi dmigs pa.gloss: object of observation that is a thorough affliction

senses.gloss: object of observation that is a thorough affliction
senses.context: Renders Sanskrit saṃkleśa-ālambana, i.e. an ālambana (object of observation, focal object) consisting of, or characterized by, saṃkleśa (thorough affliction). Used where the objects taken as the focus of observation are classified as belonging to the afflicted side, in contrast to purified objects.

kun nas nyon mongs can.gloss: thoroughly afflicted; that which has thorough affliction

senses.gloss: thoroughly afflicted; that which has thorough affliction
senses.context: Renders saṃkliṣṭa (also saṃkliṣṭatva, the state of being such), attested in Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra and Madhyāntavibhāga materials. The Tibetan is adjectival (can, "possessing"), designating whatever is characterized by saṃkleśa, thorough affliction.
In Conze's usage saṃkliṣṭa is glossed simply "afflicted" or "polluted," describing minds, phenomena, or states contaminated by affliction.

Renders saṃkleśa-prātipakṣika (Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra), literally that which is the counteragent (prātipakṣa) of saṃkleśa. Tibetan gnyen po here has the sense of remedy or counterforce applied to thorough afflictions.

A paired expression joining kun nas nyon mongs (thorough affliction, saṃkleśa) with rnam byang (purification, thorough purity). It marks the two contrasting classes under which phenomena or states are surveyed.

kun nas nyon mongs dang rnam byang gnyis.gloss: the two: the thoroughly afflicted and the purified

senses.gloss: the two: the thoroughly afflicted and the purified
senses.context: The pair kun nas nyon mongs and rnam byang taken explicitly as two (gnyis), i.e. both the afflicted class and the purified class. Rendered by Hopkins as "both the thoroughly afflicted and the purified."

A paired term joining kun nas nyon mongs (thorough affliction, saṃkleśa) with rnam byang (purification, i.e. the thoroughly pure side). The compound names the two contrasting classes of phenomena — the afflicted and the purified — treated together as a topic.

Rendering Sanskrit saṃkliṣṭa: that which is thoroughly afflicted or has thorough affliction. Used of persons, minds, or phenomena described as afflicted or polluted; the abstract saṃkliṣṭatva (the state of being afflicted) is also attested for this expression.
Rendering saṃkleśasyānurakṣaṇā: protecting, guarding, keeping, maintaining, or safeguarding oneself against the thorough afflictions (saṃkleśa).
Rendering saṃkleśa-nirdeśa: the teaching, indication, or exposition of thorough affliction (saṃkleśa), as a topic set forth in a text.

kun nas nyon mongs pa dang rnam par dag.gloss: meaning of being neither afflicted nor purified

senses.gloss: meaning of being neither afflicted nor purified
senses.context: Rendering niḥsaṃkleśa-viśuddhy-artha: the object or meaning that is free of both thorough affliction (saṃkleśa) and purification (viśuddhi), i.e. that which is neither afflicted nor purified.

kun nas nyon mongs pa dang rnam par byan.gloss: affliction and purification; the afflicted and the pure

senses.gloss: affliction and purification; the afflicted and the pure
senses.context: A paired term rendering Sanskrit saṃkleśa-vyavadāna (also saṃkleśa-viśuddhi), naming the two sides of experience treated together in Yogācāra texts such as the Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra and Madhyāntavibhāga. It covers both the processes — becoming afflicted and becoming purified — and the two classes of phenomena so characterized (saṃkleśika / vaiyavadānika).

senses.gloss: the class of afflicted phenomena and the class of purified phenomena
senses.context: Used substantively of the two divisions of dharmas: those belonging to defilement and those belonging to purification. In this usage the compound functions as an inclusive rubric for all phenomena.

kun nas nyon mongs pa dang rnam par byan.gloss: absence of conceit regarding a division between the afflicted and the purified

senses.gloss: absence of conceit regarding a division between the afflicted and the purified
senses.context: Rendering saṃkleśa-vyavadāna-bhede nirmāṇaḥ in the Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra material, this describes the lack of pride or conceit that would take affliction and purification to be truly separate. It qualifies an attitude in which the pair (see kun nas nyon mongs pa dang rnam par byang ba) is not reified as two distinct things.

kun nas nyon mongs pa dang rnam par byan.gloss: the side/sphere of affliction and of purification

senses.gloss: the side/sphere of affliction and of purification
senses.context: Rendering saṃkleśa-vyavadāna-pakṣa, the term designates the two 'sides' or classes into which phenomena are grouped, the afflicted and the purified. The final dag here marks the pair, so the phrase may also be read simply as 'the afflicted and the purified.'

kun nas nyon mongs pa dang rnam par byan.gloss: not viewing (i.e., not observing) affliction and purification

senses.gloss: not viewing (i.e., not observing) affliction and purification
senses.context: Rendering saṃkleśa-vyavadānādarśana in Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra contexts, this denotes the non-seeing or non-perception of the pair of the afflicted and the purified. It expresses a state in which this duality is not apprehended as an object of view.

kun nas nyon mongs pa dang rnam par byan.gloss: correct teaching of affliction and purification

senses.gloss: correct teaching of affliction and purification
senses.context: Rendering saṃkleśa-vyavadāna-saṃdeśanatā, this names the act or quality of thoroughly and correctly setting forth the two topics of defilement and purification. It is presented as a mode of instruction concerning how beings become afflicted and how they become purified.

kun nas nyon mongs pa dang rnam par byan.gloss: thorough investigation of the afflicted and the purified

senses.gloss: thorough investigation of the afflicted and the purified
senses.context: A compound naming the full search or examination (yongs su tshol ba, paryeṣṭi) directed at the two classes of phenomena, those belonging to affliction (saṃkleśa) and those belonging to purification (vyavadāna). Attested in Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra literature as saṃkleśa-vyavadāna-paryeṣṭi.

kun nas nyon mongs pa dang rnam par byan.gloss: characters of the afflicted and the purified

senses.gloss: characters of the afflicted and the purified
senses.context: The defining characteristics (mtshan nyid, lakṣaṇa) of the two categories of phenomena: the afflicted (kun nas nyon mongs pa, saṃkleśa) and the purified (rnam par byang ba, vyavadāna). Given in the Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra as saṃkleśa-vyavadāna-lakṣaṇa.

That which pertains to affliction (saṃkleśa) considered as an object of abandonment (spang bar bya ba, prahāṇa). The Sanskrit saṃkleśa-prahāṇa points equally to the act of abandoning affliction and to what is to be abandoned.

kun nas nyon mongs pa spangs pa.gloss: having abandoned affliction; free of affliction

senses.gloss: having abandoned affliction; free of affliction
senses.context: The state in which affliction (kun nas nyon mongs pa, saṃkleśa) has been discarded or is absent, rendering saṃkleśa-varjita in the Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra. Describes a person or state marked by the absence of what has been given up.

The negation of kun nas nyon mongs pa (saṃkleśa), i.e. asaṃkleśa: the absence of affliction, or, adjectivally, that which is not afflicted. In Prajñāpāramitā contexts it is glossed both as 'non-affliction' and as 'without affliction, non-afflicted'.

Negative form corresponding to Sanskrit asaṃkliṣṭa / asaṃkleśa / niḥsaṃkleśa, i.e., not thoroughly afflicted, free of the thorough afflictions (kun nas nyon mongs pa, saṃkleśa). Used adjectivally of persons, states, or activities that are not tainted by affliction.
Also equated with saṃkleśa-abhāva, the mere absence or non-existence of thorough affliction, hence usable as a substantive ('non-affliction') as well as an attribute.

Rendering asaṃkleśāṅga: a yan lag (aṅga, branch/limb/member) characterized by absence of thorough affliction. The compound joins the negated saṃkleśa (kun nas nyon mongs pa med pa) with 'branch', i.e., a constituent factor that is free of affliction.

Rendering niḥkleśatopasaṃhārākāra: an aspect or mode (rnam pa, ākāra) of bringing about / accomplishing (sgrub pa, upasaṃhāra) the state of being free from afflictions (niḥkleśatā). Named as one of the ākāras in Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra-related enumerations of aspects.

Rendering asaṃkleśādhimokṣa: belief in, zeal or inclination toward (mos pa, adhimokṣa) the absence of thorough affliction. The term thus denotes an attitude of confident aspiration directed at the unafflicted state.

Rendering asaṃkliṣṭa-paribhoga: partaking of or fully enjoying (yongs su longs spyod pa, paribhoga) something without being thoroughly afflicted in doing so. The negated saṃkliṣṭa qualifies the manner of enjoyment as untainted by affliction.

kun nas nyon mongs pa yang med.gloss: there is no thorough affliction; without affliction

senses.gloss: there is no thorough affliction; without affliction
senses.context: A phrase negating the presence of saṃkleśa (kun nas nyon mongs pa, thorough affliction), rendered by Lokesh Chandra's comparandum na saṃkleśaḥ. Used in Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra-type contexts to state that a given state or basis is free of affliction.

kun nas nyon mongs pa las ldog pas.gloss: due to turning away from afflictions

senses.gloss: due to turning away from afflictions
senses.context: Ablative/instrumental construction on kun nas nyon mongs pa (saṃkleśa) with ldog pa 'turn away, reverse', corresponding to saṃkleśān nirvṛttitaḥ. It gives the reason for something as the reversal of, or turning back from, thorough affliction.

Verbal phrase with bsal ba 'remove, clear away' taking kun nas nyon mongs pa (affliction) as object; the Madhyāntavibhāga comparandum is kleśāpaśama (pacification/removal of afflictions). Hopkins' renderings include eradicate, remove, clear away, eliminate, avoid, exclude affliction.
Genitive compound saṃkleśa-hetu: that which produces or gives rise to thorough affliction (kun nas nyon mongs pa). Attested in Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra contexts.

A dharma that is afflicted or belongs to the class of affliction, corresponding to kliṣṭo dharmaḥ and sāṃkleśika-dharma. Typically contrasted with purified phenomena (rnam byang) in Yogācāra presentations.

kun nas nyon mongs pa'i nad kyi gnyen po.gloss: antidote to the disease of the afflictions

senses.gloss: antidote to the disease of the afflictions
senses.context: Compound designating that which counteracts the afflictions (kleśa), the afflictions being figured as a disease (vyādhi) and the remedy as its opposing factor (pratipakṣa). Attested in Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra-type literature as kleśa-vyādhi-pratipakṣatva.

kun nas nyon mongs pa'i phyogs.gloss: the afflicted class; sphere/side of thorough affliction

senses.gloss: the afflicted class; sphere/side of thorough affliction
senses.context: Renders saṃkleśa-pakṣa, the 'side' or class of phenomena belonging to thorough affliction (kun nas nyon mongs pa, saṃkleśa), as opposed to the pure or purifying side. Glossed also as 'sphere of the afflicted' or 'afflicted quarter'.
Renders saṃkleśa-pakṣa-nirodha: the stopping or blocking ('gag pa, nirodha) of the class or side of thorough affliction. Also glossed 'ceasing the sphere of the afflicted / the afflicted quarter'.

Renders saṃkleśa-lakṣaṇa, the defining characteristic or mark (mtshan nyid) of that which is thoroughly afflicted. Attested in Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra and Madhyāntavibhāga contexts, where such a character is typically contrasted with that of purification.

kun nas nyon mongs par 'gyur pa.gloss: becomes thoroughly afflicted; will be afflicted

senses.gloss: becomes thoroughly afflicted; will be afflicted
senses.context: Verbal expression rendering saṃkliśyate, the process of coming to be afflicted (kun nas nyon mongs pa, saṃkleśa). Hopkins gives the future-oriented gloss 'will be afflicted'.

kun nas nyon mongs med rnam dag.gloss: purity free from thorough affliction; unafflicted purity

senses.gloss: purity free from thorough affliction; unafflicted purity
senses.context: Renders Sanskrit niḥsaṃkleśa-viśuddhitā, a compound describing a purity (viśuddhi) characterized by the absence of thorough affliction (saṃkleśa). Attested in Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra literature as a quality of purification.

A term for the apprehending conception (gzung rtog) that takes as its objects phenomena belonging to the class of thorough affliction (kun nas nyon mongs). Glossed in English as 'conception of thoroughly afflicted objects.'

Corresponds to Sanskrit suvimokṣāya saṃkleśāt, 'for the sake of thorough liberation from affliction,' attested in Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra materials. Glossed as complete freedom or release from the afflictions.

Renders Sanskrit paryutthāna (also paryupasthāna), given in Conze's glossary as 'obsession'; the negated form niṣparyutthāno bhavati indicates being free of such obsession. In this use it names an affliction that surges up and overwhelms the mind.

senses.gloss: to rise up, arise, get up
senses.context: Corresponding to Sanskrit samutthāna, the term is also used in the more literal verbal sense of rising or arising. Further glosses recorded include 'flow' and 'suffice.'
Given as an equivalent of Sanskrit āghāta, a term of injury or striking down. The English glosses render it as thoroughly harming, torturing, or tormenting.

A mental state of hostility or malice toward others, rendering Sanskrit āghāta-citta. The compound joins kun nas mnar sems (harmful, tormenting intent) with sems (mind, attitude), naming the mind or attitude that wishes to injure.

Verbal form corresponding to Sanskrit āghātayati: to harbour ill will toward someone, to feel anger or cherish malice. The finite form (byed de) marks the ongoing act of entertaining such hostile intent.

Corresponds to Sanskrit saṃdṛśyate, 'is seen, appears'; the Tibetan intensifier kun nas ('thoroughly, from all sides') with snang ba ('appear, shine, illuminate') yields the sense of appearing fully or being clearly beheld. The comparanda also record the nuances 'appears bright' and, uncertainly, 'be equal to'.

Honorific-negative phrase (ma mchis pa, 'there is not') built on kun nas byung ba, 'arising, origination', rendering Sanskrit asamutthāna. Used where something is said not to arise or have no origination.

Negation of kun nas ldang ba ('rise up, arise, originate'), corresponding to Sanskrit asamutthāna. The comparanda gloss the positive verb ldang ba as 'rise up, get up, flow, suffice', while the negated compound is given the sense 'no arising, non-arising'.

kun nas mdzes pa.gloss: beautiful in every way, lovely on all sides

senses.gloss: beautiful in every way, lovely on all sides
senses.context: Renders Sanskrit samanta-prāsādika (samanta-prasādika), 'pleasing/agreeable on every side'. Used as an epithet of what is fair or attractive from all points of view, without any unpleasing aspect.
Verbal expression combining kun nas ('entirely, from all sides') with zhi ('pacify, be at peace'), glossed by Hopkins as 'thoroughly pacify'. No Sanskrit equivalent is supplied in the comparanda.

kun nas langs pa nyid las byung ba.gloss: arisen from, produced from a complete arising

senses.gloss: arisen from, produced from a complete arising
senses.context: Corresponds to Sanskrit samutthita, glossed 'arisen from'. The Tibetan analyses the term literally as that which comes about (las byung ba) from the very fact of complete arising or rising up (kun nas langs pa nyid).

Renders Sanskrit asamutthāna-yoga, i.e. lacking connection with samutthāna (kun nas slong ba, complete arising/instigation). Hopkins gives the interpretive rendering 'not joined up with the world of appearance'.
Corresponds to Sanskrit samutthāpaka, the agent of samutthāna (kun nas slong ba). Hopkins' range of glosses covers one who raises, gathers, incites, arouses, urges on, or causes something to arise.

kun nas slong ba med pa gtogs pa.gloss: not included in [that which has] motivation/arising

senses.gloss: not included in [that which has] motivation/arising
senses.context: Rendering Skt. asamutthāna-paryāpanna, describing what is not comprised within the sphere of that which is aroused or made to arise. Hopkins records the Conze-style gloss 'not included in the world of appearance', i.e. not belonging to what is stirred up or produced.

kun nas slong ba'i thabs.gloss: means of motivating, method of urging on

senses.gloss: means of motivating, method of urging on
senses.context: Rendering Skt. samutthāna-upāya, the technique or method by which something is raised up, set in motion, or motivated. Glossed as 'means of raising up/motivating/urging on'.

kun nas slong bar mi bgyid pa.gloss: does not arouse, does not raise up

senses.gloss: does not arouse, does not raise up
senses.context: Negated honorific verbal form corresponding to Skt. asamutthāpika, said of what does not induce, incite, or cause anything to arise. Hopkins gives 'which raises nothing' alongside the range 'does not ask/beg/collect/gather/raise/inspire/excite/arouse/cause to rise/urge on'.

A designation among the minor marks (dpe byad) of a buddha, characterized by purity of overall behavior or deportment (kun spyod). Attested only through the English phrase gloss 'minor mark of pure proper conduct'.

kun byang gi 'grib 'phel.gloss: decrease and increase of the afflicted and the purified

senses.gloss: decrease and increase of the afflicted and the purified
senses.context: A paired expression treating the waning and waxing of the thoroughly afflicted class (kun nas nyon mongs) and the purified class (rnam byang / byang ba). Attested only through the English phrase gloss 'increase and decrease of the thoroughly afflicted and the purified'.

A compound of kun byed (all-creating, doing everything) with las rlung (the wind or energy of karma/action); designates the karmic wind held to produce or bring about everything. Attested in Hopkins as "all-creating wind of karmic action"; the comparanda give no further doctrinal specification.

kun 'byung chos bzod.gloss: doctrinal forbearance with respect to origins of sufferings

senses.gloss: doctrinal forbearance with respect to origins of sufferings
senses.context: Formed from kun 'byung (origin[s] of suffering, the second truth) and chos bzod (doctrinal forbearance). It names the forbearance directed at the doctrine concerning origins, one member of the set that pairs forbearance (bzod) and knowledge (shes) in doctrinal (chos) and subsequent (rjes) modes.

kun 'byung chos shes.gloss: doctrinal knowledge with respect to origins of sufferings

senses.gloss: doctrinal knowledge with respect to origins of sufferings
senses.context: From kun 'byung (origins of suffering) and chos shes (doctrinal knowledge); the knowledge of the doctrine concerning origins, following upon the corresponding doctrinal forbearance (kun 'byung chos bzod).

kun 'byung rjes bzod.gloss: subsequent forbearance with respect to origins of sufferings

senses.gloss: subsequent forbearance with respect to origins of sufferings
senses.context: From kun 'byung (origins of suffering) and rjes bzod (subsequent forbearance); the subsequent-type forbearance regarding origins, paired with the doctrinal-type members of the same set (kun 'byung chos bzod, kun 'byung chos shes).

kun 'byung rjes shes.gloss: subsequent knowledge with respect to origins of sufferings

senses.gloss: subsequent knowledge with respect to origins of sufferings
senses.context: From kun 'byung (origins of suffering) and rjes shes (subsequent knowledge); the subsequent-type knowledge regarding origins, completing the fourfold series of doctrinal forbearance, doctrinal knowledge, subsequent forbearance, and subsequent knowledge.

kun 'byung mthong spang nyon mongs bcu.gloss: the ten afflictions abandoned by the path of seeing in relation to the truth of origins

senses.gloss: the ten afflictions abandoned by the path of seeing in relation to the truth of origins
senses.context: An enumeration of ten afflictive states (nyon mongs) that are eliminated by the path of seeing (mthong lam) insofar as it observes the noble truth of the origin of suffering (kun 'byung). The set is defined by two factors: the level of path at which the abandonment occurs, and the truth in relation to which the afflictions are classed.

kun 'byung bden pa'i khyad chos bzhi.gloss: the four distinguishing features (attributes) of the truth of origination

senses.gloss: the four distinguishing features (attributes) of the truth of origination
senses.context: A set of four characteristics that mark off the second noble truth, the truth of the origin of suffering (kun 'byung bden pa), as distinct from the other truths. Such fourfold sets of attributes are standardly enumerated for each of the four noble truths.

kun 'byung ba'i don rnam pa gsum.gloss: the three aspects of the meaning of origination

senses.gloss: the three aspects of the meaning of origination
senses.context: Sanskrit trividhaḥ samudaya-arthaḥ; a threefold analysis of what is meant by 'origin/origination' (samudaya, kun 'byung ba), i.e. of the sense in which suffering is said to arise. The term is a topical heading in scholastic presentations of the noble truth of origins.
Renders Sanskrit saṃśuddhi, the complete purifying or washing clean of something. Used of removing stains or defilements so that what remains is entirely pure.

The same verbal form is also glossed as thorough practicing or training, i.e. refining oneself through repeated cultivation. This sense extends the image of cleansing to the disciplining of the practitioner.
Renders Sanskrit asaṃgraha, the absence of grasping or clinging. Attested in Perfection of Wisdom contexts as a quality of not holding on to or appropriating objects.

kun rdzob nyid.gloss: mere conventionality; the state of being a conventional truth

senses.gloss: mere conventionality; the state of being a conventional truth
senses.context: Abstract noun formed on kun rdzob (saṃvṛti), rendering Sanskrit saṃvṛti-satyatā, the quality or status of being conventional truth. Hopkins glosses it as 'just a conventionality', i.e., something that is nothing more than conventionally true.

Verbal phrase indicating that something is stated or verbalized on the level of kun rdzob, conventional truth, rather than ultimately. Hopkins gives both a passive rendering ('expressed as conventionalities') and an active one ('conventionally express, verbalize').
A chos can (subject, topic possessing qualities) that belongs to the conventional level, kun rdzob pa. Hopkins glosses the term as 'conventional subjects'.

kun rdzob la ltos pa'i zhi mtha'.gloss: extreme of peace relative to the conventional

senses.gloss: extreme of peace relative to the conventional
senses.context: One of the extremes to be avoided, here the zhi mtha' (extreme of quiescence/peace) considered in relation to (ltos pa) conventionalities. Hopkins renders it 'extreme of peace relative to the conventional'.

kun rdzob las bzlog pa don dam pa'i ngo.gloss: the ultimate nature opposite to conventionalities (i.e. emptiness)

senses.gloss: the ultimate nature opposite to conventionalities (i.e. emptiness)
senses.context: A descriptive phrase for the don dam pa'i ngo bo nyid, the ultimate own-nature, characterized as the reverse or opposite (bzlog pa) of what is merely conventional. Hopkins identifies the referent as emptiness, 'the ultimate nature which is the opposite of conventionalities'.

kun rdzob/ tha snyad.gloss: convention; the conventional and the nominal

senses.gloss: convention; the conventional and the nominal
senses.context: A paired expression rendering Sanskrit saṃvṛti (the concealing/conventional) together with vyavahāra (everyday usage, transactional designation). Glossed simply as "convention," it refers to what is established by ordinary worldly usage and designation rather than by ultimate analysis.

A figurative expression for offerings arrayed in vast, cloud-like abundance, likened to those emanated by Samantabhadra (kun bzang). The Hopkins gloss is a provisional rendering: "clouds of offerings [like those] of Samantabhadra."

An epithet combining the names Samantabhadra (kun bzang) and Vajradhara (rdo rje 'chang) with the honorific "great" (chen). Attested only through the provisional English gloss "great Samantabhadra Vajradhara."
Denotes an emanated or magically manifested display (rnam 'phrul) associated with Samantabhadra (kun bzang). Given only as a provisional rendering, "magical display of Samantabhadra."

Renders Sanskrit samuccaya (also samuddhṛta, sarva...samuccaya), literally what is gathered together from everything. Used for a collection or abbreviated digest of material, and as a verb-like expression for grouping or collecting.
As a title or abbreviated title, kun las btus pa stands for a work called a "Compendium"; in particular it serves as the short title of Asaṅga's Summary of Manifest Knowledge (Abhidharmasamuccaya).

Said of what has gone entirely beyond everything, i.e. transcends all (states, objects, or categories). Hopkins renders it both as a verbal phrase, 'passed beyond all / completely transcended', and adjectivally, 'is beyond all'.
Abstract noun (nyid marking the abstract state) for the quality of knowing everything, corresponding to Sanskrit sarvajñatā. Hopkins glosses it 'knowledge of all'.
Possessive form (dang ldan pa, 'having, endowed with') describing one who possesses complete or thorough knowledge, for Sanskrit parijñātāvin. Hopkins: 'endowed with all-knowingness'.

kun shes pa rig pa'i dbang po.gloss: dominant faculty of one who has fully understood

senses.gloss: dominant faculty of one who has fully understood
senses.context: Rendering of Sanskrit ājñātāvīndriya, a term for a controlling faculty (dbang po, indriya) attributed to one who has already fully understood. Hopkins, following Conze, gives 'the dominant faculty of one who has fully understood'.
Rendering of Sanskrit ājñendriya, the controlling faculty (dbang po, indriya) of 'understanding'. Hopkins, following Conze, gives "the dominant (faculty) of 'understanding'".

Renders Sanskrit ājñāsyāmi-iti, a quoted first-person resolve, "I shall fully understand," marked in Tibetan by the future verb form kun shes par bya'o plus the quotative zhes. It expresses the aspiration or vow to come to complete knowledge of something.

Corresponds to the Sanskrit passive ājñāyate, glossed "is noticed," i.e. is completely or thoroughly known/recognized. The Tibetan continuative particle shing links this clause to a following one within a sentence.

Instrumental phrase rendering Sanskrit samutthānayā vācā, "by speech together with its motivating impulse." Here kun slong ba renders samutthāna, the motivation or instigating intention that accompanies an act of speech.
The motivating intention (kun slong) directed toward [the attainment of highest] enlightenment (byang chub sems). Given only as an English paraphrase in the comparanda, without a Sanskrit equivalent.

A descriptive expression, "all-illuminating enclosure" (kun gsal + ra ba, "enclosure, courtyard"), given as a poetic designation for the sky. Attested only through the English paraphrase supplied in the comparanda.

A place or point that is contested or under dispute. The comparanda give only the English rendering "disputed place"; the exact sphere of use (e.g. territory, or a debated point in a text) is not specified.

keng rus kyi gzugs brnyan yid la byed pa.gloss: taking to mind the image of a skeleton

senses.gloss: taking to mind the image of a skeleton
senses.context: A meditative act of bringing to mind (yid la byed pa, manasi-kurvataḥ) a reflected image or likeness (gzugs brnyan, pratibimba) of a skeleton (keng rus). The Sanskrit phrase pratibimba-saṃkalikāṃ ca manasikurvataḥ pairs the image with the skeletal frame as an object of mental attention.

see_also: rnam par rtog pa dang bcas pa'i gzugs brnan

ko.gloss: emphatic/contrastive particle: still, again; but, yet

senses.gloss: emphatic/contrastive particle: still, again; but, yet
senses.context: Rendered by Sanskrit api and tu, as in kiṃ tena jīvitenāpi ("what use even that life?") and ahaṃ kasmāttu kātaraḥ ("but why should I be faint-hearted?"). English glosses "still," "still again," and the note that it functions as an emphatic particle.
Also equated with Sanskrit carma, hide or leather, the sense underlying compounds such as ko gru, a leather boat.
A boat made of hide or leather; ko in the sense of carma (hide, leather) plus gru (boat).
A river of Kong-po; the name combines kong (Kong-po) with chu (water, river). The comparanda supply only this identification.

kye'i rdo rje zhes bya ba rgyud kyi rgya.gloss: Hevajratantra, the King of Tantras called "Hevajra"

senses.gloss: Hevajratantra, the King of Tantras called "Hevajra"
senses.context: Title of a tantric scripture, Sanskrit Hevajratantrarāja (also given as Hevajratantra-rāja-nāma), classed as a Highest Yoga Tantra and located at P10, vol. 1. The Tibetan renders the Sanskrit title element by element: kye'i rdo rje (Hevajra), zhes bya ba (nāma), rgyud kyi rgyal po (tantrarāja).

see_also: kye'i rdo rje mkha' 'gro ma dra ba'i sdom pa'i rgyud kyi rgyal po
kye'i rdo rje zhes bya ba'i rgyud kyi rgyal po'i 'grel pa
kye'i rdo rje'i rgyud kyi dka' 'grel padma can
kye'i rdo rje bsdus pa'i don gyi rgya cher 'grel pa

senses.context: Tibetan transliteration of the Sanskrit kriyā, meaning action or activity.
As a tantric class-name, the transliterated kriyā designates Action Tantra, the first of the tantra sets.
Tibetan transliteration of the Sanskrit kriyā, meaning action or activity; an orthographic variant of kri ya.
Used as the name of the tantra class called Action Tantra.
Renders Sanskrit mlecchajana, a compound of mleccha (barbarian, kla klo) and jana (person, people). In Conze's materials it is glossed collectively as "barbarous populations."

Verbal phrase rendering Sanskrit vācyate, the passive of the verb "to speak/recite"; Conze glosses it as "is recited." The construction klag pa (to read, recite) plus bya ba expresses the action as something to be done or undergone.

Rendering Sanskrit nāgapati, nāgādhipati and bhujagādhipa, this term designates the ruler or chief of the nāgas (klu), the serpent beings. Used as a title for the sovereign among a class of nāgas, and hence also as a proper epithet of particular nāga kings.
A malevolent or harmful being of the nāga (klu) class, glossed as 'nāga demon' or 'nāga spirit'. The element bdud marks the being as demonic rather than as a nāga sovereign.

klu dbang.gloss: lord of the serpents, nāga lord

senses.gloss: lord of the serpents, nāga lord
senses.context: Corresponding to Sanskrit nāgendra and bhujagendra, 'Lord of the Serpents': the powerful one or ruler among the nāgas (klu). Frequently functions as a title or epithet of a nāga king.

klu yi bdag po.gloss: chief of serpents, lord of the nāgas

senses.gloss: chief of serpents, lord of the nāgas
senses.context: An expanded form with the genitive, corresponding to Sanskrit bhujagādhipa, 'Chief of Serpents'. It designates the ruling nāga (klu) and is used interchangeably with the contracted form klu bdag.

A compound of klu (serpent being, nāga) and srin (harmful spirit, vermin-demon), glossed 'serpent spirit' or 'serpent vermin spirit'. It names a class of noxious serpentine spirits rather than nāga sovereigns.
Corresponds to Sanskrit pāṇḍu/pāṇḍura, denoting a pale or whitish coloration. Used of colors that are not pure white but off-white, grayish or wan.
A list or index of contents, e.g. of a collection of texts or of items in a library. Lokesh Chandra associates it with sūcīlipi, 'index writing'.
Lokesh Chandra tentatively adduces svakṣara, sulikhita, and suvyañjana, suggesting the notion of well-formed letters or clearly written text; these equivalents are marked as doubtful.

dkar po rnam par mthong ba'i sa.gloss: ground of seeing the white/wholesome; stage of bright insight

senses.gloss: ground of seeing the white/wholesome; stage of bright insight
senses.context: Renders śukla-vidarśanā-bhūmi (with the variant śukla-vipaśyanā-bhūmi), a named stage or level (bhūmi) on the path. Here dkar po, 'white', carries the sense of pure or wholesome phenomena that are seen, or alternatively the brightness of the insight itself.
Renders samudghātita-śukla-dharma, describing the state in which the white (i.e. wholesome, virtuous) dharmas have been completely uprooted or overcome.

Renders śukla-pakṣa, the 'white' portion or party, i.e. the class of wholesome qualities or practices as opposed to their dark counterpart. Occurs in Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra and Madhyāntavibhāga contexts.

see_also: dkar po'i chos rnams kun tu bcom

dkar dmar mdangs gsal.gloss: clear complexion, white tinged with red

senses.gloss: clear complexion, white tinged with red
senses.context: Descriptive compound for a bright, clear (gsal) glow or luster (mdangs) that is white (dkar) with a reddish (dmar) tinge. Attested in Hopkins only as a description of a fair complexion suffused with red.
Rendered by Hopkins as "radiant white" and equated by Lokesh Chandra with Sanskrit pāṇḍuraka (pale/whitish) and śuci (pure, bright, clean). It combines dkar (white) with gsal (clear, bright).
Lokesh Chandra records pāṇḍuraka as the name of a nāga king (nāgarājā), so the term also serves as the Tibetan rendering of that proper name.

Given by Hopkins only with the provisional English gloss "confidence." No Sanskrit equivalent is supplied, so the precise nuance and range of the term cannot be determined from the available comparanda.
Corresponds to Sanskrit ratnamegha, "cloud of jewels," used as the title of a sūtra. Equivalent in reference to the form dkon mchog sprin, the fuller title being dkon mchog sprin gyi mdo.
Proper name of a Tibetan author, dated 1728-1791 in Hopkins. Only the identification and dates are supplied by the comparanda.

dkon mchog rjes dran.gloss: Sūtra on the Recollection of the Three Jewels

senses.gloss: Sūtra on the Recollection of the Three Jewels
senses.context: Title of a scriptural text concerned with calling to mind (rjes dran) the Three Jewels (dkon mchog). Cited by Hopkins as the "Sutra on the Recollection of the Three Jewels".
Proper name of a Tibetan scholastic author, also known as Gung-tang Jam-pel-yang. Hopkins gives his dates as 1762–1823.
Renders Sanskrit ratnamegha, literally "jewel cloud," used as the short title of the sūtra known in full as dkon mchog sprin gyi mdo.
Full title corresponding to Sanskrit ratnameghasūtra. Hopkins locates it at P897, vol. 35.
An expanded designation of the three objects of refuge, dkon mchog ("jewel, rare and supreme one") qualified as rin chen ("precious") and enumerated as three.

Rendered by Sanskrit maṇḍalavidhi and maṇḍalopāyikā, i.e., the procedure or ritual method of the maṇḍala. The Tibetan literally suggests the maṇḍala in its entirety, and is glossed both as 'the complete maṇḍala' and as the rite by which it is accomplished.

An abbreviated form corresponding to Sanskrit maṇḍalavidhi and maṇḍalopāyikā, the ritual procedure or method for the maṇḍala. It shares its equivalents with dkyil 'khor gyi cho ga and dkyil 'khor yongs rdzogs.
Glossed simply as 'lower half', with dkyil indicating the middle or waist and smad the lower portion. No Sanskrit equivalent is supplied.
Glossed as a kha-ta (offering scarf) of ordinary quality, i.e., a plain or standard-grade btags. The element dkyus carries the sense of 'ordinary, common' as in dkyus ma.
Corresponds to Sanskrit veṣṭayati, veṣṭana and upanāha, the act of wrapping, winding or binding something around. Also given as bandhanīya, that which is to be bound or wrapped.
In the sense of Sanskrit parīta, 'surrounded, beset', rendered by Hopkins as 'entangle' and (in Conze's usage) 'overcome'. Here what wraps around is figured as encompassing or overwhelming.

Attested only with the English gloss 'turn/face upwards', i.e. directed or oriented in an upward direction. No Sanskrit equivalent is supplied, so the grammatical status (verbal form or adjectival) cannot be determined from the comparanda.

Glossed as 'order; command', i.e. an authoritative injunction issued by one in authority, or the act of issuing it. The form is closely allied to (and evidently a variant spelling of) bka' bsgo ba, which carries the same gloss.

A provisional rendering ({PH}) for a strict injunction of secrecy — a 'sealed' command (bka' rgya) that is 'tight' or firm (dam po), binding the recipient not to divulge what has been transmitted. Only the English gloss is attested; no Sanskrit equivalent is given.

Provisionally glossed ({PH}) as 'order; command', corresponding to Sanskrit ājñāsaṃkathā, literally speech or discourse (saṃkathā) of authoritative injunction (ājñā). Used of an authoritative instruction given by a superior, and of the act of giving it.
Also equated with Sanskrit āhava, a calling out or summoning, suggesting a use in which the authoritative word is a call or challenge issued to another.
Rendering Sanskrit kathā and saṃkathā, and also lapita, i.e. talk, converse, or what is spoken. The honorific bka' marks the speech as that of an exalted or authoritative speaker.
In the sense of a set discourse or narration — a sermon or story told (kathā) — as when the words of a teacher are related at length.
Corresponding to Sanskrit udanta, pravāda, and janapravāda: tidings or an account of what has happened, and by extension what is commonly said or reported among people.
An authoritative pronouncement issued by one in authority, glossed as a decree, command, or sealed order.

senses.gloss: signifier (mark) of the Word of the Buddha
senses.context: A distinguishing mark by which teachings are identified as authentic Word (bka') of the Buddha. In this use it appears in the set of four such signifiers (bka' rtags kyi phyag rgya bzhi).

bka' rtags kyi phyag rgya bzhi.gloss: four seals that signify the Word of the Buddha

senses.gloss: four seals that signify the Word of the Buddha
senses.context: A set of four 'seals' (phyag rgya) serving as the marks by which a teaching is recognized as authentic Word (bka') of the Buddha. The compound combines bka' rtags, 'signifier of the Word,' with the number four.

bka' dang bstan bcos.gloss: scripture and treatise; the [Buddha's] word and [Indian] treatises

senses.gloss: scripture and treatise; the [Buddha's] word and [Indian] treatises
senses.context: A paired expression contrasting the Buddha's own pronouncements (bka') with the expository treatises (bstan bcos) composed by later, principally Indian, masters. It designates the two classes of authoritative literature taken together.

Designation of the branch of the Ka-dam tradition following the line of oral precepts or instructions (gdams ngag), rendered 'Preceptual Ka-dam.' It is distinguished from the Textual Ka-dam (bka' gdams gzhung pa ba).
Designation of the branch of the Ka-dam tradition emphasizing the study of texts (gzhung), rendered 'Textual Ka-dam.' It is distinguished from the Preceptual Ka-dam (bka' gdams gdams ngag pa).

bka' bsdu bzhi pa.gloss: the fourth council; (one) of a fourth compilation of the word

senses.gloss: the fourth council; (one) of a fourth compilation of the word
senses.context: Literally the "fourth" (bzhi pa) gathering or compilation (bsdu ba) of the Buddha's word (bka'). Used to characterize a doctrinal statement as having the authority or significance of a fourth Buddhist council.

senses.gloss: short title of Dol-po-pa's Bka' bsdu bzhi pa'i don bstan rtsis chen po
senses.context: Abbreviated title of the work by Dol-po-pa Shay-rap-gyel-tsen (dol po pa shes rab rgyal mtshan), rendered by Hopkins as The Great Calculation of the Doctrine, Which Has the Significance of a Fourth Council.
The descent or handing down of authoritative scriptural word (bka'); the line through which teaching is passed on.

senses.gloss: doctrine that has befallen one through transmission
senses.context: By extension, the particular teaching or instruction that has come down to a person by way of such transmission, as glossed by Hopkins.
Formed from bka' blon, a minister of the council or cabinet, plus rogs, assistant or helper. Hopkins gives this only as a provisional rendering (marked {PH}).

A set of seven topics declared by the Buddha (bka' stsal, that which was pronounced/spoken). Hopkins lists them as the mental and physical aggregates, the sense-spheres, dependent-arising, the foods, the noble truths, the constituents, and the harmonies with enlightenment.
Title of a work attributed by Hopkins to Jang-chup-dzü-trül (byang chub rdzu 'phrul), P5839. The components are bka' yang dag pa, the true or correct word, and tshad ma, validity or valid cognition.

One of the similes used to classify the generation of the altruistic mind (sems bskyed), here likened to bkod ma'i chu, a spring or well of water. The comparison indicates a mind-generation characterized by the qualities of such a water-source; the comparanda give no further specification of the point of similarity.

A logical sign (rtags) as it is set forth or formulated in a statement of proof, i.e., the sign in the form in which it has been laid out. The element bkod relates to the sense of setting forth, arranging, or stating.

bkor bdag rgyal po.gloss: king who is custodian of property

senses.gloss: king who is custodian of property
senses.context: A royal title designating one who acts as guardian or steward of possessions or wealth. The comparanda give only this general characterization without further specification of context.

The reference material additionally attaches the glosses respect, respectful, service, honor, and (Conze) eulogy to this entry. These may reflect the honorific element bkur; they are recorded here without independent confirmation.
Used of what is radiant or attractive to the eye, rendering Sanskrit citra and citrita. In this sense the term conveys brightness or beauty of appearance.

Corresponds to Sanskrit vicitra, śabala, śabalita, karbura, and the abstract vaicitrya (variety), all denoting mottled or many-colored appearance and, by extension, diversity. The equivalent phalaka is also listed by Lokesh Chandra.
Name of a bird, so called because it emits a bright or beautiful cry. The compound joins bkra ba (shining, beautiful) with skad 'byin (producing a sound).
Literally rendering Sanskrit maṅgalakūṭa, a compound of 'auspiciousness' (bkra shis) and 'mass, heap, peak' (lhun po). Used as a descriptive name evoking an accumulation of good fortune.
As a proper name, the monastery in Gtsang province, Tibet, which is the seat of the Paṇ-chen Lamas.

An adverbial phrase built on bkral ba ('commentary, exegesis') with ltos med du ('without depending on'). Indicates that something is understood or established without recourse to explanatory literature.
Negative of bkri ba, 'to lead, guide', corresponding to Sanskrit aneyatā, the state of not being leadable. Hopkins glosses the phrase as 'one cannot be led astray'.
Verb with the forms bkru (future), 'khrud (present), bkrus (past), khrus (imperative). Renders Sanskrit terms for washing and cleansing such as kṣālana, nirmādana, and snāpana.
Also corresponds to Sanskrit siñca, secana, snāta and ṛtusnātā, i.e. sprinkling or pouring water over something or someone, and bathing in a ritual or ceremonial sense.
Rendering Sanskrit kṣut-pipāsā-nirvartaka, where bkres pa is hunger and skom pa thirst, and bzlog pa means to turn back or avert. Describes what removes or wards off hunger and thirst.

see_also: bkres pa dang skom pas gdungs pa

senses.context: Past/perfective form in the paradigm dgrol / 'grol / bkrol, corresponding to Sanskrit parimokṣaṇa, 'setting free.' Used of releasing or liberating someone or something from bondage or confinement.
The same verb in its more concrete application, of loosening or undoing what is bound or fastened.
Rendered only by the paraphrase 'engraving'; formed on bkros, the corresponding verbal form. The comparanda supply no further specification of what is engraved.
Corresponds to Sanskrit padādhiṣṭhāna, 'support for the foot,' and pratipādaka, 'support, stand.' Glossed by paraphrase as a portable stool used to help one dismount from a horse or vehicle.

Renders Sanskrit apagata-pāda-mrakṣaṇa, literally 'free from anointing/smearing of the feet,' the Tibetan matching this with 'devoid of oiling the feet.' The abstention from such an amenity is taken as an instance of frugality.

rkang pa skong tshe yi 'thob bo.gloss: the particle yi is used when filling out a verse line

senses.gloss: the particle yi is used when filling out a verse line
senses.context: A grammatical/metrical rule-phrase: rkang pa here is a line (pāda) of verse, and the statement is that the form yi is what one obtains when a syllable is needed to complete the line.

rkang pa gnyis kyi mthil.gloss: the soles of the two feet

senses.gloss: the soles of the two feet
senses.context: Rendering pāda-tala with explicit dual reference to both feet. Used in descriptions of the body, e.g. of marks or features located on the soles.

rkang pa'i mtha' la.gloss: at the end of a line (of verse)

senses.gloss: at the end of a line (of verse)
senses.context: Here rkang pa has its metrical sense of a verse-line (pāda), and mtha' la indicates the position at its end. Used in poetics and metrics for what occurs line-finally.
Standard equivalent of Sanskrit pāda-tala, the flat underside of the foot. Frequent in descriptions of bodily marks and features.

rkang pa'i 'og na gnas pa.gloss: abiding under the foot; resting on the sole of the foot

senses.gloss: abiding under the foot; resting on the sole of the foot
senses.context: Renders pāda-tala-sanniśrita, 'supported on / situated at the sole of the foot'. Used of what is located beneath the foot or rests against its sole.
The principal sense, corresponding to Sanskrit tālu, the roof of the mouth. Occurs in listings of parts of the mouth alongside lips, teeth, and mouth.
In some contexts rkan is given as the equivalent of jihvā/jihva, 'tongue'.
Also attested as the equivalent of kākuda, the hump (as of the shoulders).

see_also: rkan dang mchu dang kha dang so skams nas

senses.context: Renders Sanskrit pratyaya-jina, literally a "conqueror (jina) through/of conditions," i.e. one whose awakening is described in terms of conditions. In the Conze-based comparanda it is glossed "Single Buddha," a solitary awakened one, and the term thus designates a type of enlightened being rather than a condition itself.
Renders pratyaya-saṃdarśana: the act of pointing out or demonstrating the condition (rkyen) responsible for something. Used where a text displays or makes evident which condition is operative.
Renders pratyayābhigamābhilāṣa, the desire (abhilāṣa) to come upon or encounter (abhigama) conditions. It expresses an aspiration to meet with the conditions required for something to occur.

Renders apratyaya, the negation of rkyen (condition): that which does not serve as a condition, or is without conditions. The comparanda allow either the reading "non-condition" or "unconditioned," depending on context.

rkyen de dang de la brten nas dngos po d.gloss: in dependence on this and that condition this and that thing arise

senses.gloss: in dependence on this and that condition this and that thing arise
senses.context: A stock formula rendering taṃ taṃ pratyayaṃ pratītya te te bhāvā bhavanti, stating that particular things (dngos po) come into being in dependence on particular conditions (rkyen). It expresses dependent arising in a distributive, one-to-one fashion: each specific effect follows upon its own specific condition.

rkyen de dang de la brten nas dngos po d.sanskrit: {MSA}taṃ taṃ pratyayaṃ pratītya te te bhāvā bhavanti

senses.context: Renders Sanskrit idaṃpratyayatā, the state of being conditioned by just these (and no other) conditions. Used to express dependence on a specific set of conditions, i.e. conditionality as such.
Renders Sanskrit pratyaya-siddhi, the achieving or establishing of the conditions (rkyen) required for something. Hopkins glosses it as accomplishing, achieving, or establishing conditions.

Glossed by Hopkins as 'reason'. The illustrative Tibetan phrase given as comparandum has a camel realizing 'this is a rkyen bu' (i.e. recognizing something as a reason or pretext); the material is too slight to specify further nuances.

rkyen bu.sanskrit: rnga mo des 'di ni rkyen bu zhig go snyam du shes te

rkyen dbang gis 'jug pa.gloss: operating through the force of conditions

senses.gloss: operating through the force of conditions
senses.context: Renders Sanskrit pratyayādhīnavṛttitva, the fact of functioning or occurring in dependence on conditions. Said of what arises or works only through the force of its conditions (rkyen).
Renders Sanskrit pratyayāvaikalya, the absence of any deficiency in the requisite conditions, i.e. that the conditions are complete.

rkyen mi zad pa.gloss: non-exhaustion of conditions; conditions not being used up

senses.gloss: non-exhaustion of conditions; conditions not being used up
senses.context: Formed on rkyen (condition) with mi zad pa (not exhausted, not depleted); Hopkins gives 'non-exhaustion of conditions'. The Sanskrit comparandum links it to (tat-)pratyaya, the condition(s) in question, qualified adverbially (bhṛśa, intensely/abundantly), i.e. conditions present in unexhausted abundance.

rkyen la rag las pa.gloss: reliance on conditions; dependence upon conditions

senses.gloss: reliance on conditions; dependence upon conditions
senses.context: Renders pratyayādhīnatva, the state of being subject to or dependent on conditions (pratyaya); Hopkins glosses 'reliance on conditions'. Used of that which does not stand on its own but comes about in dependence on causal conditions.

Corresponds to pratyaya-pravṛtti, the occurring or coming forth (pravṛtti) of something from conditions (pratyaya); Hopkins: 'arisen from conditions'. Said of phenomena whose production is due to conditions rather than being independent.
Form of rkyong 'to stretch, extend', matching Sanskrit prasārita 'stretched out, extended'; Hopkins glosses simply 'extend'. Cf. the parallel forms brkyang / brkyangs.

senses.gloss: restrain, hold in (in bag brkyang and the like)
senses.context: The comparanda also record nigṛhya for this stem, as in bag brkyang = nigṛhya, i.e. holding or keeping something in check; this usage is noted only through that equivalence.

Renders aparokṣadharma: a dharma (chos) that has not become hidden or obscured (lkog tu ma gyur pa), i.e. one that is manifest rather than out of view. Contrasts with lkog tu gyur pa / lkog gyur, the hidden or obscure.

Renders Sanskrit eka-kṣaṇa-samāyukta, describing what is joined with or occurs in conjunction with one single instant. The compound combines skad cig ('moment, instant') with gcig ('one, single') and ldan pa ('possessing, associated with').

skad cig ma gcig gis mngon par rtogs pa.gloss: clear realization in a single moment

senses.gloss: clear realization in a single moment
senses.context: A single-moment mngon par rtogs pa (clear realization), i.e. realization accomplished within one instant. Formed from skad cig ma gcig ('one moment') plus the instrumental gis and mngon par rtogs pa.

see_also: skad cig gcig gi rtogs pa
skad cig gcig mngon rdzogs byang chub

senses.context: Glossed in the comparanda as 'first moment'; skad cig ma ('moment, instant') with gcig po singling out one such instant. The gloss is marked as a supplied phrase rendering rather than an attested Sanskrit equivalent.

see_also: skad cig gcig dang ldan pa

senses.context: An emphatic form of skad cig ma gcig po, with de nyid ('that very, that itself') pointing back to the single (first) instant just spoken of. Glossed in the comparanda as 'the very first moment'.

see_also: skad cig gcig dang ldan pa

senses.context: Renders Sanskrit kṣaṇikatva, the abstract quality of being momentary, formed from skad cig ma ('moment, instant') with the abstract/emphatic nyid.
In some contexts nyid functions restrictively or emphatically, so that the term characterizes something as being only momentary or purely instantaneous.

skad cig ma re re la.gloss: in each moment, moment by moment

senses.gloss: in each moment, moment by moment
senses.context: Adverbial phrase rendering Sanskrit pratikṣaṇam, indicating that something occurs in every single moment. The distributive re re la ("in each") applied to skad cig ma stresses that the action is repeated in one instant after another.
Abstract expression corresponding to Sanskrit kṣaṇika-hetutva: the fact or state of being a cause that is momentary. Used where a cause is characterized as lasting only an instant.

Abstract expression corresponding to Sanskrit kṣaṇika-phalatva: the fact or state of being an effect that is momentary. It pairs with skad cig ma'i rgyu yin pa (being a momentary cause) in discussions of instantaneous cause and effect.

Renders Sanskrit kṣaṇikaprayoga, a training or practical application characterized as momentary, i.e., accomplished in a single instant. It is naturally associated with the notion of complete enlightenment in one moment (skad cig gcig mngon rdzogs byang chub).

see_also: skad cig gcig mngon rdzogs byang chub
