skad cig gcig gi rtogs pa

skad cig re re la.gloss: in each instant, at every moment

senses.gloss: in each instant, at every moment
senses.context: Adverbial phrase for Sanskrit pratikṣaṇam, marking something as occurring in every single instant, moment, or period. Equivalent in force to skad cig ma re re la.

skad cig re re la byung ba.gloss: arising in each moment; momentary arising

senses.gloss: arising in each moment; momentary arising
senses.context: Renders Sanskrit pratikṣaṇotpāda, 'production/arising at every instant'. Used of what comes into being anew in each single moment (skad cig) rather than enduring.

skad cig la 'jig pa'i don.gloss: the meaning/fact of disintegrating in a moment

senses.gloss: the meaning/fact of disintegrating in a moment
senses.context: Corresponds to Sanskrit kṣaṇa-bhaṅgārtha, the sense (don) of momentary destruction or breaking-up (bhaṅga) within an instant (kṣaṇa). It designates the topic of momentariness — that things perish in the very moment of their arising.
An enumeration of four principal languages, glossed as Sanskrit, Prakrit, Apabhraṃśa, and Pisachi. Here skad rigs means 'type/class of language'.

skad sor bzhag tu bzhag.gloss: the language was left as it was

senses.gloss: the language was left as it was
senses.context: Said of wording that has been retained unchanged rather than emended or re-translated; skad, 'language/wording', is placed (bzhag) just as it stood (sor bzhag).

skabs khyad par can yod pa'i bstan pa.gloss: teaching in relation to which there is occasion for something more special

senses.gloss: teaching in relation to which there is occasion for something more special
senses.context: Designates a teaching that is not final in its own right, since there remains an occasion (skabs) for a further, more distinguished (khyad par can) explanation. The term is used to classify a doctrinal statement by whether anything more special can still be taught with respect to it.

skabs dang po'i spyi don.gloss: general meaning of the first chapter

senses.gloss: general meaning of the first chapter
senses.context: A commentarial rubric formed from skabs in the sense of a chapter or section of a text, here the first one, plus spyi don, 'general meaning'. It designates the general exposition of the topics of the opening chapter, as distinct from word-by-word explanation.

see_also: skabs 'dir dngos su bstan pa'i mtshan nyid ngo bo nyid med pa'i don

skabs 'dir dngos su bstan pa'i mtshan ny.gloss: meaning of the character-non-nature explicitly indicated on this occasion

senses.gloss: meaning of the character-non-nature explicitly indicated on this occasion
senses.context: A doctrinal phrase identifying, within a particular passage or context (skabs 'dir), that which is explicitly (dngos su) taught concerning the non-nature in terms of character (mtshan nyid ngo bo nyid med pa), one of the three non-natures. The phrase points to what is stated directly at that point rather than what is implied.

skabs 'dir bstan.gloss: indicated on this occasion; indicated in this context

senses.gloss: indicated on this occasion; indicated in this context
senses.context: Used of whatever a text sets forth at the point under discussion, skabs 'dir meaning 'here, in this context or occasion' and bstan meaning 'indicated, taught, shown'. It commonly qualifies a following term, marking it as the item taught in the passage at hand.

see_also: skabs 'dir dngos su bstan pa'i mtshan nyid ngo bo nyid med pa'i don

skabs 'dir bstan gyi yid mngon.gloss: mental direct perception indicated on this occasion

senses.gloss: mental direct perception indicated on this occasion
senses.context: A specification of yid mngon (mental direct perception) as it is presented in the particular text or passage under discussion — according to Hopkins, Dharmakīrti's Commentary on (Dignāga's) Compilation of Prime Cognition (tshad ma rnam 'grel, pramāṇavārttika). The qualifier skabs 'dir bstan restricts the term to the variety taught at that point, as opposed to other presentations.
Said of something that is of suitable proportion or measure for its occasion or place; skabs here carries the sense of a fitting opportunity or context.
Rendering Sanskrit mṛṣṭa in the Perfection of Wisdom materials edited by Conze ({C}). In such contexts the term describes a polished or smooth quality.

Renders Sanskrit ulkā-pāta / bhraṣṭolkā, literally the falling or dropping (ltung ba) of a shooting star (skar mda'). Used of the phenomenon of meteors descending, often listed among portents or striking natural occurrences.
In the Prajñāpāramitā vocabulary recorded by Conze the phrase is rendered collectively as 'shower of meteors', i.e. the event of meteors falling rather than a single object.
Translates tārakopama-kalpa, an aeon (bskal pa) said to be 'like the stars' (skar ma lta bu). Conze's material identifies it as the aeon associated with the Tathāgata Suvarṇapuṣpa.

skar ma'i tshogs.gloss: collection of stars; host of stars

senses.gloss: collection of stars; host of stars
senses.context: Renders tāraka-gaṇa, tāra-gaṇa, jyotir-gaṇa, tārā-nikara: a group, host, or assemblage (tshogs) of stars or heavenly luminaries (skar ma). Used of the multitude of stars taken together, often in similes contrasting them with the sun or moon.

see_also: skar ma lta bu'i bskal pa

skal mnyam gyi rgyu.gloss: cause of equal lot; cause of similar lot

senses.gloss: cause of equal lot; cause of similar lot
senses.context: Translates sabhāga-hetu, one of the causes discussed in Abhidharma; it is the cause whose effect shares the same class, lot, or share (skal) as itself. The Tibetan analyses the term as the cause (rgyu) that is of equal or matching (mnyam) portion.

skal mnyam pa.gloss: of equal lot; those of similar share

senses.gloss: of equal lot; those of similar share
senses.context: Renders sabhāga / sabhāgatā, said of what shares an equal lot, share, or fortune (skal) with something else. Used both adjectivally of persons or phenomena of the same class and abstractly for the state of being of like lot.

An object not accessible to ordinary sense perception, glossed by Hopkins as "supersensory object." Lokesh Chandra records the equivalent form bskal don, indicating that this headword is a variant spelling of that term.

The allotment or share that falls to someone, hence one's fortune or destiny. Lokesh Chandra's Sanskrit adṛṣṭa (the "unseen" factor determining what befalls one) supports this sense of an unseen allotted destiny.
Corresponding to Sanskrit bhavya as attested in the Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra, the term can denote one who is fit or worthy — i.e., one possessing the requisite fortune or capacity.

see_also: skal pa rab tu gyur pa

skal pa can.gloss: having the lot; fortunate; possessing a share

senses.gloss: having the lot; fortunate; possessing a share
senses.context: One who possesses the allotted portion or good fortune, glossed by Hopkins as "having the lot, having the share, having the fortune." Lokesh Chandra gives Sanskrit bhāgīya (Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra) and bhāgin, both formed from bhāga "share, portion."
With the further Sanskrit equivalent bhavya, the term indicates one who is fit or worthy — that is, endowed with the capacity or fortune for something.

see_also: skal pa rab tu gyur pa

senses.context: An outstanding or fortunate share, corresponding to Sanskrit subhaga ("of good fortune, blessed") in Lokesh Chandra.
Hopkins records the provisional rendering "auspicious age," reflecting the use of the phrase (also spelled bskal pa bzang po) for a fortunate eon. The comparanda give no further detail on this usage.
One whose lot or share has become supremely excellent; Hopkins gives the provisional rendering "most fortunate." The phrase is built on skal pa ("lot, share, fortune") intensified by rab tu gyur pa.

Renders Sanskrit yathā-bhavyam, expressing that something is allotted or distributed as befits the recipient's share. Hopkins glosses it in Perfection of Wisdom contexts as 'which corresponds to the merit', i.e. proportionate to what one is due or fit for.

skal ba mnyam pa.gloss: having an equal lot; equal share

senses.gloss: having an equal lot; equal share
senses.context: Corresponds to Sanskrit sabhāgatā / sahabhavyatā, the state of sharing the same portion or fortune as another. Hopkins gives 'having equal lot'.
In Perfection of Wisdom materials the term is rendered 'companionship', i.e. the condition of those who share a common lot or class.
Negative of skal ba, corresponding to Sanskrit abhavya / abhāgya. Hopkins gives 'without the lot; without the fortune', i.e. not endowed with the requisite share or good fortune.
In Perfection of Wisdom contexts the same term is rendered 'impossible; unable; unfit; uncapable', reflecting abhavya as lacking the capacity or eligibility for something.
Attested only through Hopkins' provisional English gloss 'backbone'; here skal is not the usual 'lot, share' but part of an anatomical term.
Hopkins gives the provisional gloss 'dowry', i.e. the portion or share sent along with a bride. The element skal reflects the sense of an allotted share.

sku dang gsung dang thugs sprul pa.gloss: emanations of exalted body, speech, and mind

senses.gloss: emanations of exalted body, speech, and mind
senses.context: Honorific compound rendering Sanskrit kāya-vāk-citta-nirmāṇa, the threefold set of emanations (sprul pa) manifested from a buddha's body (sku), speech (gsung), and mind (thugs). Used where the three doors of an exalted being are each said to produce manifestations.

Corresponds to Sanskrit sat-kāya, glossed in the Conze materials as the '(true) individuality' or '(true) individual body'. Here sku is the honorific term for body and dam pa renders the sense of 'true, genuine'.
A set of seven regions or parts of the body, enumerated honorifically with sku. The comparanda supply only the enumeration itself, not the identity of the seven.
Renders Sanskrit pratimā, mūrti, and śarīra in the sense of a sacred figure or representation of a holy being, made with the honorific sku for 'body'.
Answers also to pratinidhi ('substitute, representative') and pratibimba ('reflected image, counterpart'), i.e. something standing in for or resembling the body of another.
Honorific term for the shoulder, literally composed of sku ('body', hon.) and dpung ('shoulder'). Used of the shoulders of a revered person.
An honorific term for a sacred image or statue, understood as one that is poured or cast — hence a metal image. The element sku is the honorific for 'body, form, image'.
Equivalent in sense to sku blugs, a poured or cast image; the suffix ma marks the nominal form. Glossed simply as 'metal image'.
Negation of sku (honorific 'body'), rendering Sanskrit akāya. Used of what lacks or is free from a body.
Literally 'body-life-long', an honorific expression for longevity, corresponding to Sanskrit dīrgha-āyuṣkatā, 'long life'.
Literally 'body-equal', i.e. one who is the equal or match of a person's own body; used honorifically for a husband or wife.

sku yi kho lag.gloss: the round contour of the [Buddha's] body

senses.gloss: the round contour of the [Buddha's] body
senses.context: Reflecting Sanskrit maṇḍalagātratā, the term points to the well-rounded, perfectly proportioned shape of an exalted body. 'kho lag' here designates the encircling outline or curvature of the body.
Corresponding to maṇḍala-paryanta, the compound denotes the encircling edge or boundary of a rounded form; Hopkins accordingly glosses it simply as 'boundary'.

sku la dbang 'byor ba nyid.gloss: mastery with respect to the body

senses.gloss: mastery with respect to the body
senses.context: Rendering Sanskrit kāya-vibhutva (Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra), the term names the state of having attained sovereign power or command over the (exalted) body. Hopkins gives 'attainment of mastery with respect to the body'.

Title of a work, Sanskrit Kāyatrayastotra, a hymn of praise to the three exalted bodies (of a buddha). Hopkins identifies it as 'Praise of the Three Exalted Bodies', attributed to Nāgārjuna (P2015, vol. 46).

For Sanskrit kāyācintya (Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra): an exalted body that cannot be encompassed by thought or imagination. The phrase 'bsam gyis mi khyab' marks what lies beyond the reach of conceptual thought.

sku'i khyad par.gloss: distinguishing feature of an exalted body

senses.gloss: distinguishing feature of an exalted body
senses.context: Rendering Sanskrit kāya-viśeṣa (Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra), the term designates a special attribute or distinctive quality belonging to an exalted body. Hopkins gives 'attribute/feature of exalted body'.
In less honorific application the compound may simply mean a bodily or physical distinguishing characteristic, as Hopkins's third gloss 'physical attribute' indicates.

sku'i phrin las.gloss: activity of (buddha) body; exalted physical activity

senses.gloss: activity of (buddha) body; exalted physical activity
senses.context: Corresponds to Sanskrit kāya-karman, the 'action/deed of body'. In the context indicated by the comparanda it designates the enlightened activity performed through the exalted body (sku) of a buddha, one member of the triad of body, speech, and mind.

see_also: sku dang gsung dang thugs sprul pa

senses.context: Past-tense form of the verbal expression skur ('debs), glossed as deprecate, depreciate, deny. It refers to having falsely disparaged or repudiated something, i.e., denying what does in fact exist or possess a given quality.
A completed-action construction of skur pa 'debs, glossed as negate or deny. It expresses that the denial or disparagement has already been carried out.

senses.gloss: {C} having withdrawn from, gone away from
senses.context: In Conze's usage the underlying Sanskrit apodya is rendered 'go away from, withdraw from', i.e., setting something aside or removing oneself from it.
Verbal stem (also spelled bskul) corresponding to Sanskrit codana and preraka, glossed as rouse, arouse, entreat, urge on, incite, exhort. It denotes stirring or prompting someone to act.
As reflected by preraka and parikṣeptṛ in the comparanda, the term can name the agent or factor that sets something in motion.
Continuative (cing) form of skul, corresponding to Sanskrit codayati, 'urges, incites, exhorts'. It links the act of urging or rousing to a following clause.
In Conze's renderings of codayati the sense extends to admonishing or reproaching, i.e., warning someone against something or bringing a charge.
Name of a bird, glossed in English as 'magpie'. Used as an ordinary zoological term for the bird.
Tibetan rendering of the Indian place-name Pāṭaliputra, the city so called in Sanskrit sources. The Tibetan form translates the name element by element, taking -putra as 'son, offspring' (bu).
A descriptive phrase indicating something thoroughly churned or agitated with a paddle or churning-stick (skya ba). Attested only as a phrase, glossed in English as 'churned well by a paddle'.
A paired expression enumerating monastics together with lay people. The two colour terms (pale/white and yellow-ochre) stand by convention for the two groups.
The vows or restraints (sdom pa) undertaken in connection with going for refuge (skyabs 'gro). Rendered in English simply as 'refuge vows'.

Predicative expression stating that something (in the Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra context, the Buddha or the Three Jewels) is a refuge than which there is none higher. The Sanskrit śaraṇatva-ānuttarya combines 'being a refuge' with 'unsurpassedness'.
Used abstractly of the quality of being supreme among objects of refuge, i.e., the state of a refuge's being unexcelled.
Refers to the point or circumstance at which one goes for refuge. The Sanskrit śaraṇa-gamana-adhikāra indicates the topic or occasion under which going for refuge is treated.

senses.gloss: section (of a text) on going for refuge
senses.context: As adhikāra can designate a topical section, the term may also mark the portion of a treatise devoted to going for refuge.

skyabs su 'gro ba'i khyad par.gloss: distinguishing features of going for refuge

senses.gloss: distinguishing features of going for refuge
senses.context: Denotes the special qualifications or characteristics that mark the practice of going for refuge. The Sanskrit śaraṇa-pratipatti-viśeṣaṇa refers to what qualifies the undertaking (pratipatti) of refuge.

see_also: skyabs bla na med pa yin pa

senses.context: The formal ritual procedure (cho ga) by which one takes refuge. Related to the vows of refuge conferred on such an occasion.

skyabs su 'gro bar nges pa.gloss: being certain to go for refuge

senses.gloss: being certain to go for refuge
senses.context: Describes one who is definite or settled in going for refuge, as opposed to being wavering or undecided.
The Sanskrit śaraṇa-gamana-vyavasāya suggests firm resolution with respect to going for refuge, i.e., the settled decision to take refuge.

Rendering Sanskrit śaraṇa-vipravādana, this term names the condition of being thoroughly misled or deluded about what constitutes a refuge. It concerns error regarding the object of going for refuge rather than refuge itself.
A proper name corresponding to Sanskrit pāṇḍu, identified in the comparanda as Pāṇḍu, the father of the five Pāṇḍavas. Here the Tibetan functions as a name, not as a term of the refuge vocabulary.
A water bird, glossed in English as 'heron'; the Sanskrit comparandum given is amlikā. The form belongs with the related entries built on skyar.
Corresponds to Sanskrit paryaṅka, the cross-legged sitting posture. It appears as the shortened form of skyil mo krung and occurs in expressions for assuming or sitting in that posture.

Corresponds to Sanskrit paryaṅka (also cited as udrā), the cross-legged manner of sitting. The full form of skyil krung, it occurs in phrases describing assuming the posture and remaining seated in it.

see_also: skyil mo krung bcas te bzhugs so

senses.context: Instrumental/adverbial phrase built on skyil mo krung (cross-legged posture, paryaṅka), rendering eka-paryaṅkena: by means of one cross-legged session. Used of an act completed during a single uninterrupted sitting of cross-legged meditation.

skyu na gsal.gloss: it is clear in the run of the text

senses.gloss: it is clear in the run of the text
senses.context: A remark that the point at issue is evident from the flow or continuity of the passage itself, requiring no further comment. Only an English gloss is attested for this phrase; no Sanskrit equivalent is given.

Renders Sanskrit āmalakī / āmalaka (also ambla, amlaka, tiṣyaphalā, rucaka, dhātrī), glossed in English as 'olive' or 'sour medicinal fruit'. A sour fruit used in medicine, frequently named in materia medica lists.
Present/continuative form of skyug pa, corresponding to Sanskrit vamat, 'vomiting'; used also of something spurting or gushing out.
In some Prajñāpāramitā contexts the form is matched with āgacchati, 'comes (along), approaches, comes to'. This correspondence is attested only in the Conze materials.
Literally 'vomit-turning-out' (skyug + log pa), i.e. the upset or turning of the stomach that precedes vomiting. Only an English gloss is attested; no Sanskrit equivalent is given.

skyung ka.gloss: a black bird with a red beak

senses.gloss: a black bird with a red beak
senses.context: Hopkins glosses skyung ka as a black bird with a red beak, i.e. a bird-name of the jackdaw/myna type. This is the ordinary lexical sense of the term.

Lokesh Chandra registers the Sanskrit bhagavatī for this headword, an epithet meaning 'the Blessed Lady'. The comparanda give no further explanation of how the bird-name and this Sanskrit equivalent are connected, so the equation should be treated as unexplained (possibly a name-usage or a homophonous transcription).

Hopkins glosses 'sour', matching Lokesh Chandra's āmla/amla, cukra and śukta (sour, acid, fermented). The abstract amlatā indicates that the term can also render 'sourness' as a quality, one of the standard tastes.

Lokesh Chandra also records apanud ('to drive away, remove'), reflecting the verbal use of skyur ba in the sense of discarding or throwing something away. The comparanda give only this bare equivalence.

skye dgag gnas gsum.gloss: the three: production, abiding, and cessation

senses.gloss: the three: production, abiding, and cessation
senses.context: Per Hopkins, this is the standard set of three phases—being produced, abiding, and ceasing—applied in analysing phenomena. Related headwords contrast phenomena for which these three are possible with those for which they are not.

see_also: skye dgag gnas gsum mi rung ba'i chos
skye dgag gnas gsum rung ba'i chos

skye dgag gnas gsum mi rung ba'i chos.gloss: phenomenon for which production, abiding, and cessation are not possible

senses.gloss: phenomenon for which production, abiding, and cessation are not possible
senses.context: Hopkins glosses this as a phenomenon of which the three—production, abiding, and cessation—are not possible, i.e. one that does not undergo the three phases. It is the explicit counterpart of skye dgag gnas gsum rung ba'i chos.

see_also: skye dgag gnas gsum rung ba'i chos

skye dgag gnas gsum rung ba'i chos.gloss: phenomenon for which production, abiding, and cessation are suitable

senses.gloss: phenomenon for which production, abiding, and cessation are suitable
senses.context: Hopkins glosses this as a phenomenon of which the three—production, abiding, and cessation—are suitable, i.e. one to which the three phases can apply. It stands in contrast to skye dgag gnas gsum mi rung ba'i chos.

see_also: skye dgag gnas gsum mi rung ba'i chos

senses.context: Compound of skye dgu (beings, creatures) and don (aim, benefit), used adverbially or as a purpose-phrase, 'for the sake/benefit of [all] beings.'

Hopkins also records a provisional gloss 'Prajapati [n. of the fourth constellation]' for this form; this sense properly belongs to skye dgu'i bdag po ('lord of creatures') and should be used with caution here.

see_also: skye dgu'i bdag po dang bcas pa'i lha rnams

senses.context: Literally 'master/lord (bdag po) of beings (skye dgu)', rendering Sanskrit prajāpati, the divine lord of created beings.

senses.gloss: Prajāpati, name of the fourth lunar mansion (rohiṇī)
senses.context: Lokesh Chandra also equates the term with rohiṇī-nakṣatra, i.e. the constellation Prajāpati, counted as the fourth constellation in Hopkins.

see_also: skye dgu'i bdag po dang bcas pa'i lha rnams

senses.context: Renders saprajāpatikā devā, a phrase for an assembly of gods accompanied by (or gathered around) Prajāpati, the lord of creatures.
Renders ṣaḍāyatana, the set of six āyatanas or sense-bases/sources; also rendered 'six sense-spheres.'
Renders āyatana-kauśalya, expertise or proficiency with regard to the āyatanas (sense-spheres, sources).
Renders Sanskrit puruṣottama, literally the highest (mchog) among persons or born beings (skye). Used as an epithet of an exalted human or creature who stands foremost among living beings.

A phrasal rendering in which skye is taken as generation/production and thebs as a section or portion thereof. The comparanda give only this English phrase, without a Sanskrit equivalent or further specification of context.
The dual form of skye thebs, i.e., a pair of sections of generation. Only the English phrase is attested in the comparanda; the identity of the two sections is not specified.
Corresponds to Sanskrit janana-maraṇa, the coupled terms skye (birth, being born) and 'chi (dying). Names the pair of events bounding a lifetime.

skye po bdag 'dzin can.gloss: one who holds a self of the person; Proponent of Permanent Existence

senses.gloss: one who holds a self of the person; Proponent of Permanent Existence
senses.context: Formed from skye po (person) and bdag 'dzin can (having/holding self-apprehension), designating one who asserts a self with respect to the person. The comparanda render it as a doxographical label, 'Proponent of Permanent Existence.'
Refers to a series of births strung together like a garland ('phreng), i.e., the succession of lives or incarnations of a being. Used for accounts tracing a person's successive rebirths.
Renders Sanskrit śukla-janman, literally a 'white' (dkar po) birth, understood as a virtuous or wholesome rebirth.
Renders upapatti-viśeṣaṃ prāpya: having attained a distinguished or superior rebirth. The phrase is a gerund clause introducing what follows upon such an attainment.
Designates a ninefold classification of birth or birth-realms.
By extension the term is used for living beings in general, i.e., all those born in the ninefold birth realms; compare skye dgu, 'creatures, people'.

Renders utpatti-niḥsvabhāvatā, one of the ways in which phenomena are said to lack an own-nature, namely with respect to [self-]production or arising. The Tibetan uses the honorific negative ma mchis pa for 'lacking, non-existent'.

skye ba dang mthun pa.gloss: concordant with birth; conducive to production

senses.gloss: concordant with birth; conducive to production
senses.context: Renders Sanskrit utpatti-anukūla, i.e. that which accords with or is favorable to arising/birth. Used of factors that are in harmony with, and hence conducive to, the production of something.

Corresponds to Sanskrit cayāpārthya as attested in the Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra: a production or birth that serves no purpose. The compound joins skye ba (birth, production) with don med pa (without aim, meaningless).

Renders Sanskrit caturdaśa-vidha utpāda, a set enumeration of fourteen modes of birth or production cited in the Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra. The term designates the group as a whole (the particle po marking the enumerated set).
Renders Sanskrit jantu, glossed in Conze's materials as including scorpions and the like, hence sometimes translated 'vermin'; more generally any born creature.

senses.gloss: the born one (as an imputed self)
senses.context: Appears among the terms for a falsely imputed personal identity, in the series self, sentient being, life-force, person (ātma-sattva-jīva-pudgala-dṛṣṭi), where 'the one who is born' is one of the designations grasped as a real self.
A type of sprul sku (nirmāṇakāya) specified by skye ba, birth: an emanation body manifested by way of taking birth, i.e. an incarnation.

skye ba 'phongs shing.gloss: having passed beyond (the present) birth; after death

senses.gloss: having passed beyond (the present) birth; after death
senses.context: Renders jāti-vyativṛtta, glossed as having gone to another birth (janma-antara-gata) through relinquishing one's own present nature (sva-prakṛti-parityāga). Used of what happens once beings have passed through this present life, i.e., after they have died.
For anutpāda-vijñāpanatā: the state of informing about or communicating non-production (anutpāda).
For anupapadyamāna: not undergoing (further) birth, without ever being reborn.
Corresponds to anupapatti, the absence of (re)birth or coming into existence.
A paired expression (Skt. anupāda-upāda) contrasting the absence of arising with arising.
Renders anutpādādi, i.e., non-production (or birthlessness) together with the further items of a series beginning with it.
Rendered by Sanskrit jñānājāti (Mahāvyutpatti), i.e. the knowing/cognition that there is no [more] birth. Used of the realization that rebirth has ceased or that phenomena are unproduced.

skye ba med pa'i chos la bzod pa.gloss: forbearance with respect to the doctrine of non-production

senses.gloss: forbearance with respect to the doctrine of non-production
senses.context: Glossed as forbearance, patience, tolerance, or endurance regarding the teaching that phenomena are not produced. The term names a capacity to accept and abide in the doctrine of non-production (skye ba med pa) without recoiling from it.

Corresponds to Sanskrit hīnopapattiḥ śritā (Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra), 'relying on / based upon an inferior rebirth.' Describes a state or quality that rests upon a low or inferior birth (skye ba dman pa).
Corresponds to Sanskrit janma-kṣaya (Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra), the wearing away or exhaustion of birth. Indicates that (re)birth has been used up or brought to an end.
Corresponds to Sanskrit śubha-janman and śobhana ... janman (Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra). Denotes a birth that is fine, excellent, or auspicious, in contrast to a low or inferior birth.

A negation-pair phrase (Skt. notpādo na nirodhaḥ) denying both arising and ceasing of a phenomenon. Rendered variously as "no production and also no cessation," "neither production nor cessation," or "both no production and no cessation."

skye ba la nges par 'gyur ba.gloss: definite to be born; certain of rebirth

senses.gloss: definite to be born; certain of rebirth
senses.context: Corresponds to Skt. upapatti-niyatipāta, indicating that birth or rebirth is fixed/certain for the being in question.
Glossed by Skt. cayāpārthya, characterizing production (arising) as lacking purpose or aim.
Corresponds to Skt. janma-saṃkleśa (also utpatti-/utpāda-saṃkleśa), the class of thorough afflictions associated with birth or arising.

skye ba'i skad cig ma dang po phyin chad.gloss: from the first moment of birth onward

senses.gloss: from the first moment of birth onward
senses.context: Corresponds to Skt. (prathama-)janma-kṣaṇād ūrdhvam, marking the period beginning with the initial moment of birth and continuing thereafter.

skye ba'i sgo.gloss: door of production; source of arising

senses.gloss: door of production; source of arising
senses.context: Renders Sanskrit āya-dvāra, literally the "door" or gateway through which something comes to be. Used for that which serves as the avenue or means of production of a thing.
With skye ba in the sense of birth or rebirth, the compound denotes the gateway through which birth takes place.

Formed on skye ba'i sgo (door of production/birth) with bcom pa, "to destroy, demolish." Glossed as destroying the possibility (of something's arising), i.e. blocking off the avenue by which it could be produced.

skye ba'i chos can.gloss: subject to production; having the quality of arising

senses.gloss: subject to production; having the quality of arising
senses.context: Renders Sanskrit utpāda-dharmin, said of what has production as its nature or attribute, i.e. what is liable to arise.
Renders Sanskrit janma-nirmāṇakāya, a type of emanation body (sprul sku) specified by janma, birth. Hopkins gives "construction emanation body."

skye ba'i phreng ba.gloss: garland of lives; sequence of rebirths

senses.gloss: garland of lives; sequence of rebirths
senses.context: Literally a "garland" or string (phreng ba) of births, hence a series of successive lives or incarnations.

skye ba'i lus bor te sprul pa'i lus 'dzi.gloss: abandoning the body of birth and assuming an emanation body

senses.gloss: abandoning the body of birth and assuming an emanation body
senses.context: Renders Sanskrit janma-kāyaṃ tyaktvā nirmāṇa-kāyaṃ gṛhṇāti: to give up the body produced by (ordinary) birth and take on a body of magical emanation. Used of the transition from an ordinary birth-body to a nirmāṇakāya.
Corresponds to Sanskrit durjana, duṣṭajana, khala, asatyajana: a person of bad character. The term designates the individual (skye bo) qualified as ngan pa, 'bad, evil, base'.
Renders kujana-vāsa, 'dwelling/keeping company with bad people'. It denotes the act of consorting with or befriending evil beings, typically cited as a fault or unfavorable circumstance.
Corresponds to kliṣṭajanānukampā: sympathy or mercy (rjes su brtse ba) directed toward beings who are beset by the afflictions (nyon mongs pa, kleśa).

Renders duṣṭa-jana-vāsa, 'dwelling with malicious people'. Here skye bo sdang ba are beings characterized by hatred or malice, and 'grogs pa is keeping their company — again presented as an unfavorable association.

skye bo phal cher.gloss: most beings, the majority of people

senses.gloss: most beings, the majority of people
senses.context: A compound of skye bo (person, being) with phal cher (most, the majority), rendering Sanskrit jana in the sense of people or a crowd of people. Attested in Prajñāpāramitā-related (C) vocabulary, where it denotes beings at large rather than a specified group.
Renders Sanskrit mūrkha-jana (Madhyāntavibhāga), a person characterized by mūrkha, stupidity or folly. The term qualifies skye bo, an individual being or person, by the fault of dullness.

skye bo mang po dga' ba.gloss: liking many beings; dear to many people

senses.gloss: liking many beings; dear to many people
senses.context: Corresponds to Sanskrit bahu-jana-supriya (Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra), literally 'very dear to/of many people'. The Tibetan phrasing skye bo mang po dga' ba is glossed 'liking many beings', i.e. affection involving a large number of persons.
Renders Sanskrit vimūḍha ... jana (Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra), a person who is deluded or bewildered. Here rmongs pa qualifies skye bo with the fault of confusion or obscuration.

skye bo mdza' ba la byams pa.gloss: loving friendly beings; affection for dear ones

senses.gloss: loving friendly beings; affection for dear ones
senses.context: Corresponds to Sanskrit priya-jana-preman (Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra), love (preman) directed toward dear or friendly persons (priya-jana). The Tibetan renders this as byams pa, loving kindness or affection, toward skye bo mdza' ba, beings who are friends or dear ones.

skyed mos tshal gyi sa.gloss: grounds of a pleasure grove; site of a park

senses.gloss: grounds of a pleasure grove; site of a park
senses.context: Corresponds to Sanskrit udyāna-bhūmi, the ground or locality occupied by a pleasure garden. Formed from skyed mos tshal (pleasure grove, park) plus sa (ground, place), thus designating the place where such a grove is located.
Rendered by Sanskrit udyāna (pleasure garden, park), upavana (grove adjoining a settlement), and nikuñja (thicket, arbor). Used for a cultivated or planted pleasure ground.
Corresponds to Sanskrit java (speed) and vikramin (striding vigorously, swift), describing something that moves or acts rapidly.
As an adverbial rendering of śīghram, āśu, and kṣipram, translated 'soon,' 'quickly,' 'speedily,' and in imperative contexts 'hurry up with.'

Glossed by Hopkins as 'reason'; the attested illustrative phrase rnga mo des 'di ni rkyen bu zhig go snyam du shes te shows the camel recognizing that 'this is some reason (for it).' Evidently equivalent to, and interchangeable in spelling with, rkyen bu.

skyen bu.sanskrit: rnga mo des 'di ni rkyen bu zhig go snyam du shes te

skyem tsam re.gloss: just briefly, for a short while

senses.gloss: just briefly, for a short while
senses.context: Glossed only as 'just briefly'; the expression indicates a brief span or small measure, with tsam re conveying 'merely as much as.' The available comparanda give no further specification of the underlying image or of any Sanskrit equivalent.

skyes 'phreng.gloss: garland of lives, series of births

senses.gloss: garland of lives, series of births
senses.context: Compound of skyes (birth, life) and 'phreng (garland, string), used for a strung-together sequence of one life after another. Rendered as 'garland of lives' or 'sequence of lives'.
By extension, the succession of embodiments taken by one continuum, i.e. successive incarnations considered as a connected series.
Corresponds to Sanskrit puruṣapudgala, a compound doubling two words for a person (skyes bu = puruṣa, gang zag = pudgala). Glossed simply as 'person'.

A person classed among beings of lesser or lower capacity (skyes bu chung ngu) but marked out as distinguished or special (khyad par can) within that class. The term presupposes a scheme grading persons by scope of capacity.

skyes bu chung ngu khyad par can gyi lam.gloss: path of a special being of small capacity

senses.gloss: path of a special being of small capacity
senses.context: The path (lam) belonging to a special being of small capacity, i.e. the practice appropriate to that distinguished member of the class of lesser-capacity persons. Formed by adding gyi lam to skyes bu chung ngu khyad par can.

skyes bu chung ngu dang thun mong pa'i l.gloss: path in common with those of lesser capacity

senses.gloss: path in common with those of lesser capacity
senses.context: A path (lam) that is shared in common (thun mong pa) with persons of small or lesser capacity (skyes bu chung ngu), rather than being exclusive to those of greater capacity.

A designation within the graded classification of practitioners (beings of small, middling, and great capacity) for a distinguished or particular subtype of the being of small capacity, marked by 'khyad par can' (special, distinguished). The comparanda give only the phrase itself, without further specification of what makes such a being 'special'.

skyes bu chung 'bring thun mong gi lam.gloss: path in common with beings of small and middling capacity

senses.gloss: path in common with beings of small and middling capacity
senses.context: Refers to a portion of the path that is shared with, or held in common by, practitioners classed as beings of small capacity and beings of middling capacity. The term presupposes the threefold division of beings into small, middling, and great capacity.

skyes bu che 'bring thun mong gi lam.gloss: path in common with beings of great and middling capacity

senses.gloss: path in common with beings of great and middling capacity
senses.context: Refers to a portion of the path that is shared with, or held in common by, practitioners classed as beings of middling capacity and beings of great capacity. As with the parallel term for small and middling beings, it presupposes the threefold classification of practitioners by capacity.
Translates Sanskrit mohapuruṣa: a person characterized by delusion or bewilderment (gti mug). Glossed also as beclouded, ignorant, confused, or befuddled.

Corresponds to Sanskrit satpuruṣa-saṃsevā, satpuruṣāśraya/satpuruṣāpāśraya: attending upon, associating with, or taking as one's support a true, holy, or excellent person (skyes bu dam pa). Rendered variously as relying on or acquainting oneself with a holy, excellent, or true being.

see_also: skyes mchog ka lo sgyur ba

skyes bu dam pa'i las byed pa.gloss: performing the actions of a holy being

senses.gloss: performing the actions of a holy being
senses.context: Renders Sanskrit satpuruṣa-karma-karaṇatā (Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra): the state of doing the deeds proper to a true, holy, or excellent person (skyes bu dam pa). The term names the activity or conduct itself rather than the person.

skyes bu byed pa'i 'bras bu.gloss: personally made effect; fruit of human agency

senses.gloss: personally made effect; fruit of human agency
senses.context: Equivalent to Sanskrit puruṣa-kāra-phala, an effect (phala, 'bras bu) produced by a person's own action or effort (puruṣa-kāra, skyes bu byed pa) rather than arising otherwise. Attested in Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra and Madhyāntavibhāga contexts.
Sanskrit avidagdha, an unrefined or dull person; skyes bu 'person, being' qualified by blun po 'stupid, foolish'.
In Conze's Prajñāpāramitā vocabulary the term corresponds to mohapuruṣa, a person under the sway of delusion or bewilderment (moha).

skyes bu 'bring gi lam.gloss: path of a being of middling capacity

senses.gloss: path of a being of middling capacity
senses.context: Sanskrit madhyapuruṣamārga: the path (lam, mārga) assigned to a person of middling ('bring, madhya) faculties, as distinguished from paths for lesser and superior persons.
A person (skyes bu) characterized by rmongs pa, bewilderment or confusion. Only an English gloss is attested for this compound in the comparanda.

skyes bu tshad ma.gloss: valid person, being who is a valid authority

senses.gloss: valid person, being who is a valid authority
senses.context: Renders Sanskrit pramāṇabhūta, literally one who has become (bhūta) a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa). Applied to a person (skyes bu) who is authoritative or trustworthy, i.e., a valid being whose word or knowledge can be relied upon.

skyes bu gsum ka.gloss: all three types of beings, beings of the three capacities

senses.gloss: all three types of beings, beings of the three capacities
senses.context: Hopkins glosses this as a paraphrase, 'beings of the three capacities'; gsum ka signals 'all three' together. Used for the threefold classification of persons (skyes bu) by scope or capacity, taken collectively.

skyes bu'i rgyud kyis bsdus pa'i rdul du.gloss: atomically established phenomenon included within a being's continuum

senses.gloss: atomically established phenomenon included within a being's continuum
senses.context: Hopkins: 'that which is atomically established and is included within the continuum of a being.' Designates matter established as (composed of) atoms that belongs to the mental-physical continuum (rgyud) of a person, i.e., inner or bodily matter, as opposed to that not so included.

skyes bu'i rgyud kyis ma bsdus pa'i rdul.gloss: atomically established phenomenon not included within a being's continuum

senses.gloss: atomically established phenomenon not included within a being's continuum
senses.context: Hopkins: 'that which is atomically established and is not included within the continuum of a being.' The complementary category to atomically established phenomena belonging to a person's continuum, i.e., outer matter not part of any being's continuum.

Renders Sanskrit puruṣakāra (also cited as puruṣakāru), the capacity or power (mthu) of a person (skyes bu). Conze's glosses give '(manly) doing' and 'work', i.e., human exertion or activity as an effective force.

skyes bu'i 'dod pa tsam gyis bzhag pa'i.gloss: relation established by mere convention/intention of the speaker

senses.gloss: relation established by mere convention/intention of the speaker
senses.context: Designates a connection that holds only because a person wishes or intends to posit it, rather than one grounded in the nature of the things related. Hopkins glosses it as 'a relation established by the mere intention of the speaker', i.e. a merely stipulated or conventional linkage.
The ongoing stream of consciousness (shes rgyud) belonging to a person or being (skyes bu). Used to identify what is one's own mind-stream, as distinct from what is external to it.

skyes bu'i shes rgyud kyis bsdus pa'i gz.gloss: form included within the mental continuum of a being

senses.gloss: form included within the mental continuum of a being
senses.context: A form (gzugs) that is contained within a being's own mind-stream — i.e. counted as part of the person's continuum rather than as external matter. It is the positive member of the pair contrasted with form not so included.

skyes bu'i shes rgyud kyis ma bsdus pa'i.gloss: form not included within the mental continuum of a being

senses.gloss: form not included within the mental continuum of a being
senses.context: A form (gzugs) that is not contained within any being's mind-stream, i.e. external material form. It is the negative counterpart of 'form included within the mental continuum of a being'.

skyes bu'i shes rgyud bsdus pa.gloss: included within the mental continuum of a being

senses.gloss: included within the mental continuum of a being
senses.context: Predicated of what is contained or subsumed within a person's mind-stream. Frequently used as a qualifier, as in the case of forms that are or are not so included.

skyes bu'i shes rgyud ma bsdus pa.gloss: not included in the mental continuum of a person

senses.gloss: not included in the mental continuum of a person
senses.context: Said of something that is not comprised within (ma bsdus pa) the continuum of consciousness (shes rgyud) of a person or being (skyes bu). Used to exclude a phenomenon from what belongs to an individual's own stream of awareness.
A result (’bras bu) that is brought about through the agency of a person (skyes bu), i.e., one personally made or produced by an individual agent rather than arising otherwise.

skyes zin pa yang skye ba ni ma yin.gloss: what has already been produced is not produced again

senses.gloss: what has already been produced is not produced again
senses.context: A formulaic statement (Skt. utpannaṃ punar na utpadyate) denying that something already born or arisen (skyes zin pa) undergoes production a second time. Cited in analyses of production (skye ba) where repeated arising of what has arisen is rejected.

skyes zin pa yang skye ba ni ma yin.sanskrit: skye/ skye/ skyes/ skyes/; {MSA}utpannaṃ punar utpadyate (na-)

senses.context: Rendered tentatively as “quarrel” in the available comparanda; no Sanskrit equivalent is attested here, so the gloss should be treated as provisional. The first element belongs to the skyo family (sadness, weariness, distress).

skyo bcas sems can smin par byed.gloss: ripening sentient beings who are afflicted with distress

senses.gloss: ripening sentient beings who are afflicted with distress
senses.context: Skt. sodvegā sattva-pācanā: the maturing (smin par byed) of sentient beings who are accompanied by (bcas) weariness, sadness, or distress (skyo ba). Rendered by Hopkins as “ripening poor sentient beings.”

An expanded form of the name of the bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, incorporating kun tu ('all-around, thoroughly'), spyan ras gzigs ('who looks with the eye'), and dbang po ('lord, powerful one'). Attested as an equivalent of Sanskrit avalokiteśvara.

Renders Sanskrit asamudācāra, the negation of samudācāra ('manifest activity, habitual operation'). Glossed as 'habitual absence' — i.e., the state in which a given activity or factor does not operate or come into play.
Corresponds to Sanskrit samudācarati, the verb of manifest or habitual activity. Glossed as 'issue forth,' and, in context-sensitive renderings, 'befall,' 'use,' 'commit to,' 'nurse,' 'credits with.'
Verbal sense corresponding to Sanskrit saṃyunakti, 'to join together, connect.' Extended in usage to applying or affixing one thing to another, and to practising.

As an equivalent of Sanskrit saṃyojana, the nominal sense of that which binds or thoroughly enwraps; glossed 'entanglement,' 'thorough enwrapment.' In some attested renderings also 'deprivation, loss.'

Causative construction ('to make thoroughly joined') corresponding to Sanskrit saṃyojayati. Shares the semantic range of kun tu sbyar: uniting, applying, affixing, and, nominally, binding or entanglement.

Renders Sanskrit visaṃyojayati, causative in force: to cause something to be un-joined or not connected. Hopkins glosses the term as 'disunite'; the Tibetan is literally 'to cause not to be joined/connected in all respects'.
Renders Sanskrit saṃmohabīja, the latent 'seed' (sa bon) of complete bewilderment or obscuration (saṃmoha). Hopkins gives 'seeds of obscuration', i.e. the potentialities from which delusion arises.
Standard equivalent of Sanskrit saṃmoha (also sammohana, sambhrama), attested in Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra and Prajñāpāramitā literature. Hopkins renders it 'thorough obscuration; ignorance; delusion'.
Also corresponds to the participial saṃmūḍha (sammūḍha), describing a person or mind that is completely bewildered or deluded.

Renders Sanskrit paryeṣamāṇa ('searching'), the sense being an exhaustive seeking or looking for. Hopkins extends the range to 'thoroughly seek/search/examine/analyze/investigate', so the term can also cover investigative searching.
Renders Sanskrit saṃharṣa-jāta, 'in whom delight (saṃharṣa) has arisen'. Hopkins gives 'generate thorough satisfaction' and, for the Conze materials, 'thrilled'.

Renders Sanskrit paryeṣaṇa in the sense of searching out or investigating something completely. Hopkins gives 'thorough investigation/examination/search' and, in the Conze-attested usage, 'search for'.
Corresponds to saṃparigraha, āgraha, ādhi: taking hold of or appropriating something completely. Also attested for sandhara/sandhā in the sense of holding or upholding.
In an affective sense, the tight holding onto possessions; Hopkins glosses 'miserliness' alongside 'thoroughly holding onto'.
Renders parigraha-hetu: that which causes one to take hold of or appropriate something. Formed from kun 'dzin pa ('thoroughly holding onto') plus rgyu ('cause').
Where kun 'dzin pa is taken in its affective sense of miserly grasping, the compound denotes the cause of such miserliness.

A rtog pa (conception, conceptual consciousness) qualified as kun rdzob, i.e. conventional. Hopkins also allows the reading 'conceptual consciousness of a conventionality', where kun rdzob is the object rather than the character of the conception.

Renders saṃvṛti-satyatva, the abstract form (-tva, Tibetan nyid) of kun rdzob kyi bden pa, 'conventional truth'. Hopkins reflects the etymology of saṃvṛti as concealing with the alternative rendering 'concealer-truth itself'.

dka' ba byed pa yin pa.gloss: doer of what is hard; one who performs difficult deeds

senses.gloss: doer of what is hard; one who performs difficult deeds
senses.context: Renders Sanskrit duṣkara-kāraka, describing a person who does what is hard to do. Formed from dka' ba (what is difficult) plus byed pa yin pa (is a doer of), it characterizes someone by the difficulty of the deeds undertaken.

Corresponds to Sanskrit dīrgha-kālika-duṣkarākheda: absence of fatigue or discouragement (mi skyo ba) in the face of difficult practice (dka' ba) sustained over a long period (yun ring po). Used of one who remains undaunted by prolonged austerity or arduous endeavor.
Given by Lokesh Chandra as an equivalent of Sanskrit umā, the name of the goddess. Attested as a Tibetan naming-rendering rather than a literal translation.

Hopkins glosses the term as 'ascetic,' i.e., one engaged in hard practice. The two comparanda are compatible in that Umā is renowned for austerity, but only the equivalences themselves are certain here.
Hopkins glosses this compound as one who has faith in (dad) Durgā, expressed by dka' zlog. Attested only as this identification; no Sanskrit equivalent is supplied.
Literally 'difficult place' (dka' = difficult, sa = place, point), used for a hard or problematic point in a text or topic of study.
Continuative (absolutive) phrase corresponding to Sanskrit baddhvā, 'having bound.' The disjunctive sam links two near-synonymous verbal forms, giving 'having wound up or bound (it).'

dkrug par bya.gloss: should be disturbed; should deflect from

senses.gloss: should be disturbed; should deflect from
senses.context: Future/gerundive form rendering Sanskrit vikopayitavya, expressing what is to be stirred up, upset, or turned aside. Hopkins glosses the Perfection-of-Wisdom usage as 'should deflect from.'
Past-stem continuative of dkrug pa, corresponding to Sanskrit samākulīkṛta 'thrown into confusion, troubled' and samāhata. Used for having troubled, agitated, or stirred up something or someone.
Given by Hopkins with the sense of turning or facing something upwards. No Sanskrit equivalent is supplied in the comparanda.
Phrase combining bkan ('turn/face upwards') with bzhag ('place, set down'), i.e., to set something down so that it faces upwards. No Sanskrit equivalent is supplied in the comparanda.

A title/degree given in the Tibetan scholastic system, formed on bka' (authoritative word, scripture) with rab 'byams (vast, unlimited), i.e. one learned in the full breadth of the scriptural word. Rendered by Hopkins simply by transliteration, 'Rap-jam-pa [degree]'.

Corresponds to Sanskrit ājñā (command) and śāsturājñayā (by the command of the Teacher), also śiṣṭi (instruction, correction) and śāpa (curse, imprecation). Used of an authoritative pronouncement that must be obeyed.

Answers to adhikāra (authority, charge), adhikṛta (one placed in charge) and adhyakṣa (overseer, superintendent), and to kārya (matter of office, business to be done). Hopkins accordingly glosses simply 'power'.

As bka' (authoritative word) combined with lung (scriptural statement), the term can indicate an authoritative verbal pronouncement or account; Lokesh Chandra also records ākhyāyikā (narrative, tale).

bkar ba.gloss: to set apart, single out, separate

senses.gloss: to set apart, single out, separate
senses.context: Hopkins gives 'select; put aside; separate' — the action of marking something off from a larger group and treating it on its own.

senses.gloss: to specify, restrict to, tie down to
senses.context: By extension of the sense of setting apart, the term is used for narrowing something down to a particular case, Hopkins: 'tie down to; specify'.
Lokesh Chandra equates the term with uccāṭana, driving out or eradicating; in this sense it approaches bskrad pa and skrod pa.

Past-tense verbal form built on bkas (instrumental of bka', authoritative word/command) with bcad pa (cut off, decided): something settled or established by authoritative decree. Hopkins glosses simply 'decreed'.

bkur rnyed.gloss: honor and gain; respect and acquisitions

senses.gloss: honor and gain; respect and acquisitions
senses.context: Rendering Sanskrit satkāra-lābha, the pair of veneration (satkāra, bkur sti) and material acquisition or profit (lābha, rnyed pa). Hopkins glosses the compound as 'wealth and respect', i.e. the honor and material gain that may accrue to a person.

bkur stir bgyis par 'gyur.gloss: will treat with respect, will honor

senses.gloss: will treat with respect, will honor
senses.context: A verbal phrase (with the honorific/elegant auxiliary bgyid) rendering Sanskrit satkaroti, 'treats with respect, reveres, honors'. The form marks a future or resultant occurrence: one will come to pay honor and show reverence.

bkur stir bya ba.gloss: to honor, to attend upon with respect

senses.gloss: to honor, to attend upon with respect
senses.context: Nominalized verbal phrase corresponding to Sanskrit paryupāsanā, glossed 'to honor'. It expresses the act of rendering honor and respectful attendance as something to be done.
Present-tense verbal phrase for Sanskrit satkaroti, 'treat with respect, honor, revere'. It denotes actively showing respect and veneration toward someone.

Nominal form corresponding to Sanskrit gaurava/garava and satkāra, glossed 'respect, dignity'. It names both the attitude of reverence and the honor or service rendered to a worthy person; also associated with sarvajananamratā, deference toward all people.

senses.gloss: a title or status deserving respect
senses.context: In an extended usage the term denotes the dignity or honorific standing that entitles someone to be respected.

bkod ma'i chu.gloss: spring water, water of a fountain

senses.gloss: spring water, water of a fountain
senses.context: Rendering Sanskrit prasravaṇodaka, water issuing from a spring or fountain. The term names naturally flowing water as it wells up.

see_also: bkod ma'i chu lta bu'i sems bskyed

senses.context: Negated form of bkra shis, corresponding to Sanskrit amaṅgala; said of things or acts that bring or portend ill fortune. In the cited usage some people say that keeping a garbled or damaged text is inauspicious (bkra mi shis pa yong).
Used substantivally for the misfortune or ill omen itself, as opposed to auspiciousness.

bkra mi shis pa.sanskrit: chos sems can 'ga' zhig gis dpe 'khrug pa nyar na bkra mi shis pa yong zer; {LC}amaṅgala

senses.context: Proper name, the fuller form of bkra shis 'khyil, literally something like 'auspiciousness swirling/gathered from all sides.' Attested only as a name in the comparanda.
Name of a monastic university in the province of A-mdo (a mdo). A shortened form of bkra shis kun nas 'khyil ba.
A standard set of eight emblems regarded as signs of good fortune; also rendered 'eight good luck symbols.' Formed from bkra shis (auspicious) plus rtags brgyad (eight signs).
Abstract/nominalized form of bkra shis, corresponding to Sanskrit maṅgalatva, i.e., the state or fact of being auspicious. Its opposite is bkra mi shis pa (inauspicious).
Standard term for one who steals, rendering Sanskrit taskara, muṣaka, and dasyu (bandit, brigand). Frequently paired with related forms such as rkun ma (theft, thief) and rkun rdzas (stolen goods).

Some equivalents cited (cara, and the phrase caro dhvaja-baddhakaḥ) belong to the vocabulary of covert agents rather than simple thievery, suggesting the term can extend to one who moves secretly or acts by stealth. This extension is attested only in the lexical comparanda and should be applied with caution.
Corresponds to Sanskrit pāyu, guda, apāna, and buli, the lower orifice of the body. In this sense it aligns with terms for the excretory passage such as gzhang and bshang lam.
By extension the hindquarters or the part of the body one sits on, matching Sanskrit āsana (seat). This underlies compounds such as rkub kyag (chair).
A seat for sitting on, formed from rkub (rear end, seat) plus kyag. Glossed simply as 'chair'.

rkyen gyi dbang gis 'jug pa.gloss: operating through the force of conditions

senses.gloss: operating through the force of conditions
senses.context: Renders Sanskrit pratyayādhīnavṛttitva, the state of functioning in dependence upon conditions (rkyen). Used of phenomena whose occurrence or activity is not autonomous but comes about by the power of conditioning factors.

A type of lineage (rigs) characterized as developing or being transformed through conditions (rkyen). The comparanda give only the English rendering 'developmental lineage', with the Tibetan indicating that its unfolding depends on conditions.
Adverbial phrase (locative) corresponding to Sanskrit carame kṣaṇe, 'in the last moment'. Used of what occurs at the final instant or final period of a series or process.

skad cig ma dang po dang khyad par med p.gloss: not different from the first moment

senses.gloss: not different from the first moment
senses.context: Renders ādi-kṣaṇa-nirviśiṣṭatva, the state of being indistinguishable from the initial instant. Predicated of something later in a sequence that is held to be in no way distinct from its first moment/instant/period.
Negation of skad cig ma, corresponding to Sanskrit akṣaṇika: that which is not momentary, i.e. not arising and perishing instant by instant.

skad cig ma ma yin pa las skad cig ma 'b.gloss: it is not suitable for the momentary to arise from the non-momentary

senses.gloss: it is not suitable for the momentary to arise from the non-momentary
senses.context: A full sentence rendering na tv akṣaṇikāt kṣaṇikaṃ bhavitum arhati, a reasoning statement denying that something momentary can be produced from something non-momentary.

Corresponds to Sanskrit kṣaṇikatva, the quality of being momentary; hence also rendered adjectivally as 'momentary, instantaneous'. To be distinguished by context from a reading as the negation of skad cig ma.

Honorific compound of sku (body, person) and skye (birth), used for the reincarnated person of a lama or master. The cited usage — khyed rje'i 'gos kyi sku skye yin pas — identifies someone as the incarnation of a particular teacher.

sku skye.sanskrit: khyed rje'i 'gos kyi sku skye yin pas ...

senses.context: Honorific term formed from sku (body, person) and chas (articles, gear), used for the belongings or effects of a venerable person. Hopkins glosses it simply as things or possessions in honorific register.
Abbreviated form describing a body that is broad/large (che) and straight (drang). It corresponds to the fuller phrase sku che zhing drang ba.

sku che zhing drang ba.gloss: having a broad and straight bodily frame

senses.gloss: having a broad and straight bodily frame
senses.context: Renders Sanskrit bṛhad-ṛju-gātratā, the quality of a body (gātra) that is large or broad and upright/straight. Hopkins glosses: his bodily frame is broad and straight.

Honorific term corresponding to Sanskrit gātratā, the state or quality of having a body; Hopkins glosses it as body or limbs. It appears in descriptions of bodily attributes, as in sku che zhing drang ba (bṛhad-ṛju-gātratā).

Continuative (cing) form of skul ba, 'to exhort, urge on, incite'. Lokesh Chandra gives Sanskrit codye, corresponding to Hopkins' passive rendering 'I am exhorted', so in context the phrase may render a form of the verb 'to exhort/urge' where the agent stirs another to action.

Name of a female deity, given by Lokesh Chandra as cundā/cundī and, in the Guhyasamāja context, reconstructed as *cundavajrī (Hopkins: Cundavajrī). Literally the term means 'she who exhorts/incites', from skul ba 'to urge on' plus the feminine ma.
A swelling or goitrous growth on the neck, from ske 'neck' and lba ba 'goiter, wen, tumor'. Attested only through Hopkins' gloss 'neck goiter', apparently in medical or illustrative contexts.
Continuative (shing) form of skem pa, 'to dry, dry up, parch', corresponding to Sanskrit tapeti (Hopkins: 'dry up'). Used where one action of drying or scorching accompanies another.

Continuative (cing) form of skems par byed pa, the causative 'to make dry, dry up, parch', matching Sanskrit tapeti (Hopkins: 'dry up'). The construction marks the drying/scorching as accompanying or coordinate with another action.

Given as an equivalent of 'fill' or 'fulfill' in the sense of making something full or bringing it to completion. The form is a non-present stem (imperative/past) of the verb, so it typically renders a command or completed action of filling or fulfilling.

skom pas gdungs pa.gloss: tormented by thirst, pained by thirst

senses.gloss: tormented by thirst, pained by thirst
senses.context: Renders Sanskrit pipāsā-tapta, pipāsita, and tṛṣṇārtta, i.e. one who is afflicted or scorched by thirst. The phrase combines skom pa (thirst) with gdungs pa (to be tormented, pained).
Corresponds to Sanskrit kṛśa, 'thin, emaciated, lean.'

senses.gloss: a lean hybrid cow yielding much milk
senses.context: Used as a term for a hybrid cow that is thin in body yet gives abundant milk; the sense of leanness (kṛśa) underlies this specialized usage.
A numerical phrase, 'eleven' plus skor (cycle, round, circuit), rendered provisionally as 'eleven cycles.' Parallel in formation to skor dgu, 'nine cycles.'

see_also: skor ba bya bar 'os par 'gyur te

skor ba bya bar 'os par 'gyur te.gloss: worthy of being honored by circumambulation

senses.gloss: worthy of being honored by circumambulation
senses.context: Renders Sanskrit pradakṣiṇīya, said of one who deserves to be circumambulated as a mark of respect. The Tibetan literally states that (someone) becomes fit or worthy (' os par 'gyur) to be circumambulated (skor ba bya bar).

skye ba'i ngo bo nyid med pa.gloss: absence of an inherent nature of production; production-non-nature

senses.gloss: absence of an inherent nature of production; production-non-nature
senses.context: A term for the lack of any own-being consisting in production — i.e., that phenomena are without a nature of being produced. Formed from skye ba (production) with ngo bo nyid med pa (absence of inherent nature).

skye mi rung gi chos can.gloss: that which has the quality of being unsuitable to be produced

senses.gloss: that which has the quality of being unsuitable to be produced
senses.context: Designates a subject characterized by not being fit or able to be produced (again). Hopkins glosses it provisionally as 'having the quality of not being suitable to be produced again'; the element skye mi rung indicates unsuitability for production.

see_also: skye dgag gnas gsum mi rung ba'i chos
skye dgag gnas gsum rung ba'i chos

senses.context: Locative phrase rendering Sanskrit anupādapade, the 'place' or 'track' of non-arising. Hopkins gives both 'in the state of non-production' and, following Conze, 'to the track of non-production'.

skye med blo ldan.gloss: one whose mind is set on non-production

senses.gloss: one whose mind is set on non-production
senses.context: Renders Sanskrit anupādadhī, describing someone whose intelligence or thought (blo) is directed toward non-arising. Conze's rendering given by Hopkins is 'his thought on non-production'.
Hopkins offers the provisional gloss 'confused being', taking skye as a being (a birth, one born) and rmongs as bewildered or obscured. The comparanda do not indicate further technical usage.

skyes mchog ka lo sgyur ba.gloss: supreme being, bull among men; hero

senses.gloss: supreme being, bull among men; hero
senses.context: Rendered by Sanskrit puṅgava ("bull [of men]," i.e. an outstanding or foremost person), and glossed in Conze's Perfection of Wisdom vocabulary as "hero." The compound joins skyes mchog, "supreme/excellent person," with ka lo sgyur ba, "one who wields command," describing a preeminent person who holds sway.

skyes pa tsam gyis 'jig par mi 'gyur.gloss: is not destroyed merely by having been produced

senses.gloss: is not destroyed merely by having been produced
senses.context: A phrase from Mahāyāna-sūtrālaṃkāra literature corresponding to Sanskrit (na) utpanna-mātraṃ vinaśyet, i.e. the negation of the position that something perishes simply in virtue of its having arisen. Used in discussions of production (skyes pa) and disintegration.
Translates Sanskrit jātaka, an account of a former birth; in Buddhist usage, discourses narrating the Buddha's previous lives. Conze renders it "birth-story."

skyes pa'i rabs kyi sde.gloss: the jātaka class [of scripture]; collection of birth stories

senses.gloss: the jātaka class [of scripture]; collection of birth stories
senses.context: An expanded form of skyes pa'i rabs (jātaka) with sde, "section, class," designating the division of scripture consisting of accounts of [the Buddha's] previous births; also rendered simply "life stories, birth-story."
Rendered by Sanskrit dahara/dahra, "young, small," and yuvan, "youth"; Hopkins gives the phrase rendering "boy."
The equivalents given include the feminine yuvati, so the term can also denote a young person generally rather than a male child specifically.

Renders Sanskrit khedavat, 'possessing khedaḥ (fatigue, dejection)'; the suffix can marks a person or mind endowed with such weariness. Used of one who is discouraged or worn out, in contrast to those free of such weariness.

see_also: skyo ba med pa yid la byed pa

senses.context: Corresponds to Sanskrit nirvit-sahagata, 'accompanied by nirvid (weariness, turning away)'; the phrase dang ldan pa marks accompaniment or possession. Glossed as discouraged or weary, i.e. a state of mind conjoined with such weariness.

see_also: skyo ba med pa yid la byed pa

senses.context: Translates Sanskrit kheda-vivarjita, 'devoid of, having discarded, khedaḥ (fatigue, dejection)'. It describes one from whom weariness or discouragement has been eliminated; the Hopkins gloss 'abandoned disregard for' reflects a further contextual reading of skyo ba.

see_also: skyo ba med pa yid la byed pa

senses.context: Corresponds to Sanskrit akheda, akheditva, and khedābhāva — the state or quality of being without fatigue or dejection. Used as an abstract quality (the fact of not being wearied).

senses.gloss: untiring, not wearied; forbearance of fatigue
senses.context: Also equated with aparikhinna ('not wearied out') and khedasahiṣṇutā ('endurance of fatigue'), i.e. the capacity to bear hardship without becoming discouraged.

see_also: skyo ba med pa yid la byed pa

senses.context: Renders Sanskrit akheda-manaskāra, 'attention/mental application devoid of khedaḥ'. It denotes taking to mind, or directing attention, in a manner untouched by fatigue or discouragement.

skyo bar mi 'gyur.gloss: does not become weary; does not get discouraged

senses.gloss: does not become weary; does not get discouraged
senses.context: Verbal phrase corresponding to Sanskrit na khedam āpadyate, 'does not fall into exhaustion/weariness'. Used of one who persists in an activity without tiring.
Also rendering nodvegam āyāti, 'does not come to agitation/dejection', i.e. does not lose heart or become disheartened.
Corresponds to Sanskrit akhinna, 'not wearied, not exhausted'. Describes a person or activity free of fatigue, weariness, or discouragement.

skyod pa.gloss: to move, stir, set in motion

senses.gloss: to move, stir, set in motion
senses.context: Transitive sense supported by ādhūta ('shaken, stirred') and the glosses 'arouse, stir, move, cause to go'. Used of causing something to move or go.
Corresponding to cañcala ('moving, wavering, restless') and saṃbhrama ('flurry, agitation'), the term can denote the state of being in motion or in commotion.
Renders Sanskrit guṇa-doṣa-bheda, the distinction or division between good qualities (yon tan) and faults (skyon). Refers to discriminating what is advantageous from what is disadvantageous.

see_also: skyon dang yon tan du so so yang dag par rig pa

skyon dang yon tan du so so yang dag par.gloss: thorough individual knowledge of faults and good qualities

senses.gloss: thorough individual knowledge of faults and good qualities
senses.context: Renders Sanskrit doṣa-guṇa-pratisaṃvedana, the full experiential awareness of faults and good qualities taken one by one. Emphasizes knowing each disadvantage and advantage individually and correctly.

see_also: skyon dang yon tan dag dbye ba

skyon du mi bya'o.gloss: should not be taken as a fault

senses.gloss: should not be taken as a fault
senses.context: Verbal phrase indicating that something is not to be regarded as a defect, flaw, or disadvantage. Hopkins gives 'not take as a fault/defect/disadvantage'.
Corresponding to Sanskrit anaparād(d)ha in the {C} materials, the phrase is glossed 'free from guilt', i.e. nothing has been offended against and no blame attaches.
The act of hurling or pointing out faults (skyon) at something or someone; hence critique, criticism.
By extension the agent, one who casts faults, i.e. a critic. Hopkins lists 'critique; critic' alongside 'casting faults'.
Honorific-register negation of skyon ('fault, flaw'), rendering Sanskrit nirdoṣa. Hopkins glosses it 'flawless; faultless', both in the general sense and in the {C} materials.

Corresponds to Sanskrit adoṣodbhāvana in the {VN} materials. Hopkins offers 'non-fault-statement', noting the phrase can be read either as (1) not pointing out the fault, or (2) pointing out the non-fault.
Rendering Sanskrit niyāmāvakrānti in the {MSA} materials; Hopkins glosses 'entry into flawlessness', i.e. the entering into a state without fault or flaw (skyon med pa).

skyon med par 'jug pa yang dag par 'grub.gloss: thorough establishment of entry into flawlessness

senses.gloss: thorough establishment of entry into flawlessness
senses.context: Rendered in the Madhyāntavibhāga context as niyāmāvakrānti-samudāgama, the full accomplishing (samudāgama) of the entry ('jug pa, avakrānti) into the state free of fault or error (skyon med pa). It names an attainment consisting in the completed achievement of such faultless entry.

Corresponds to doṣa-parijñāna in the Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra context: complete or thorough (yongs su) knowing (shes) of faults, flaws, or disadvantages (skyon, doṣa). It presupposes discernment of what is defective as opposed to what is of good quality.

see_also: skyon dang yon tan du so so yang dag par rig pa

skyon sel mi nus pa.gloss: unable to clear away the fault

senses.gloss: unable to clear away the fault
senses.context: Said of an opponent or position that cannot avoid, remove, or eliminate (sel ba) a fault or objection (skyon) that has been raised. Typically used in argumentative contexts where a consequence has been fastened on a thesis.

Continuative form (cing) of the verb skyob pa (present skyob; past bskyabs; future bskyab; imperative skyobs), 'to protect, defend, shelter'. Attested in the Conze materials for paritrāṇanā (glossed trāṇabhūta) 'sheltering', and in Lokesh Chandra for saṃvāhana.
Agentive noun (pa po) from skyob pa (present skyob; past bskyabs; future bskyab; imperative skyobs), 'to protect, shelter'. Designates the one who protects — a protector, guardian, or refuge/shelter.

Verbal form of skyob pa 'protect, guard, defend, shelter' (Skt. trā-, trayate), here in the present/continuative construction with byed and the connective particle cing, i.e. 'and protects...', linking to a following clause. Related past and imperative forms are given as bskyab, bskyabs, skyobs.
The same verb in the sense of giving shelter or refuge to someone; the comparanda list 'shelter' alongside 'protect' and 'defend' as renderings of skyob pa.
Compound of skra 'hair' and khang 'house', glossed as a barber-shop, i.e. an establishment where hair is cut. Only the English gloss is attested in the comparanda.
Rendering Sanskrit vāla, glossed simply as 'hair'. The element nyag ma indicates a single fine strand, so the term is used for hair viewed as individual filaments.

Phrase rendering Sanskrit keśa-bhramara-ādi, an enumeration beginning with hair (keśa) and bees (bhramara) and continuing with 'and so forth' (la sogs pa). The comparanda give only the literal listing, without further specification of the context in which the items are enumerated.
Compound of skra 'hair' and snum 'oil, grease', glossed as oil applied to the hair. Only the English gloss is attested in the comparanda.

Renders Sanskrit muṇḍa/muṇḍita, 'shaven, shorn'; describes one whose head-hair has been cut off, hence 'shaven head'. Formed from skra ('hair (of the head)') plus the past of the verb 'to shave, shear'.

skra zla la sogs pa med pa.gloss: non-existent hairs, moons, and so forth

senses.gloss: non-existent hairs, moons, and so forth
senses.context: Renders asat-keśa-candra-ādi, 'non-existent hairs, moons, etc.' The phrase names illusory appearances — falling hairs, a double moon and the like — that appear although they do not exist.

see_also: skra dang sbrang bu la sogs pa

skra la phog par.gloss: splitting a hair; hitting a hair

senses.gloss: splitting a hair; hitting a hair
senses.context: Renders bālavedha / bālavedhanā, the piercing or splitting of a hair; the Tibetan is literally 'striking upon a hair'. Used for the feat of hitting so fine a target, hence 'splitting a hair'.
Renders keśoṇḍuka, a 'hair-net', i.e. a mass of hairs appearing tangled together. The Tibetan compound adds 'dzings pa, 'entangled, matted', to skra, 'hair'.

see_also: skra zla la sogs pa med pa
skra dang sbrang bu la sogs pa

senses.context: Continuative form of skrag pa, corresponding to Sanskrit trasati / uttrasati and participial trasyan, trasta: to dread, be alarmed, be terrified. Typically links the fright to what follows in the sentence.

skrag dang dngang.gloss: fear and dread; fear and panic

senses.gloss: fear and dread; fear and panic
senses.context: A coordinate pair expressing intensified fright, corresponding to Sanskrit trāsa (fear, terror) in the Madhyāntavibhāga compound trāsatā-māna. The two Tibetan terms skrag and dngang reinforce one another, conveying alarm together with panic.
Renders Sanskrit trāsa-pratiṣedha (Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra), the negation or blocking of fear. It names the act or condition by which fright is prevented or brought to an end.
Renders Sanskrit atrāsa (Madhyāntavibhāga), the privative of trāsa 'fright, dread'. Used of a person or state in which fear or dread is absent.
Renders Sanskrit trāsa-kāraṇa (Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra), that which produces or occasions dread. It designates the causal factor from which fright arises.
Renders Sanskrit uttrāsa-pada and trāsa-sthāna (Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra), literally a 'place' or 'ground' of terror. It indicates a situation or basis constituting an occasion for dread.

bskal pa gang gā'i klung gi bye ma snyed.gloss: eons as numerous as the sands of the Ganges

senses.gloss: eons as numerous as the sands of the Ganges
senses.context: A stock simile of immensity of time, rendering Sanskrit gaṅgā-nadī-vālikā-sama ... kalpa, 'eons equal (in number) to the sand grains of the river Ganges.' Used to indicate a practically uncountable span of eons, e.g. in describing the length of a bodhisattva's practice.

see_also: bskal pa grangs ma mchis pa

senses.context: Renders Sanskrit asaṃkhyeya-kalpa, an 'incalculable' number of eons. The honorific negative ma mchis pa ('there are none/it is not') marks the number as beyond counting.

see_also: bskal pa gang gā'i klung gi bye ma snyed
bskal pa grangs med pa gsum

senses.context: The passing or elapsing ('da' ba) of innumerable (grangs med) eons. Expresses duration measured by the going-by of incalculable eons.

see_also: bskal pa grangs ma mchis pa
bskal pa grangs med pa gsum

senses.context: Renders Sanskrit naikasahasra ... kalpa, literally 'not one thousand' i.e. many thousands of eons. A large but numbered measure of time, as distinct from the strictly incalculable.

see_also: bskal pa grangs ma mchis pa
bskal pa gang gā'i klung gi bye ma snyed

senses.context: Renders Sanskrit kalpa-sahasra-koṭi, a thousand koṭi (ten million) of eons. A specific enumerated multiple used to express an enormous span of time.

see_also: bskal pa grangs med pa gsum
bskal pa gang gā'i klung gi bye ma snyed
bskal pa grangs ma mchis pa

bskal pa rdzogs ldan.gloss: the perfect age, age of completeness (kṛtayuga)

senses.gloss: the perfect age, age of completeness (kṛtayuga)
senses.context: Designates the first of the four ages (yuga) into which an aeon (bskal pa) is divided, the age in which perfection or completeness prevails. Literally 'the aeon/age endowed with completeness', corresponding to Sanskrit kṛtayuga.

bskal pa'i me 'bar ba.gloss: blazing fire of the eon; universal conflagration

senses.gloss: blazing fire of the eon; universal conflagration
senses.context: Renders Sanskrit kalpoddāha, the conflagration said to rage at the end of an aeon (bskal pa). Used for the world-consuming fire that destroys the universe at an aeon's close, and hence as an image of overwhelming blazing.

Past/gerundive form of bskur ('to bestow, render, pay [honor]') translating Sanskrit satkṛtya, 'having honored.' The Sanskrit commentarial glosses explain the honoring in terms of conferring marks of distinction (e.g., binding on the glorious head-band, establishing one in a special position) and of preparing a maṇḍala and the like.

Continuative (cing) form of bskul, translating Sanskrit codayati: to arouse, urge on, incite, entreat, or exhort. Depending on context it can also carry the sense of admonishing, warning against, or pressing a charge.
Conditional/temporal (na) form of bskul: 'if or when one is aroused, entreated, urged on, or exhorted.'
Corresponding to Sanskrit preṣita, of a person or thing sent or dispatched; the Sanskrit saṃghaṭṭita further suggests being struck together or stirred up as the impetus.

A named monastic offense (spang ba, a fault to be abandoned) incurred by urging or prompting others — per the gloss, in connection with donations. The entry combines bskul ba 'urging, exhorting, soliciting' with spang ba, the class of offenses requiring relinquishment; only the English gloss supports this reading.
Verbal form for Sanskrit codayati: to spur, prompt or press someone to act. Rendered in the comparanda as 'urge on', 'incite', 'exhort', 'entreat'.
Used where the object is a mental state or capacity that is stirred into activity rather than a person who is commanded; the gloss offers both 'arouse' and 'cause to arouse'.
Tibetan rendering of the Sanskrit name Cunda, treated as a proper name in the comparanda.
Literally an agentive formation from bskul 'to urge, exhort, incite', hence 'inciter, exhorter'; this is the sense underlying its use to translate the name Cunda.

bskul byed rdo rje ma.gloss: Cundavajrī (proper name of a female deity)

senses.gloss: Cundavajrī (proper name of a female deity)
senses.context: Tibetan rendering of Sanskrit Cundavajrī, attested in the Guhyasamāja context. Formed from bskul byed (= cunda) plus rdo rje ma (= vajrī), the feminine 'Vajra' element typical of tantric goddess names.
