An adverbial phrase, 'just as [he/she] exhorted', built on bskul ma 'exhortation, urging' with the honorific verb mdzad pa and bzhin 'in accordance with'. It indicates that an action follows upon or conforms to a request or prompting made by another.

Renders Sanskrit upādāya (upādu) in the idiomatic sense of taking something as a starting point, i.e. 'beginning with (such and such)'. Formed from bskyed with the phrase nas bzung ste, 'taking from', the expression marks the point from which an enumeration or a range is reckoned.
Equivalent of Sanskrit upādāya (upādu), indicating the starting point of a series or range. Functions like bskyed nas bzung ste, marking that from which the reckoning begins.
An elegant/honorific finite verb form (bgyid for byed) corresponding to Sanskrit janayati. Used where a subject brings something into being, e.g. generating an attitude or a quality.

bskyed par bya ba.gloss: that which is to be produced/generated

senses.gloss: that which is to be produced/generated
senses.context: Corresponds to Sanskrit gerundives and related forms such as utpādayitavya, utpāditavya, utpādanīyatva, and utpādya, i.e. what ought to be or is to be brought into being.

senses.gloss: that which is produced; the produced/generable
senses.context: Also renders janana, janya, janyatva, and janyamāna, i.e. the effect or object that is produced or is being produced, as opposed to that which produces it.

Continuative form (byas la) rendering Sanskrit saṃjanayati, 'produces, generates, creates'; the Tibetan presents the action as completed and leading on to what follows, i.e. 'having generated (it), ...'.
Rendering Sanskrit asaṃprakampya, describing what cannot be shaken or stirred by anything. Used adjectivally of a state or being that is impervious to disturbance.
Literally 'not able to move/shake', the negated potential of the verb bskyod pa. In this reading the emphasis is on an agent's incapacity to set something in motion.

bskyod mi nus so.gloss: cannot be moved; cannot be shaken

senses.gloss: cannot be moved; cannot be shaken
senses.context: A finite negated statement ('one is unable to move it'), formed on bskyod pa, corresponding to the Sanskrit causative cālayati 'moves, shakes, deflects'. Hopkins also gives 'cannot be deflected' and 'cannot move'.
Corresponds to Sanskrit utpādita, 'produced, brought forth'; Hopkins gives 'craft, make, form, produce'. The causative counterpart of bskyed pa, said of what an agent brings about.
In the idiom rendering avarupta/avaropita kuśalamūla, of virtuous roots that have been sown or planted; also glossed by āropaṇa 'planting, setting up'.

see_also: bskrun pa ste bskyed pa =btsugs pa

senses.context: Hopkins glosses this as filling out something deficient, e.g. supplying a missing syllable in a line of verse with an extra syllable so that the metre is complete.
Hopkins gives only the provisional rendering 'facing backward', i.e. the side or aspect (ngos) that is turned to the rear (kha rgyab).

kha ton byang bar byas.gloss: mastered by recitation, learned by heart

senses.gloss: mastered by recitation, learned by heart
senses.context: Renders Sanskrit vacasā paricita, literally 'made familiar by speech', i.e. having become thoroughly acquainted with a text through repeated oral recitation. Hopkins glosses it as 'learned recitation', and in some contexts the phrase is associated with (religious) texts that have been so mastered.
A phrase-level term glossed by Hopkins as 'oral tradition', i.e. what is transmitted by word of mouth rather than in writing. Formed on kha ('mouth', hence speech).
Locative phrase glossed by Hopkins as 'upon; above', indicating position on or over the surface of something. Built on kha in the sense of surface or upper face.
Glossed by Hopkins as 'downwards', indicating orientation toward the lower direction, i.e. with the opening or face turned down. Cf. the adverbial form with the terminative particle.
Adverbial (terminative) form glossed by Hopkins as 'downwards', expressing motion or orientation toward what is below. Equivalent in meaning to the same phrase without the terminative particle.
A dune or heaped mound of sand; formed on the element bye "sand." Attested in the comparanda only as a phrase-level gloss ("sand dune").

The term isolates color per se, as distinct from any particular instance or shade of it. In this use it designates a merely hypothetical or posited color-in-general rather than an actual blue, yellow, etc.

kha dog gi gzugs.gloss: color-form; form that is a color

senses.gloss: color-form; form that is a color
senses.context: Sanskrit varṇarūpa: a visible form (gzugs) which is a color (kha dog), as opposed to a form which is a shape. Used where visible forms are divided into those consisting of color and others.
Sanskrit nīla-varṇa; the color blue as a particular instance of kha dog (color).

kha dog gcig tu.gloss: of one color, as one color

senses.gloss: of one color, as one color
senses.context: Sanskrit eka-varṇa; adverbial/terminative form indicating that something is uniform in color or is taken as a single color.
Used of speech or manner that is direct and honest. The comparanda give only an English rendering, glossing the term as 'straight-forward, forthright'.

Designates the side or aspect that faces to the front, in contrast to the rear side. Formed with kha ('face, surface') and ngos ('side, surface'), it parallels the corresponding expression for the back side.

Corresponds to Sanskrit anu-mātra ... avadya, 'a fault of merely atomic measure'. The phrase emphasizes that even the most minute blameworthy element is at issue, typically in contexts denying its presence.

Honorific form (mi mnga' ba, 'does not possess') rendering Sanskrit anavadya / niravadya. Said of a person or quality that is free of anything blameworthy or unseemly; also rendered 'not involving unseemliness'.
Standard (non-honorific) equivalent of Sanskrit anavadya / niravadya, indicating the absence of anything blameworthy. Also rendered 'not involving unseemliness'.

kha na ma tho ba med pa'i las can yin pa.gloss: having faultless activities; having deeds free of unseemliness

senses.gloss: having faultless activities; having deeds free of unseemliness
senses.context: Predicated of a being whose actions are without blame or reproach. Rendering Sanskrit anavadya-karmatva, the state of having activities (las) that are without unseemliness or fault (kha na ma tho ba med pa).
Corresponds to Sanskrit anavadya-viṣaya, an object or field of activity (yul) that is free of blame or unseemliness. Used of objects or areas of engagement that are beyond reproach.
The aspect or factor (cha) of an awareness that faces inwards. In one epistemological usage it denotes an internal cognition that apprehends the objectal aspect of an external object.
Designates a class or manner ('gros) of that which faces inwards, i.e. is directed within rather than towards outer objects.
Said of something whose face or orientation (kha) is turned inward. Contrasts with what is turned outward toward external objects.

Said of something whose face or opening (kha) is turned toward the inside. Used of orientation or of a mental factor or aspect that is directed inwards rather than towards outer objects, in contrast to kha phyir bstan (facing outwards).

Rendering Sanskrit pragalbha in the vocabulary of the Perfection of Wisdom translations, glossed as 'arrogant'. Literally involving the raising or lifting of the mouth/face (kha), the term denotes an attitude of boldness or self-assertion.
The aspect or portion (cha) of a mind that faces outwards, i.e. is turned towards objects external to itself, as opposed to a factor facing inwards.
In the terminology of the Collected Topics tradition, a cognition characterized as outwardly directed, that is, one that apprehends an object external to the mind itself.
A kind or manner ('gros) of something whose orientation (kha) is towards the outside, i.e. outward-looking. Parallel in formation to kha phyir lta'i cha, the outwardly directed factor.

Said of something whose face or opening (kha) is turned toward the outside. Used of physical orientation and of aspects of mind that are directed towards external objects, in contrast to kha nang du bstan pa (facing inwards).
Said of something whose face, opening, or surface (kha) is turned away from the observer or from a center. Used descriptively of orientation, i.e., directed or turned toward the outside.
A designation of the country (yul) possessed of snow (kha ba can), understood as Tibet. The Hopkins gloss is a paraphrase rendering of the epithet.
The taste (ro) that is bitter, kha ba here functioning as the flavor-term 'bitter'. Given only as a taste designation in the comparanda.
Corresponds to Sanskrit utphulla, phullita, vikasita, puṣpa, i.e., of a flower whose mouth (kha) has opened. Used of blossoms bursting open.
The Sanskrit comparandum prakāśa suggests an extended sense of being opened out and hence evident or manifest, by analogy with a flower unfolding.

kha 'bus pa.gloss: to form buds, be in bud

senses.gloss: to form buds, be in bud
senses.context: Rendered by Sanskrit kuḍmalakajāta, koraka, and mukulajāta, all terms for a bud or the budding state. Describes a plant at the stage where the flower's mouth (kha) is still closed or just swelling.
In the Conze-based material the term is glossed as opening out blossoms, i.e., the transition from bud to bloom.
Rendering Sanskrit pṛthumukha, literally 'having a broad mouth or opening'. Used of something whose mouth, face or surface is of great breadth.
Extended by Hopkins to the sense 'vast and open', i.e. broadly expansive rather than narrow or constricted.

Verbal phrase corresponding to Sanskrit alpa-āhāra, 'having little food'. Hopkins gives both 'seek a little food' and 'takes little food', the Tibetan using the honorific 'tshal ba for eating/partaking.
Glossed simply as 'food' (Hopkins); no Sanskrit equivalent is supplied in the comparanda.
Rendering Sanskrit sārathi, one who steers or drives a chariot; the Tibetan literally means 'one who turns the steering'.
In the compound puruṣadamyasārathi, 'charioteer of men to be tamed', the term denotes one who guides and disciplines those amenable to training.
Corresponds to Sanskrit ruru and nyaṃku, names of species of deer or antelope; Hopkins glosses 'spotted deer'.
Rendered by Hopkins as 'dispute; argue', denoting verbal contention between parties. Used of disagreement carried on in speech rather than physical conflict.
Hopkins also gives 'use rough language', i.e. abusive or contentious speech. The sense stays close to the element kha (mouth, speech).
A temporal adverb glossed by Hopkins simply as 'yesterday', i.e. the day preceding today.
Hopkins offers the provisional gloss 'everyday expressions', suggesting words used to fill out or round off ordinary speech. The comparanda do not support a more precise technical rendering.
Glossed by Hopkins as 'magpie', the name of a bird. No further comparanda are available.

khang steng.gloss: upper storey of a house, rooftop level

senses.gloss: upper storey of a house, rooftop level
senses.context: Hopkins gives the provisional gloss 'upper level of a house', and Lokesh Chandra records Sanskrit talakopari, i.e. the part above a floor or storey. The compound joins khang (house, building) with steng (upper part, top).

Lokesh Chandra further equates the term with aṭṭa (an upper room or turret) and prāsāda (a lofty building, mansion, terraced structure). In such uses the word denotes the elevated portion of a fine dwelling rather than merely a roof.

Renders Sanskrit koṭṭarāja (koṭṭa-rājan), where koṭṭa denotes a fort or stronghold and rājan its lord; hence the Conze gloss 'commander of a fort'. Here khams does not carry its usual sense of 'constituent/element' but corresponds to the fortified place or district over which such a ruler presides.

khams rgyas pa.gloss: increase of the constitution, improved health

senses.gloss: increase of the constitution, improved health
senses.context: Corresponds to Sanskrit dhātu-puṣṭi, the nourishing or increasing of the bodily constituents (dhātu). Used of increasing the constitution in the sense of improving physical health.
A phrase combining khams (constituent, element, dhātu) with chen (great, major), glossed as 'major constituents'. No Sanskrit equivalent is attested in the material at hand.
Renders Sanskrit dvaya-dhātu-puṣṭatā, the nourishing or strengthening of the two constituents (dhātu). Glossed as increasing or improving the two constituents, hence improving health.

khams rtas pa.gloss: increase of the constituents, improved health

senses.gloss: increase of the constituents, improved health
senses.context: Corresponds to Sanskrit dhātu-puṣṭatā / dhātu-puṣṭi, the state of the bodily constituents (dhātu) being nourished or strengthened; hence 'increase/improve the constituents, improve health'. The verbal element appears with the spelling variants brta'/brta/brtas/rtas.

Given as a Tibetan equivalent of Sanskrit nigraha and glossed 'refutation' in the Perfection of Wisdom (Conze) vocabulary. The phrase is cited with the terminative particle la, i.e. as the complement of a verb of refuting or censuring.

A reduplicated expression indicating an amount beyond expression or reckoning. It is cited in the passage stating that the relics (sku gdung ring bsrel) of as many Tathāgatas as 'khar yas khar yas' are present there.

khar yas khar yas.sanskrit: de bzhin gshegs pa khar yas khar yas zhes bya ba snyed kyi sku gdung ring bsrel rnams gnas so

senses.context: Equivalent of Sanskrit pratijñā, the taking of something as one's own position; literally 'to take by mouth'. Used for asserting or claiming a thesis.
In the sense of verbally accepting or committing oneself to something, i.e. giving one's word.

khas blang bar bya ba.gloss: that which is to be asserted/accepted

senses.gloss: that which is to be asserted/accepted
senses.context: Future/gerundive form corresponding to Sanskrit abhyupagantavya, indicating what is to be accepted, asserted, or promised.
A fault whereby a position conflicts with what one has oneself asserted or accepted (khas blangs). Recorded as 'contradiction of opinion'.

khas len pa med cing.gloss: without asserting, making no claim or promise

senses.gloss: without asserting, making no claim or promise
senses.context: Negated phrase built on khas len pa 'assertion, acceptance, promise', used adverbially or as a qualifier ('and without asserting...'). Hopkins glosses it as 'without assertion/acceptance/promise'.

In the Conze (C) materials the phrase corresponds to Sanskrit anupagata, rendered 'unapproachable'. This reading construes the negation as 'not come to / not taken up' rather than as the refusal of an assertion.
Verbal expression with khas len 'assertion, acceptance, promise' plus byed, i.e. to make such an assertion or undertaking. Hopkins: 'make assertion/acceptance/promise'.
Lokesh Chandra records Sanskrit anumanye 'I concede, approve' and samupeta (MSA), suggesting the sense of assenting to or endorsing a position.

Standard name of the bird, rendering a wide range of Sanskrit synonyms recorded by Lokesh Chandra: kokila, pika, parapuṣṭa, parabhṛta ('nourished/reared by another', alluding to the cuckoo's brood parasitism), vanapriya ('fond of the forest'), and harikaṇṭha.
Transcription of the Chinese name; Hopkins gives it as a phrase-level rendering (PH) for Confucius, and by extension for the tradition named after him, Confucianism.

khums.gloss: past and imperative stem of 'khum pa

senses.gloss: past and imperative stem of 'khum pa
senses.context: Lokesh Chandra cites khums only within the verb paradigm khum / 'khums / khums / khums, i.e. as the perfect and imperative form beside the present khum and 'khums. The lexical meaning must therefore be taken from the paradigm's base verb.
Hopkins glosses the form as 'listen; hear; understand; realize', a reading not corroborated by the Sanskrit comparanda, which supply only the verb paradigm.

khur 'dor ba.gloss: to cast off a burden, lay down a load

senses.gloss: to cast off a burden, lay down a load
senses.context: Corresponds to Sanskrit bhāra-nikṣepaṇa, the setting down or discarding of a load (khur). Used of forsaking or throwing off a burden, whether a physical load or figuratively a responsibility.
Renders Sanskrit bhāra, a load or burden. The nominal form of khur, denoting the thing carried; hence also figuratively a burden or charge.
Corresponds to Sanskrit bhāravāha, 'load-bearer'. Formed from khur po (load, bhāra) with the agentive -ba, designating one whose work is carrying loads.
Renders Sanskrit apahṛta-bhāra / apagata-bhāra, and also apahṛta alone, i.e. (a load) taken off or set down. Used of one whose burden has been laid down or put aside.
Glossed as dandelion; the Sanskrit comparandum darvikā (ladle-shaped) may reflect the leaf or flower form. Attested as a plant name distinct from khur 'load'.

senses.gloss: name of a bird (partridge; a water bird)
senses.context: Also equated with Sanskrit tittiri, the partridge, and (uncertainly) plava, a water bird or diver. The zoological identification is unsettled in the sources.

khur mi khyer ba.gloss: not carrying a burden; not taking on a load

senses.gloss: not carrying a burden; not taking on a load
senses.context: Negated form of khur khyer ba "to carry a burden." Hopkins gives "not carry a burden/load," and in the Conze-based (C) material the corresponding Sanskrit anāropaṇatā is rendered "not put on (of a burden)", i.e. the abstract state of not having a load laid on or taken up.

khur rin.gloss: porter's fee, wages for carrying a load

senses.gloss: porter's fee, wages for carrying a load
senses.context: A compound of khur (burden, load) and rin (price, payment): the payment made for transporting a load. Hopkins glosses it (as a phrase) "wages for carrying a load."
Hopkins glosses nang khul simply as "inside," i.e. the inner part or interior region of something, in contrast to what is outside.

In the illustrative phrase supplied with this entry — nang khul phan tshun khe bzang mi za bar rang yod dngos po 'tshong ba, selling one's own goods without taking profit off one another nang khul — the term marks a transaction as taking place internally, within the group or circle concerned.

nang khul.sanskrit: nang khul phan tshun khe bzang mi za bar rang yod dngos po 'tshong ba

senses.context: The only comparandum available is Hopkins's gloss "stale," said of something no longer fresh. No Sanskrit equivalent is attested in the material at hand, so the range of the term cannot be further specified.

A privative phrase built on khengs pa (haughtiness, arrogance, being puffed up) with dang bral ba "separated from, devoid of." Hopkins renders it "free of haughtiness; free of arrogance; free of being puffed up."

In the Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra (MSA) material the phrase corresponds to Sanskrit kharatvapāgama, the going away or disappearance (apagama) of kharatva (harshness, roughness), which the Tibetan renders as separation from khengs pa.

Negated form of khengs pa (being puffed up, arrogant), corresponding to Sanskrit anunnati as attested in the Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra literature. Used to describe the absence of haughtiness or self-inflation.

khem pa gcig las med pa min te.gloss: it is not the case that there is only one brief moment

senses.gloss: it is not the case that there is only one brief moment
senses.context: A sentence-phrase denying that something is limited to a single khem pa, i.e., a single short interval of time. The Hopkins comparandum renders it as a denial that the matter is confined to just one brief period.
First-person plural pronoun, glossed simply as 'we'. Formed on kho with the plural/collective particle cag; compare the singular kho bo, 'I'.

Rendering Sanskrit eva-śabdenāvadhāraṇaṃ: a restriction or determination effected by attaching the particle kho na ('only', eva) to a term. Used in scholastic analysis of how the exclusive particle narrows the scope of what is asserted.
A debate formula introducing an opponent's statement or objection, literally 'if they say...'. It sets up a position that is then answered or refuted.

Formed from kho na ('only, that alone') plus ma 'dres ('unmixed'), designating what belongs solely to one thing and is not commingled with anything else. The Sanskrit comparandum āveṇika supports the sense 'peculiar to, special', i.e. proper to one subject alone.

kho bos sngon po mthong ngam ma mthong s.gloss: a sense direct perception apprehending blue that induces doubt

senses.gloss: a sense direct perception apprehending blue that induces doubt
senses.context: An illustrative technical phrase: a direct perception by a sense faculty which takes blue as its object, yet which gives rise to a subsequent doubting consciousness thinking, 'Did I see blue or not?' It is cited as an instance of a valid direct perception that nonetheless fails to produce ascertainment.

kho bos bris pa las shes par bya'o.gloss: these are to be known from my own writings

senses.gloss: these are to be known from my own writings
senses.context: An authorial cross-reference formula, with kho bo ('I, myself') in the instrumental: the points at issue are to be understood from what the author has composed elsewhere.
An authorial announcement formula, with kho bo ('I, myself') in the instrumental followed by bshad par bya, 'is to be explained', i.e. the author undertakes to set the matter forth.
Hopkins glosses the term as 'limb', i.e. a bodily member or extremity.
Lokesh Chandra records the Sanskrit equivalents pariṇāha and maṇḍala, pointing to the sense of extent or girth, and of a round enclosure or disc.

khong du chud par bgyi ba.gloss: to make understood; to cause to penetrate/internalize

senses.gloss: to make understood; to cause to penetrate/internalize
senses.context: Verbal-noun/honorific form built on khong du chud 'to take inside, understand, internalize, realize, penetrate'. Rendered by Sanskrit avataraṇa, which carries the sense of causing to enter or descend into something, hence 'introducing' someone to a teaching.
Used substantively for the act of comprehending or fully entering into a topic, in accord with the glosses 'understand, internalize, realize, penetrate'.

Future/resultative construction on khong du chud, corresponding to Sanskrit avatarati (enters into, descends into) and avasīyate (is ascertained). Conveys arriving at understanding, internalizing, or penetrating a subject.

khong du chud par 'dod pa.gloss: wishing to understand; desiring to penetrate

senses.gloss: wishing to understand; desiring to penetrate
senses.context: Formed from khong du chud par 'to understand, penetrate' plus 'dod pa 'to wish, want'. Sanskrit avaboddhu-kāma, 'desirous of comprehending', i.e. one who wants to look through to and fully grasp the matter.

khong du chud par bya ste.gloss: should be understood; is to be penetrated

senses.gloss: should be understood; is to be penetrated
senses.context: Gerundive construction corresponding to Sanskrit anugantavya, 'to be followed/known'. Marks what a reader or practitioner ought to comprehend or realize, often closing an explanation.

khong du chud par bya ba.gloss: that which is to be understood; object of understanding

senses.gloss: that which is to be understood; object of understanding
senses.context: Gerundive/nominal form matching Sanskrit anugantavya, pratipattavya, pratipādayitavya — what should be comprehended, practiced, or conveyed.
As a noun it renders such Sanskrit terms as abhisamaya, pratipatti, pratipādana, and nirukta, i.e. the act of grasping, realizing, or elucidating the meaning.
Ablative form of khong ("inside, interior"), rendered "from within." In the Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra material it corresponds to Sanskrit -gata, i.e. what has gone forth or proceeds from an inner source.

A place or area (sa) falling within (khongs) a given jurisdiction or sphere; glossed "territory." The sense derives from khongs, the inside or compass of something, combined with sa, ground or locale.
Glossed "vast expanse," i.e. a wide, broadly extended spread or layout, from khod (arrangement, extent) qualified by yangs po (wide, spacious).
Glossed "anger; resentment," i.e. the harboring of ill will or grudge. It belongs with the khon family of terms concerning enmity and the holding of a grudge.

Corresponds to Sanskrit avaira / nirvaira, the absence of enmity or hostility; also attested in the compound nirvairasattva, a being free of enmity. Rendered "non-enmity" and "lack of hostility" (also spelled "non-emnity" in some sources).

see_also: khon du 'dzin pa med pa yin

senses.context: The state of being habituated or well-acquainted with something through repeated practice. Hopkins gives the nominal sense 'familiarization'.
Used verbally of making oneself or another accustomed to something, i.e. conditioning to it. Hopkins renders it both 'familiar' and 'familiarize; condition to'.
A designated stage of the path characterized by repeated familiarization (khoms) with what has been previously understood. Hopkins glosses the compound as 'path of familiarization'.
A passage drawn out of a larger work; also the act of extracting or excerpting such a passage. Hopkins glosses it 'extract; excerpt [from a text]'.
The chief or principal among the distinguishing characteristics (khyad chos) of something. Hopkins offers the provisional rendering 'main distinguishing feature'.
A distinguishing characteristic (khyad chos) that belongs to one thing alone, gcig pu marking its sole or exclusive status. Hopkins glosses it 'unique distinguishing feature'.

A distinguishing quality (khyad chos) that is comparatively great or outstanding, i.e. the chief attribute setting something apart. Used when one feature among several is singled out as the most significant.
A word or expression (sgra) that states a distinguishing quality or attribute (khyad chos) of something, as opposed to naming the thing itself.
Rendering Sanskrit viśiṣyate: to be marked off as special, to surpass or be superior to something else. Often used in comparisons where one item is said to be distinguished above another.

Corresponds to Sanskrit kutsayati and vimānayati (vi √man), 'to disparage, to slight'; the nominal form renders atimananatā/vimānana, 'contemptuousness, contempt'. Denotes the act or attitude of treating another with scorn.

A joy (dga' ba) marked off as distinct or special (khyad par) within an enumerated series of joys; the Sanskrit comparanda (viramānanda and related forms of vi-ram, 'to cease') associate it with a joy connected to cessation. The comparanda support only the general sense of a particular, differentiated joy.

Negative compound corresponding to Sanskrit viśeṣa-kāraṇābhāva: the lack of any cause that would make one thing distinct from another. Used where no special or differentiating causal factor can be identified.

khyad par gyi tshul can.gloss: having a distinctive mode; conducive to distinction

senses.gloss: having a distinctive mode; conducive to distinction
senses.context: Renders viśeṣa-bhāgīya, characterizing something that partakes of or possesses a special, superior mode. The comparanda indicate the quality of being marked off as distinctive rather than ordinary.
Corresponds to viśeṣa-gatva, literally 'going to distinction': the process of attaining a superior or distinctive state. Hopkins also gives the transitive sense 'enhance'.

khyad par can gyi snang bas.gloss: by means of a special appearance

senses.gloss: by means of a special appearance
senses.context: Instrumental phrase built on khyad par can ('having distinction, special') with snang ba ('appearance'), glossed by Hopkins as 'by means of a special appearance'. It indicates that something occurs through an appearance that is distinctive rather than ordinary.

Renders viśeṣabhāgīya, marking a factor that shares in or accords with the attainment of distinction or enhancement. The element cha mthun conveys concordance with, or partaking of, the distinguished state.

Corresponds to Sanskrit viśeṣādhigama (MSA): the attaining or realizing of what is distinctive, superior, or special. Here khyad par carries the sense of a distinguishing or superior quality, and rtogs pa the sense of realization/attainment.

Term of reasoning, glossed as 'involving a qualification': said of something (e.g. a sign or reason) that depends upon (ltos pa) an added qualification or distinguishing specification (khyad par). Contrasts with what is free of qualification (khyad par dag pa pa).

khyad par ltos pa pa'i rang bzhin gyi rt.gloss: correct nature sign involving a qualification

senses.gloss: correct nature sign involving a qualification
senses.context: A subdivision of the correct sign of nature (rang bzhin gyi rtags yang dag) in logic: a valid nature-sign that depends upon an added qualification (khyad par ltos pa pa). It is paired in classification with the correct nature sign free of qualification (khyad par dag pa pa'i rang bzhin gyi rtags yang dag).

khyad par dag pa pa'i rang bzhin gyi rta.gloss: correct nature sign free of qualification

senses.gloss: correct nature sign free of qualification
senses.context: A subdivision of the correct sign of nature (rang bzhin gyi rtags yang dag) in logic: a valid nature-sign that is purified of (dag pa) any added qualification. It is paired in classification with the correct nature sign involving a qualification (khyad par ltos pa pa'i rang bzhin gyi rtags yang dag).
Rendered by Hopkins as 'become distinctive'; the verbal phrase expresses coming to have a distinguishing or superior quality (khyad par).
Equated with Sanskrit viśeṣa (MV) and vaiśeṣika (LC), i.e. that which is particular, special, or distinguishing.

Verbal expression for progressing to a state of distinction or superiority. Hopkins gives 'become distinguished'; the same form is also rendered causatively as 'enhance', i.e., to make (something) advance to a superior state.

khyad par du 'gro ba.gloss: becoming distinguished; progress to a superior state

senses.gloss: becoming distinguished; progress to a superior state
senses.context: Nominalized form corresponding to Sanskrit viśeṣa-gamana, viśeṣa-gati, and viśeṣa-gāmitva/viśeṣagāmitā (MSA, MV): a 'going to distinction', i.e., the process of advancing to a higher or more excellent state.
Hopkins also glosses the term as 'enhance', reflecting the sense of causing or undergoing an increase in excellence.
Rendering Sanskrit viśeṣādhigama, a realization or attainment (adhigama) marked by distinction (viśeṣa), i.e., a superior or extraordinary realization.

khyad par gdags pa yongs su tshol ba.gloss: thorough investigation of the designation of attributes

senses.gloss: thorough investigation of the designation of attributes
senses.context: Corresponds to Sanskrit viśeṣa-prajñapti-paryeṣaṇā (MSA): the full examination or research into how distinguishing features (viśeṣa) are imputed or designated (prajñapti). A variant spelling of khyad par 'dogs pa yongs su tshol ba.

khyad par 'dogs pa yongs su tshol ba.gloss: thorough investigation of the designation of attributes

senses.gloss: thorough investigation of the designation of attributes
senses.context: Corresponds to Sanskrit viśeṣa-prajñapti-paryeṣaṇā (MSA): the complete search into or examination of the imputed designation of distinguishing features. A variant of khyad par gdags pa yongs su tshol ba.

khyad par phyi ma phyi ma.gloss: successively later distinctions; each further superior feature

senses.gloss: successively later distinctions; each further superior feature
senses.context: Renders Sanskrit uttarottara-viśeṣa, the distinguishing features (viśeṣa) that come in an ascending series, each later one surpassing the earlier. Hopkins gives 'latter features/distinctions/differences', i.e. the qualities pertaining to the later members of a progressive sequence.

A verbal phrase, glossed by Hopkins as 'distinguish the different features': to separate out and set forth the features (khyad par) in which things are not alike (mi 'dra ba). Used where an exposition differentiates items by their unshared qualities.
Renders Sanskrit nirviśiṣṭatā, the state of being without any distinguishing feature (viśeṣa) that would set one thing apart from another. Hopkins glosses it 'non-difference; non-distinction'.
The defining mark (mtshan nyid) that functions to distinguish one thing from another, as glossed by Hopkins: 'differentiating characteristic'.

khyad par zhugs pa.gloss: differentiator as superior; qualifier marking distinction

senses.gloss: differentiator as superior; qualifier marking distinction
senses.context: Hopkins glosses 'differentiator as superior', i.e. that which enters in (zhugs pa) as a distinguishing factor (khyad par) and thereby marks something as higher or more excellent. The comparanda support no further specification of usage.

A term for setting aside or excluding features (khyad par) other than the one under consideration. Per the English comparandum, it is the act of eliminating other distinguishing characteristics or qualifications.

khyad par la kun btags pa'i kun btags su.gloss: imputation of a particular that is an imputation of attribute

senses.gloss: imputation of a particular that is an imputation of attribute
senses.context: A technical designation for one type of superimposition (kun btags): the imputation of a particular (bye brag) which is itself an instance of the imputation made with respect to an attribute or feature (khyad par la kun btags pa). It is paired with the imputation of an entity (ngo bo nyid) that likewise consists in an imputation of attribute.

Renders Sanskrit viśeṣa-vikalpa: conceptual thought (rnam par rtog pa) directed at particulars, differences, or distinctive features (khyad par). Listed among varieties of conceptualization in Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra literature.

khyad por ltos pa.gloss: involving a qualification; depending on a distinction

senses.gloss: involving a qualification; depending on a distinction
senses.context: Said of a statement or position that holds only with reference to some qualifying feature (khyad par) rather than absolutely. Per the English comparandum, it indicates that a qualification is implied or presupposed.

khyad bar la kun btags pa'i kun btags su.gloss: imputation of just the entity that is an imputation of attribute

senses.gloss: imputation of just the entity that is an imputation of attribute
senses.context: A technical designation for one type of superimposition (kun btags): the imputation of an entity or nature (ngo bo nyid) which is itself an instance of the imputation made with respect to an attribute or feature (khyad par la kun btags pa). It is paired with the corresponding imputation of a particular (bye brag).

Verbal phrase for causing something to become more distinguished or excellent, i.e., raising it to a higher or more eminent status. The element khyad here carries the sense of distinction or superiority found in related expressions of being 'especially exalted'.

Technical phrase for the joining of a qualified base (khyad gzhi) with the attribute or distinguishing feature (khyad chos) predicated of it. It names the operation of predication whereby a quality is ascribed to a subject.

A word or expression that designates the qualified base itself, as distinguished from a term expressing the attribute (khyad chos brjod pa'i sgra). The pairing marks the two sides of a predicative statement in linguistic analysis.

khyad gzhi'i gnad.gloss: the key point regarding the qualified base

senses.gloss: the key point regarding the qualified base
senses.context: Refers to the essential or crucial point concerning the substratum (khyad gzhi), the base to which an attribute is ascribed. The comparanda are tentative (marked as a provisional rendering) and support no more than 'qualified base(s)' as the referent.
Phrase for adopting a given entity as the qualified base with respect to which an attribute is then predicated. It marks the selection of the subject term in a predicative analysis.

In logic and definition-theory, the flaw (Skt. avyāpti) whereby a stated pervasion or entailment fails to cover all the instances it should, being too narrow or too limited. Also rendered as insufficient extension or under-inclusion, i.e., a definition that excludes some of what it ought to include.

The fault of an entailment or pervasion that is too extensive, i.e., that includes more than it should. It is the counterpart of the fault of too little pervasion (khyab chungs pa) and correlates with the state of being overly broad (khyab ches ba).
Skt. ativyāpti: said of a pervasion, entailment, or definition that extends too far, covering cases it should not cover. Contrasted with khyab chungs pa (too little pervasion, avyāpti).
Skt. vaiṣṇava, an adherent of the deity Viṣṇu (khyab 'jug), used in doxographical contexts for members of that non-Buddhist tradition.

The limits or scope within which a pervasion or entailment holds. Determining these boundaries is what distinguishes a correct pervasion from one that is too broad (khyab ches ba) or too narrow (khyab chungs pa).

A term of logic/debate concerning pervasion (khyab pa): the pervasion that obtains by way of the relation between the terms under consideration. Hopkins glosses it simply as "related pervasion"; the comparanda give no further detail on its technical application.
Rendered by Sanskrit aṅgana and praṃgaṇa, terms for the open court or yard of a building complex. Hopkins likewise gives "courtyard."

Corresponds to maṇḍapa (pavilion, open hall), vīthi (row, gallery, portico) and prakoṣṭhaka (inner apartment or enclosed court), i.e. the roofed or colonnaded portion adjoining a court. Hopkins gives "hall."
The equivalents geha and goha indicate the wider sense of a house or residence, the built structure of which the court and hall form parts.

khyi phag gi brtul zhugs.gloss: yogic discipline of dogs and pigs

senses.gloss: yogic discipline of dogs and pigs
senses.context: A named ascetic observance (brtul zhugs) modeled on the behavior of dogs and pigs, as glossed by Hopkins. The comparanda supply only the designation, not a description of its practices or evaluation.
In subtle-body anatomy, the name of the channel located in the western (i.e. one of the four directional) positions at the heart center, per Hopkins. No Sanskrit equivalent is given.
Literally "the poison of a mad dog," glossed by Hopkins as rabies. The comparanda identify only the disease, without further medical detail.
Compound of khyi (dog) and so (tooth), glossed simply as "dog's tooth." The available comparanda support only this literal anatomical sense.

khyim stong du.gloss: in an empty house, in an empty shed

senses.gloss: in an empty house, in an empty shed
senses.context: Renders Sanskrit śūnya-āgāra, an unoccupied dwelling or shed, here with the terminative particle du, i.e. "in/to an empty house." Glossed in the Conze materials as "empty shed," typically as a place of solitary resort.
Renders Sanskrit apuruṣa in the sense of lacking a man/husband; khyim thab means husband and med pa negates it. Said of a woman who has no husband.
Proper name: khyim bdag (householder, gṛhapati) qualifying the personal name dpal sbyin, Sanskrit Śrīdatta. Used as the designation of a particular lay householder.

khyim 'dris byed ldan zhing.gloss: intent on familiarity with families (of donors)

senses.gloss: intent on familiarity with families (of donors)
senses.context: Renders Sanskrit kula-saṃstava-saṃprayukta, "engaged in/associated with intimacy with families." Describes one—typically a renunciate—who cultivates close acquaintance with (faithful, donor) households.

see_also: khyim pa dang rab tu byung ba

senses.context: Renders Sanskrit gṛhi-bhūta, literally 'having become a householder', i.e. one who has taken up (or reverted to) household life as opposed to the renunciate state. Used both for the act of becoming a householder and, by extension, for a householder as such.

see_also: khyim pa dang rab tu byung ba

senses.context: Translates Sanskrit anagārika / anagārikā, 'without a home', designating one who has left household life; the abstract form is glossed 'homelessness'. It stands in direct contrast to the householder (khyim pa).

see_also: khyim pa dang rab tu byung ba

khyu mchog tu 'gyur ba.gloss: becoming a supreme bull; state of being the best of the herd

senses.gloss: becoming a supreme bull; state of being the best of the herd
senses.context: Corresponds to Sanskrit vṛṣabhitā, the condition or quality of being a bull-leader of the herd (khyu mchog). The image is applied figuratively to a chief or leader among people, whence the Conze-style rendering 'manliness'.

see_also: khyu mchog gi stabs su gshegs pa
khyu mchog gi mthu byung ba
khyu mchog gi gnas su dam 'cha' ba

senses.context: Personal name of a Tibetan scholar of roughly 1150–1200, identified in the comparanda as a disciple of Cha-pa Chö-kyi-seng-ge (phya pa chos kyi seng ge). Only the name-identification is supported by the material given.
Second-person pronoun khyed with the reflexive/emphatic rang and the plural marker tsho, addressing several persons politely. Corresponds to the plural of the honorific 'you'.

khyer 'khos.gloss: capacity to bear; ability to carry

senses.gloss: capacity to bear; ability to carry
senses.context: Formed on khyer/'khyer 'to carry, bear'; Hopkins glosses it as the ability or capacity to bear something, i.e. being up to carrying out or sustaining a task. Used of the strength or capability that makes bearing a load or responsibility possible.
Literally 'easy to carry', hence convenient, handy, portable. Hopkins gives the phrasal rendering 'convenient; simple'.

Passive-participial construction on khyer ba 'to carry', rendering Sanskrit uhyamāna (explained as preryamāṇa), 'being carried/driven along'. Used of something swept or borne along by an external force.

Hopkins supplies only the phrasal rendering 'manner'. The form is built on khyer ba 'to carry, take', suggesting the way in which something is carried or handled; no further specification is supported by the comparanda.

A technical formula of debate-manual logic (bsdus grwa), predicated of a subject: there is nothing that is it, i.e. its occurrence does not exist. Contrasted with khyod kyi yin pa yod pa, 'being it does exist'.

see_also: khyod kyi yin pa med pa yang yin blo'i yul du bya rung ba yang yin pa'i gzhi mthun par dmigs pa
khyod kyi yin pa yod pa
khyod kyi yin pa yod pa yang yin blo'i yul du bya rung ba yang yin pa'i gzhi mthun par dmigs pa

khyod ming dang brdas bzhag pa tsam yin.gloss: are only posited by names and terminology and are not established by way of their own character

senses.gloss: are only posited by names and terminology and are not established by way of their own character
senses.context: A stock predicate-phrase, applied for example to imputational natures, asserting that such phenomena exist merely as posited through names and conventional terminology and lack establishment from the side of their own character (rang gi mtshan nyid kyis ma grub pa). It is the negative counterpart of the formula describing things established by way of their own character and not merely posited by c

see_also: khyod tha snyad kyi dbang gis bzhag pa ma yin par rang gi mtshan nyid kyis grub pa'i dngos po

senses.context: Adverbial form built on khyon (extent, area, scope), conveying that something applies over the whole extent — hence 'thoroughly'. Hopkins gives the rendering only tentatively.
Proper name of a temple in the Yarlung valley said to have been built by Songtsen Gampo. Frequently appears in the fuller form khra 'brug lha khang, 'Tren-druk Temple'.
Full name of the temple in Yarlung attributed to the reign of Songtsen Gampo; lha khang, 'temple', is here appended to the place-name khra 'brug.

khra ma.gloss: a type of grain; quick-ripening ('sixty-day') barley

senses.gloss: a type of grain; quick-ripening ('sixty-day') barley
senses.context: Designates a variety of grain, specifically a fast-maturing barley said to ripen in about sixty days. Lokesh Chandra records the Sanskrit equivalent āyana for this entry.
Proper name of a Tibetan king, rendered by Hopkins as "King Ralpajen" (Ralpachen). The element khri is the royal title-prefix also seen in other Tibetan regnal names such as khri srong lde btsan.
Glossed by Hopkins as "enthronement year," i.e. the year in which a ruler ascends the throne (khri), used in dating reigns.

Proper name of the Tibetan emperor Tri-song-day-tsen, given by Hopkins as reigning 755-797. The name begins with the royal title-element khri, "throne," shared with other Tibetan regnal names; the spelling khri bsrong lde'u btsan is an orthographic variant.
Alternative orthography for the name of the Tibetan king Trisong Detsen, given by Hopkins as "King Trisong Deutsen." Compare the more common spelling khri srong lde btsan.

Administrative term glossed by Hopkins as "myriarch [governorship]," i.e. the district or office of a myriarch (a lord over a nominal ten thousand). The comparanda give no further detail on its scope or period.
A pair of ethical systems or codes of discipline, identified in the comparanda as those of sūtra and tantra. Formed from khrims (ethics, law, discipline) with gnyis 'two'.
Feminine agent noun built on khrus (washing, bathing), corresponding to Sanskrit rajakā, a woman of the washer/laundry occupation.
Rendered 'break-through' in the comparanda; a technical term of contemplative practice. No Sanskrit equivalent is supplied, so the analysis of the compound elements is not further specified here.

khrel dang ldan.gloss: endowed with a sense of shame/embarrassment

senses.gloss: endowed with a sense of shame/embarrassment
senses.context: Corresponds to Sanskrit hrī-yukta: possessing khrel, the sense of shame or embarrassment (in the sense of moral conscience). The construction khrel dang ldan (pa) marks endowment with that quality.
Corresponds to Sanskrit anapatrāpya / anapatrapa: the absence of khrel, i.e. lack of a sense of shame or embarrassment. It is the negative counterpart of khrel yod pa and khrel dang ldan.

khrel yod pa dang ngo tsha.gloss: sense of shame and sense of embarrassment

senses.gloss: sense of shame and sense of embarrassment
senses.context: A coordinate pair rendering Sanskrit hrī and apatrāpya, the two attitudes of self-respect and regard for others that restrain wrongdoing. Hopkins renders the pair variously as "embarassment and shame," "sense of embarassment and sense of shame," and, in the Perfection of Wisdom idiom, "sense of shame and dread of blame."

Formed with the possessive can, "one having anger," corresponding to Sanskrit krodhana; Hopkins glosses "belligerent; wrathful." Lokesh Chandra also records the equivalent kroṣṭu for this Tibetan form.
Renders Sanskrit krodhābhibhūti, the overpowering or suppression of anger. Hopkins gives "overwhlem [overwhelm] belligerence; overwhelm wrathfulness."

Hopkins glosses the phrase as to withstand, bear, forbear, endure or tolerate belligerence or wrath. The Sanskrit comparandum kṣayaḥ (glossed kṣamaḥ) kruddheḥ pairs the notions of the wearing away of anger and of patient endurance of it.

Name of a wrathful (khro bo) form associated with the uṣṇīṣa (gtsug tor) and the epithet cakravartin ('khor bsgyur), rendering Sanskrit krodhoṣṇīṣacakravartin. Hopkins offers the provisional rendering "Ulagriva-cakravarti."

khros ma nag mo.gloss: Fierce Black Goddess (name of a wrathful female deity)

senses.gloss: Fierce Black Goddess (name of a wrathful female deity)
senses.context: A proper name, rendered by Hopkins as "Fierce Black Goddess," formed from khros (wrathful, enraged), the feminine particle ma, and nag mo (black one). The comparanda identify only the name itself and give no further doctrinal or iconographic detail.
A lineage (brgyud) of preceptors or abbots (mkhan) characterized as old or ancient (rnying). The English gloss is marked as a provisional rendering ({PH}), and no Sanskrit comparandum is supplied.
Lokesh Chandra equates mkhan pa with the plant names karkoṭi and brahmamūli (the latter marked uncertain), so the term functions in botanical/medical contexts as the designation of a particular herb.

Corresponding to Sanskrit adhyāpaka, "teacher, one who instructs," and to Hopkins's provisional gloss "guide." In this use the word belongs with the mkhan/mkhan po family of terms for one who is expert or who instructs others.

Renders Sanskrit upādhyāya-kalpa, i.e. one comparable to or resembling an upādhyāya. Hopkins gives "like a preceptor/abbot/professor," the several English options reflecting the range of mkhan po itself.

Formed from nye (near, proximate) and rabs (generation, succession), designating those of a近 recent generation as opposed to earlier ones. The English rendering is marked as provisional ({PH}) and no Sanskrit equivalent is given.

mkha' khyab mkha' yi rdo rje can.gloss: one endowed with the space-vajra that pervades space

senses.gloss: one endowed with the space-vajra that pervades space
senses.context: An epithet describing a figure possessing the "space-vajra" (mkha' yi rdo rje) whose pervasion extends throughout space (mkha' khyab). The comparanda give only this descriptive rendering, without identifying the particular figure so titled.

A designation for embodied beings (lus can) whose extent is said to equal or be as infinite as space (mkha' mnyam), i.e. all sentient beings without exception. Used where the totality of beings is invoked, as in dedications and aspirations.
Astronomical/astrological name identified in the comparanda as the planet Mars, the term literally suggesting one that moves ('gro) up in ('steng) the sky (mkha').
Glossed in the comparanda as fireflies; the Tibetan literally suggests a light or appearance (snang ba) like ('dra) the sky (mkha'). No further contextual information is supplied by the sources.
Rendering Sanskrit *khecara-vidyādhara, a vidyādhara (rig 'dzin) who moves through the sky or space (mkha' spyod). Used of a tantric adept who has attained the accomplishment of traveling in the sky.

mkhas pa rnams kyi las rnam gsum po.gloss: the three(fold) activities of the wise

senses.gloss: the three(fold) activities of the wise
senses.context: A phrase from the Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra literature (Skt. budheṣu karma trividham) enumerating activity (las, karma) as threefold with respect to the learned or skilful. Occurs as a topical heading rather than as a technical term in its own right.

see_also: mkhas pa la 'byung ba'i dogs pa'i gnas

senses.context: A conditional clause (Skt. viduṣāṃ yoni-vicayāt) introducing what follows upon correct examination by the learned. The phrase presents a conclusion as established by the proper analysis of those who know.

see_also: mkhas pa rnams kyi las rnam gsum po
mkhas pa la 'byung ba'i dogs pa'i gnas

mkhas pa la 'byung ba'i dogs pa'i gnas.gloss: topic about which the learned have qualms

senses.gloss: topic about which the learned have qualms
senses.context: A point or locus (gnas) at which doubt or hesitation (dogs pa) arises even for scholars. Used to mark a difficult issue requiring clarification; no Sanskrit equivalent is attested in the comparanda.

see_also: mkhas pa rnams kyi las rnam gsum po

mkhas pa shes phyir 'jig rten.gloss: for the sake of knowing the world (?)

senses.gloss: for the sake of knowing the world (?)
senses.context: Rendering of Skt. loka-vidusya in Prajñāpāramitā materials (Conze's glossary); the construal is uncertain, and the Tibetan appears to take mkhas pa as knowing/being expert with respect to 'jig rten, the world. The gloss is offered tentatively by the comparanda themselves.

mkhas pa'i 'jug pa'i rnam bshad.gloss: Commentary on the Entry Gate of the Wise

senses.gloss: Commentary on the Entry Gate of the Wise
senses.context: Title of a treatise, a commentary (rnam bshad) on the mkhas pa'i 'jug pa (Entry Gate of the Wise), attributed to Śākya Chok-den (śā kya mchog ldan). Cited as a work title rather than as a lexical item.

Renders Sanskrit kauśalyālambana, an ālambana (object of observation) that serves as the focus of meditative attention for the sake of gaining skill (kauśalya). Used in presentations of the types of objects of observation cultivated in meditation.

mkhas pa'i rang bzhin can.gloss: having the nature of a wise person; intelligent

senses.gloss: having the nature of a wise person; intelligent
senses.context: Renders paṇḍitajātīya, describing one whose very type or nature is that of a learned, wise person (paṇḍita). Conze's materials give the simpler rendering "intelligent."
Renders kauśalya-yukta as attested in Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra materials: joined with, or possessed of, skill (kauśalya). Applied to persons qualified by learnedness or proficiency.
Renders kauśalya, which Conze's materials gloss simply as "skill." The Tibetan is formed as a verbal noun and so has the sense of proficiency itself.

senses.gloss: that in which one is to become skilled; topic of scholarship
senses.context: The gerundive form of the Tibetan can be taken as the object or topic with respect to which skill or scholarship is to be acquired.

Renders kauśalyālambana; a synonym in usage of mkhas pa'i dmigs pa. It designates the objects of observation taken as the focus of meditation in order to produce skill (kauśalya), i.e., objects that make one skillful.

A good quality (yon tan) consisting in, or arising from, the exalted knowing (mkhyen pa) of a buddha or other exalted being. Used in enumerations of the attributes of such knowledge; the comparanda specify only this general sense.

Rendering Sanskrit jānann eva, indicating that an action is performed even though the agent already knows the matter in question. In the Perfection of Wisdom context it is glossed 'although he knows the answer', as when a question is posed despite prior knowledge.
Corresponding also to saṃprajāna, i.e. acting with full, deliberate awareness rather than inadvertently.

mkhyen gsum gyi rnam pa.gloss: aspect of the three exalted knowers

senses.gloss: aspect of the three exalted knowers
senses.context: A technical enumeration item: the aspects (rnam pa) associated with the set of three exalted knowers (mkhyen gsum). The comparanda give only this identification without further specification of the three.

mkhyen gsum bsdus sgom gyi sbyor ba'i rn.gloss: aspect of the training in cultivating the three exalted knowers collectively

senses.gloss: aspect of the training in cultivating the three exalted knowers collectively
senses.context: Designates an aspect (rnam pa) of a training (sbyor ba) that consists in meditatively cultivating the three exalted knowers (mkhyen gsum) together as a combined set. The comparanda supply only this description.
A medical enumeration: the seven general indications or symptoms (spyi rtags bdun) by which a bile (mkhris pa) condition is identified. The comparanda give only the name of the set, not its members.
A medical term for a goiter or swelling (lba) classed as arising from bile (mkhris pa), i.e. a bile-type disorder of that kind. Attested here only through the English gloss 'bile goiter'.
Adjectival form describing something of firm, unyielding consistency. Equivalent in force to mkhregs pa.

Corresponds to Sanskrit drugdha and droha, i.e. spite or malicious intent directed at another. In this sense it appears in compounds such as 'khu ba'i bsam pa (thought of ill-will) and is negated in 'khu med.
Corresponds to Sanskrit spardhā, rivalry or competition, hence to contend with or set oneself against another, with the tone of scorn.
In some contexts glossed as a mistaken or perverse notion; note the equation 'khu ba'i bsam pa = log lta (wrong view), and the set of five such items in 'khu ba lnga sogs.

'khu ba lnga sogs.gloss: the five wrong ideas and so forth

senses.gloss: the five wrong ideas and so forth
senses.context: A set-phrase referring to a group of five items of 'khu ba — mistaken or malicious notions — together with further items of the same kind. The number and content of the five are not specified by the comparanda; see 'khu ba, where 'khu ba'i bsam pa is equated with log lta (wrong view).
A noun formed from 'khun, denoting a sigh or the act of sighing (also groaning of that sort); cf. the verbal 'khun par byed pa. The gloss is a paraphrastic rendering only.
Renders Sanskrit viśiṣṭa in the sense of what is distinguished or set above others. The phrase combines 'khod (being situated, established) with 'phags (exalted), i.e. exalted in one's standing.
Formed from 'khon (resentment, grudge, spite) with the possessive suffix can, hence 'one who has resentment', 'full of resentment'. Used of persons or attitudes characterized by grudge-bearing.

'khor gyi dkyil 'khor.gloss: circle of the retinue, assembled company

senses.gloss: circle of the retinue, assembled company
senses.context: Corresponds to Sanskrit parṣanmaṇḍala, the circle or assembly ('khor, retinue, attendants) surrounding a central figure. Also given for parṣatsaṃnipāta, the coming together or gathering of such an assembly.
Renders Sanskrit parijana: a person ('khor gyi skye bo) belonging to the entourage or attendants of another. Glossed as a being who is in the retinue.
Corresponds to Sanskrit parṣaddvīpa; gling (continent, island) qualified by 'khor in the sense of that which surrounds or forms the attendant circle of a central landmass.
Renders Sanskrit saṃsārābhyupagama, the acceptance or affirmation of saṃsāra. Used where a position holding cyclic existence to be the case is admitted or acknowledged.

'khor ba ji srid par.gloss: as long as cyclic existence lasts

senses.gloss: as long as cyclic existence lasts
senses.context: Corresponds to yāvat-saṃsāram, an adverbial expression of duration meaning 'for as long as there is cyclic existence'. Typically marks a commitment or activity extending throughout the whole span of saṃsāra.
Renders saṃsārātyāga, the fact of not abandoning or giving up cyclic existence. The Tibetan gtong ba med nyid marks the abstract quality of not relinquishing saṃsāra.

'khor ba bsten pa.gloss: partaking of cyclic existence; adhering to saṃsāra

senses.gloss: partaking of cyclic existence; adhering to saṃsāra
senses.context: Corresponds to saṃsāra-niṣevaṇa, resorting to, frequenting, or associating oneself with cyclic existence. bsten pa here carries the sense of attending upon or keeping company with what is indicated.

'khor ba thog ma dang tha ma med pa.gloss: cyclic existence without beginning or end

senses.gloss: cyclic existence without beginning or end
senses.context: Renders anavarāgra saṃsāra, saṃsāra characterized as having neither an initial nor a final limit. Used to describe the beginningless and endless character of the round of existence.

'khor ba dag tu yongs su bsngo.gloss: thoroughly dedicate to those in cyclic existence

senses.gloss: thoroughly dedicate to those in cyclic existence
senses.context: Renders Sanskrit saṃsāre pariṇāmanā, the act of turning over or dedicating (pariṇāmanā) toward saṃsāra, i.e., toward beings within cyclic existence. Attested in Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra materials as a form of dedication of merit.
Renders saṃsārānukūlatā, the abstract quality (-tā) of being in accord or conformity (anukūla) with saṃsāra. Attested in Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra materials.

'khor ba dang mya ngan las 'das.gloss: cyclic existence and nirvāṇa; saṃsāra and nirvāṇa

senses.gloss: cyclic existence and nirvāṇa; saṃsāra and nirvāṇa
senses.context: A paired expression rendering saṃsāra-nirvāṇa, naming the two together as a contrasting set. Attested in Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra materials.

'khor ba dang mya ngan las 'das pa la mi.gloss: not abiding in cyclic existence and nirvāṇa

senses.gloss: not abiding in cyclic existence and nirvāṇa
senses.context: Renders saṃsāra-nirvāṇāpratiṣṭhitā, the state of not being established or fixed (apratiṣṭhita) in either saṃsāra or nirvāṇa. Attested in Madhyāntavibhāga materials; compare the abstract form 'khor ba dang mya ngan las 'das pa la mi gnas pa nyid (apratiṣṭhita-saṃsāra-nirvāṇatva).

'khor ba dang mya ngan las 'das pa la mi.gloss: not abiding in cyclic existence and nirvāṇa

senses.gloss: not abiding in cyclic existence and nirvāṇa
senses.context: Renders apratiṣṭhita-saṃsāra-nirvāṇatva, the abstract quality (-tva) of not being established in either saṃsāra or nirvāṇa. Attested in Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra materials; compare the form without nyid, 'khor ba dang mya ngan las 'das pa la mi gnas pa.

'khor ba dang zhi ba ro gcig pa.gloss: the single taste of cyclic existence and peace

senses.gloss: the single taste of cyclic existence and peace
senses.context: Renders Sanskrit saṃsāra-śānty-eka-rasa, attested in Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra literature. It expresses that saṃsāra ('khor ba) and nirvāṇa/peace (zhi ba) are of one and the same taste, i.e. not ultimately differentiated.
Translates saṃsārāvacara. Used of beings who move about within the round of birth and death.

senses.gloss: belonging to saṃsāra, bound up with saṃsāra
senses.context: In Conze's renderings of saṃsārāvacara the term characterizes what operates on the plane of saṃsāra, e.g. factors 'which afflict on the plane of saṃsāra'.
Translates saṃsāra-gata, said of those who abide within the round of birth and death, i.e. who are subject to birth and death.
Translates saṃsārāvacara, like 'khor ba na rgyu ba; refers to activity carried on within the round of birth and death.

senses.gloss: belonging to saṃsāra, bound up with saṃsāra
senses.context: Conze renders saṃsārāvacara as 'bound up with samsara' or 'belonging to samsara', characterizing factors operative on the plane of saṃsāra.

'khor ba zad kyi bar du.gloss: until the exhaustion of cyclic existence

senses.gloss: until the exhaustion of cyclic existence
senses.context: Translates āsaṃsārāt, indicating a temporal extent reaching to the end of the round of birth and death; also rendered 'throughout the round of birth-and-death'.

Verbal phrase for completely giving up or forsaking saṃsāra, rendering Sanskrit saṃsāraṃ parityajeta. In the Madhyāntavibhāga context cited it appears with reference to one who, grown weary (khinna), would utterly abandon cyclic existence.
Nominal phrase corresponding to Sanskrit saṃsārāparityāga, the negation of forsaking saṃsāra. It names the state or quality of not giving up cyclic existence.
Renders Sanskrit saṃsāra-parijñāna, complete or exhaustive understanding of saṃsāra. The prefix yongs su corresponds to pari-, indicating knowledge that is full and all-round.

'khor ba len pa dang spong ba.gloss: assumption and abandonment of cyclic existence

senses.gloss: assumption and abandonment of cyclic existence
senses.context: Compound phrase rendering Sanskrit saṃsārādāna-tyāga, pairing the taking up (len pa, ādāna) of cyclic existence with its relinquishing (spong ba, tyāga).
Renders Sanskrit saṃsāra-cakra, the revolving round of saṃsāra pictured as a wheel. Also translated as the wheel of birth-and-death.
Renders Sanskrit saṃsāra-srota, the 'current' or 'flood' of birth-and-death. The image is of saṃsāra as an unbroken flow or continuum in which beings are carried along.

A favorable or elevated rebirth-condition that is nonetheless still contained within saṃsāra. The compound qualifies 'high status' (mngon mtho) as pertaining to cyclic existence rather than to liberation.
Renders saṃsāraṇa-dharmin, said of what has the nature or property of wandering about in birth-and-death. Used to characterize persons or phenomena that are still liable to transmigrate.
The defiled or contaminated (zag pa, āsrava) quality belonging to saṃsāra. It designates the taint that marks phenomena as pertaining to cyclic existence.

'khor ba'i zag pa dang bcas pa.gloss: together with a contaminated phenomenon of cyclic existence

senses.gloss: together with a contaminated phenomenon of cyclic existence
senses.context: Expanded form of 'khor ba'i zag pa, marking something as accompanied by a contaminated factor belonging to saṃsāra.

Verbal phrase corresponding to Sanskrit saṃsṛtya, an absolutive: 'after having circled/wandered about in saṃsāra'. Used of beings who have transmigrated through cyclic existence before some subsequent event.

'khor bar mngon mtho byed.gloss: cause high status within cyclic existence

senses.gloss: cause high status within cyclic existence
senses.context: Renders saṃsāre 'bhyudayāya, 'for the sake of elevation/prosperity in saṃsāra'. Denotes action or virtue whose result is attainment of a high, favourable state while still within cyclic existence, rather than liberation from it.
Corresponds to saṃsāra-gata, 'gone to / belonging to saṃsāra'. Said of persons, states or phenomena that are counted as part of cyclic existence.
Renders saṃsāre pariṇāmanā, the complete turning over (of merit) with reference to saṃsāra. Per Hopkins, the dedication is understood as being for the sake of those who dwell in cyclic existence.
Corresponds to saṃsāra-bhīta, 'afraid of saṃsāra'. Describes one who is terrified of cyclic existence and hence turns away from it.

A place-name; the comparanda identify it with Vārāṇasī, the city associated with the Buddha's first teaching. The Tibetan renders the name descriptively (lit. 'destroying the surrounding'), but only the identification as a proper name is supported here.

'khor mo 'jig gi yul du bdud.gloss: demons in the land of 'khor mo 'jig

senses.gloss: demons in the land of 'khor mo 'jig
senses.context: A phrase referring to demons (bdud) located in the country ('yul') called 'khor mo 'jig. The provided gloss renders it as the demons of the surrounding transient world, playing on the literal sense of the place-name; no further specification is supported.

'khor zhi ro gcig pa.gloss: one taste of cyclic existence and peace

senses.gloss: one taste of cyclic existence and peace
senses.context: Renders saṃsāra-śānty-eka-rasa: the state in which cyclic existence ('khor ba) and peace/nirvāṇa (zhi ba) are of a single taste, i.e. equal in nature. Here 'khor abbreviates 'khor ba, cyclic existence.
Being fond of companions or of one's circle of attendants. 'khor here has the sense of retinue/company rather than cyclic existence.

'khor lur byed par.gloss: giving weight to the assembly; preferring company

senses.gloss: giving weight to the assembly; preferring company
senses.context: Renders parṣad-guruka, said of one who values or prefers communal life, treating the assembly or retinue as important. The form 'khor lur byed par is the terminative/verbal phrase 'making (it) weighty', i.e. attaching importance to one's circle.

'khor lo rnam pa can gyi sems.gloss: mind having the aspect of a [divine] wheel/circle

senses.gloss: mind having the aspect of a [divine] wheel/circle
senses.context: A consciousness that appears in, or takes on, the form of a wheel ('khor lo) — glossed as a mind possessing the aspect of a [divine] circle. The comparanda give only this descriptive gloss, without further doctrinal specification.
Renders Sanskrit sahasrāracakra, a wheel ('khor lo) furnished with (dang ldan pa) a thousand spokes (rtsibs stong). Used in descriptions of such wheel-marks or wheel-emblems.
Renders Sanskrit cakraratna (cakra-ratana), the 'wheel jewel' — a wheel that is a precious article or treasure. Attested in Prajñāpāramitā-related (C) and Lokesh Chandra sources.

'khor lo la sogs pa rin po che sna bdun.gloss: the seven precious articles, the wheel and so forth

senses.gloss: the seven precious articles, the wheel and so forth
senses.context: Renders Sanskrit cakrādi-sapta-ratna, the set of seven precious things (rin po che sna bdun) of which the wheel ('khor lo) is listed first. Attested in the Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra (MSA).

'khor gsum gyis dag pa.gloss: pure with respect to the three spheres

senses.gloss: pure with respect to the three spheres
senses.context: Renders Sanskrit śuddha trimaṇḍalena, said of an action free of conceptualization of the three spheres ('khor gsum) — namely agent, action, and object. Attested in the Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra (MSA).

Renders Sanskrit trimaṇḍala-viśuddhatā, the abstract state of being pure with respect to the 'three spheres' — traditionally identified as agent, action, and object. Hopkins glosses it as devoidness of conceptualization of the three spheres, also rendered 'three-fold purity'.

'khor gsum rnam par dag pa.gloss: pure of the three spheres; three-fold purity

senses.gloss: pure of the three spheres; three-fold purity
senses.context: Renders Sanskrit trimaṇḍala-viśuddhi, purity with regard to the three spheres of agent, action, and object. Hopkins explains it as being devoid of conceptualization of these three; the Conze-based gloss is 'three-fold purity'.

'khor gsum yongs su dag pa.gloss: complete purity of the three spheres

senses.gloss: complete purity of the three spheres
senses.context: Renders Sanskrit trimaṇḍala-pariśuddhi (trimaṇḍalapariśuddha), where yongs su corresponds to the intensive prefix pari-, hence 'thoroughly/perfectly pure'. Hopkins glosses it as being thoroughly devoid of conceptualization of the three spheres — agent, action, and object — also rendered 'three-fold perfect purity'.
A term formed on 'khyags (freezing, ice); Hopkins gives only the provisional rendering 'ice-slip'. No Sanskrit equivalent is attested in the comparanda.
Continuative form (verb + shing) of 'khyams, 'to wander, roam'. It renders Sanskrit saṃdhāvya, a gerund, translated by Conze as 'after he has erred about', i.e. having wandered or strayed.

A paired expressive compound built on 'khyar; the only comparandum available is the English gloss 'crooked' (given as a provisional rendering). Suggests something that is bent, deviating or wavering rather than straight.

Glossed as 'ability to bear' or 'capacity to do so', i.e. the wherewithal or strength to carry/undertake something. The Sanskrit comparanda supply only transliterated forms of 'khyer and so add nothing semantically; the form khyer 'khos is an orthographic variant.
Honorific verbal compound of 'khrid with mdzad, glossed simply as 'lead'. Used where the leading or guiding is done by a respected agent.

Corresponds to Sanskrit vṛttatā, glossed 'elegant' and, in the Conze-style rendering, 'well-rounded'. Describes a quality of pleasing, rounded shapeliness; the fuller form 'khril bag chags pa carries the same sense.
Renders Sanskrit kṣubhyati, 'to be stirred up, agitated'. Used of the mind or a situation being thrown into turmoil.
By extension the same term is glossed 'become angry', 'get angry with', and 'fight', i.e. the agitation expressed as hostility or strife toward another.

Attested as the Tibetan rendering of Sanskrit anāsvādanatā, glossed 'no enjoyment; derive no enjoyment' — i.e. the state of not savoring or relishing something. The Tibetan wording (literally combining 'without disturbance' and 'without complete finishing') does not correspond transparently to the Sanskrit, so the equivalence is known only from the cited comparanda.
Renders akopanā, akṣobhaṇatā and nirupāyāsa, glossed as non-disturbance, non-agitation, undisturbed, immovability, imperturbability. Used of a mind or state that cannot be stirred or upset.
In the sense of akopanā the term is glossed 'non-anger; absence of anger', the negative counterpart of becoming angry or riled.
Corresponding to avikṣepa, glossed 'absence of distractions; non-distraction', i.e. the mind's not being scattered away from its object.

see_also: 'khrug pa med cing yongs su rdzogs pa med pa

senses.context: Renders kṣobhaṇa-citta, glossed 'mind of disturbance; disturbed/agitated mind'. Denotes a mental state that has been stirred up or upset.

see_also: 'khrug pa'i sems 'ga' tsam yang skyed par mi byed de

'khrug pa'i sems 'ga' tsam yang skyed pa.gloss: does not generate even the slightest mental disturbance

senses.gloss: does not generate even the slightest mental disturbance
senses.context: A phrase rendering cittotpādam api na kṣobhayati, glossed 'does not generate even any mental disturbance/agitation' and, in the C tradition, 'does not get angry even in his mind'. It describes one who remains wholly unagitated, not even producing an angry or disturbed thought.
Renders kṣubhyati, glossed 'become disturbed/agitated'. Used of a mind or person that is stirred up or thrown into turmoil.
In the C tradition the same verb is glossed 'get angry with', i.e. the agitation takes the specific form of anger toward someone.

see_also: 'khrug pa'i sems 'ga' tsam yang skyed par mi byed de

'khrul 'khor sbyar ba.gloss: put together a machine, fitted with a device

senses.gloss: put together a machine, fitted with a device
senses.context: Renders Sanskrit yantra-yukta, literally 'joined/fitted with a mechanical device.' Used of assembling or constructing a mechanism ('khrul 'khor).
In the Conze-based (C) material the compound designates a mechanical figure or puppet that can be made to move by pulling strings, i.e. a contrivance that seems to act on its own.

'khrul 'khor bsre ba brgya brgyad pa.gloss: Hundred and Eight Combined Yogic Exercises

senses.gloss: Hundred and Eight Combined Yogic Exercises
senses.context: A title designating a set of one hundred and eight blended or combined physical yogic exercises ('khrul 'khor). Here 'khrul 'khor has the sense of yogic exercise/physical training rather than machine.

'khrul rgyu can.gloss: having a cause of error, leading to error

senses.gloss: having a cause of error, leading to error
senses.context: Said of a consciousness or situation that possesses a cause of mistake ('khrul rgyu), and hence is liable to be erroneous. Also glossed simply as 'cause of error.'

see_also: 'khrul rgyu de ma thag rkyen la yod pa

'khrul rgyu rten la yod pa.gloss: having a cause of error in the basis

senses.gloss: having a cause of error in the basis
senses.context: One of the classifications of consciousnesses possessing a cause of mistake, here where the cause of error resides in the basis or support (rten) of the awareness.

'khrul rgyu de ma thag rkyen la yod pa.gloss: having a cause of error in the immediately preceding condition

senses.gloss: having a cause of error in the immediately preceding condition
senses.context: One of the classifications of consciousnesses possessing a cause of mistake, here where the cause of error resides in the immediately preceding condition (de ma thag rkyen).

'khrul rgyu gnas la yod pa.gloss: having a cause of error located in the abode (basis)

senses.gloss: having a cause of error located in the abode (basis)
senses.context: Said of a consciousness whose mistakenness arises from a defect situated in the abode or physical basis (gnas) of the awareness, rather than in the object or in other conditions. One of a set of classifications of causes of error ('khrul rgyu) according to where the erroneous factor is located.

see_also: 'khrul rgyu de ma thag rkyen la yod pa

'khrul rgyu yul la yod pa.gloss: having a cause of error located in the object

senses.gloss: having a cause of error located in the object
senses.context: Said of a consciousness whose mistakenness stems from a factor situated in the object (yul) apprehended, rather than in the sense-basis or in attendant conditions. One of the classifications of causes of error ('khrul rgyu) by location of the erroneous factor.

see_also: 'khrul rgyu de ma thag rkyen la yod pa

'khrul snang yod mkhan.gloss: that which is mistaken with respect to appearance

senses.gloss: that which is mistaken with respect to appearance
senses.context: An awareness in which the object appears erroneously, i.e., one that possesses mistaken appearance ('khrul snang), whatever its status may be with respect to what it ascertains.
Honorific form (mi mnga' = 'does not possess') used of an exalted being who is without mistake or error; rendered by Sanskrit aparyasta and askhalita, 'not overturned, not stumbling.'
Lacking mistake or error; corresponds to Sanskrit askhalita, 'not stumbling, unfaltering.'
In the sense of Sanskrit avyabhicārin, that which does not deviate or stray from what it should accord with, hence reliable or invariably concomitant.

Rendering Sanskrit bhrānti-mātra, the term restricts what is at issue to nothing more than error or mistakenness. It is used to say that something is merely erroneous — only a mistake and nothing beyond that.

'khrul pa'i rgyu.gloss: cause of error, cause of mistake

senses.gloss: cause of error, cause of mistake
senses.context: Corresponds to Sanskrit bhrānter nimittam, the causal factor giving rise to mistaken cognition. Compare the abbreviated form 'khrul rgyu with the same sense.

'khrul pa'i rgyu mtshan.gloss: cause of error, reason for mistake

senses.gloss: cause of error, reason for mistake
senses.context: Corresponds to Sanskrit bhrānti-nimitta; rgyu mtshan here renders nimitta as the occasioning cause or ground of mistaken apprehension. Synonymous in the comparanda with 'khrul pa'i rgyu.

Corresponds to Sanskrit bhrānteḥ saṃniśraya, that upon which error is supported or founded. Distinguished from the cause of error ('khrul pa'i rgyu) as the support rather than the producer of mistakenness.

'khrul pa'i mtshan nyid.gloss: character of mistake; definition of error

senses.gloss: character of mistake; definition of error
senses.context: Corresponds to Sanskrit bhrānti-lakṣaṇa; mtshan nyid renders lakṣaṇa either as the defining characteristic of error or as that which has a mistaken character.
Renders Sanskrit mātsarya and kṛpaṇa, glossed by Hopkins as "mean," "meanness," "niggardly." Used of the mental attitude of withholding, the opposite of generosity.
Also corresponds to Sanskrit gṛddha, i.e. greedily attached or grasping. This sense shades into the miserly grasping at possessions covered by mātsarya.
Hopkins additionally records "jealousy" for this term, reflecting the affective side of mātsarya, the inability to bear another's gain or share.
Equivalent to Sanskrit krodha; Hopkins glosses it as "belligerence." Denotes the hostile, wrathful state of mind, or the act of becoming angry.
A phonetic transcription of a Sanskrit architectural term; Hopkins gives the paraphrase "spire." The comparanda support only this architectural sense of the topmost pointed structure of an edifice.
Interrogative expression of time, per Hopkins "when?", "at what time?". Formed from the interrogative base ga with the temporal element dus.
Hopkins also records the locative interrogative sense "where?" for this form, parallel to other ga- interrogatives.
Transcription of the Sanskrit name Rūpati; according to Hopkins, the name of a minor king who fought on the side of (or with) the Kauravas. Attested only as a personal name.
Interrogative formed on the question-stem ga with the locative/terminative particle par, glossed by Hopkins as "where?". Parallel in form to other ga- interrogatives such as ga na and ga nas.
Rendering Sanskrit karpūra, the aromatic substance camphor. Here ga pur is a phonetic transcription rather than an interrogative form, despite its resemblance to ga par.
Interrogative of quantity or measure built on the question-stem ga, glossed by Hopkins as "how many?; how much?". Equivalent in sense to ga tshod.
Interrogative of quantity or amount, glossed by Hopkins as "how many?; how much?". A variant equivalent in sense to ga tshad.

Corresponds to Sanskrit akutobhaya(ā); Hopkins identifies it as the title Akutobhayā, a commentary on Nāgārjuna's Treatise on the Middle (Toh. 3829). The Tibetan renders the sense "having no fear from any quarter," i.e. fearless of anything.

gang 'dul sprul sku.gloss: Emanation Body [appearing as] whatever tames [whoever needs taming]
