senses.gloss: in order not to exhaust virtue
senses.context: Renders Sanskrit kuśalasyākṣayāya, 'for the non-extinction of virtue.' A purpose clause: an action is done so that accumulated virtue is not used up or exhausted.
Corresponds to Sanskrit śubha-daurbalya, feebleness or weakness of virtue. Indicates virtue that is deficient in strength.

dge ba yang dag len du 'jug.gloss: cause (someone) to take up pure virtue

senses.gloss: cause (someone) to take up pure virtue
senses.context: Rendered in the Sanskrit comparanda as śubhe samādāpayate, 'causes to assume (what is) pure/virtuous'. The construction is causative: one induces another to take on and undertake virtue (dge ba, śubha) properly and completely (yang dag).

dge ba yid la byed.gloss: taking virtue to mind; mental attention to virtue

senses.gloss: taking virtue to mind; mental attention to virtue
senses.context: Corresponds to śubha-manaskāra, the act of directing the mind toward, or bringing to mind, what is virtuous (dge ba, śubha). Hopkins also renders it 'contemplating virtue', i.e. holding virtue as the object of mental engagement.

dge ba rab tu sbyor ba.gloss: thoroughly engaging in virtue; intense application to virtue

senses.gloss: thoroughly engaging in virtue; intense application to virtue
senses.context: Equivalent to kuśala-prayoga, the application or engagement (sbyor ba, prayoga) in what is virtuous (dge ba, kuśala), with rab tu conveying the thoroughness or intensity of the engagement.

Corresponds to kuśala-pratiṣṭhāpana, causing another to be set or firmly placed ('god pa, pratiṣṭhāpana) in virtue (dge ba, kuśala). The idiom is transitive, describing what is done for others rather than one's own practice.

Reflects kuśala-pravṛtti-icchā, the desire ('dod pa, icchā) to enter upon or engage in ('jug pa, pravṛtti) what is virtuous (dge ba, kuśala). It names the aspiration preceding actual virtuous activity.

A causal phrase (Skt. kuśale pravartanāt) giving the reason for something as the fact of entering into or engaging in what is virtuous. Depending on context the ablative may also be rendered purposively, 'in order to engage in virtue.'

dge ba la sbyor ba.gloss: training in virtue; applying oneself to virtue

senses.gloss: training in virtue; applying oneself to virtue
senses.context: Renders Skt. kuśale niyojanāt, the joining or harnessing of oneself (or of others) to what is virtuous. Used of endeavor or application directed toward virtuous activity.
Negative counterpart of entering into virtue (Skt. kuśale 'prayuktāḥ), said of persons who have not applied themselves to or entered upon what is virtuous.

dge ba la gzhol ba.gloss: tending toward virtue; inclined to virtue

senses.gloss: tending toward virtue; inclined to virtue
senses.context: Renders Skt. kuśala-nata, 'bent toward the virtuous.' The Tibetan gzhol ba conveys sloping, flowing, or inclining, hence a natural tendency or gravitation toward virtue.
Renders Skt. kuśalācaya / śubhācaya, the heaping up or accumulation of what is virtuous or auspicious. Refers to virtue that has been amassed rather than to a single virtuous act.

Descriptive phrase rendering Sanskrit śubhācaya-prapūrṇa, said of one who is completely filled or replete (rab gang) with the accumulation (bsags pa) of virtue or goodness (dge ba, śubha). Attested in the Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra literature as a qualifier of an accumulation of merit.

Renders śubhābhirāmatā: the state of taking manifest pleasure or delight (mngon par dga', abhirāma) in virtue or goodness (dge ba, śubha). The Tibetan phrase is a split construction in which the verbal element governs the preceding term for virtue.

Equivalent to kalyāṇa-mitratā, literally the condition of being a good or beautiful friend; used for the virtuous companion who acts as a spiritual guide. The Sanskrit abstract suffix suggests it may also denote the quality or status of such friendship.
Renders kuśala-dharma-prādhānya, the predominance or principal status (gtso bo, prādhānya) among virtuous qualities, practices, or phenomena (dge ba'i chos, kuśala-dharma).

dge ba'i chos sgom pa la bar chad med pa.gloss: uninterrupted effort at meditating on virtuous qualities

senses.gloss: uninterrupted effort at meditating on virtuous qualities
senses.context: Renders kuśala-bhāvanā-nirantarābhiyoga: sustained application or effort (brtson pa, abhiyoga) that is without interruption (bar chad med par, nirantara) in the meditative cultivation (sgom pa, bhāvanā) of virtuous qualities or practices (dge ba'i chos, kuśala-dharma).

dge ba'i chos can.gloss: having virtuous qualities; virtuous in character

senses.gloss: having virtuous qualities; virtuous in character
senses.context: Possessive form (can) built on dge ba'i chos, rendering Sanskrit kalyāṇa-dharmin / kalyāṇadharma / śubhadharmaka. Describes a person or being who possesses the attribute of virtue, i.e. one whose nature or character is good and lovely.

Corresponds to Sanskrit kuśala-dharma-lābha, the obtaining or acquisition of virtuous qualities (dge ba'i chos, kuśala-dharma). Used of one who has come into possession of virtuous practices or phenomena.

Renders kuśala-dharma-saṃvardhana, the fostering or spreading abroad of virtuous qualities, practices, or phenomena. The verb spel ba indicates an agent's activity of causing such virtues to grow and multiply.

Corresponds to kuśala-dharma-vṛddhi-gamana, literally the 'going to increase' of virtuous qualities. The construction 'phel bar 'gyur ba presents the growth of virtuous qualities, practices, or phenomena as something that occurs or comes about.

Renders kuśala-dharmābhivṛddhi, the augmenting or intensified growth of virtuous qualities. The form byed pa marks the causative aspect: bringing about the increase of virtuous qualities, practices, or phenomena.

Rendering Sanskrit kuśaladharmābhyāsa, the term denotes having become habituated, through repeated familiarization, to virtuous phenomena (dge ba'i chos). The verbal element goms par byas pa indicates the acquired familiarity or practiced habit itself, not merely a single act of virtue.

Corresponding to Sanskrit kuśala-dharma-yojana, the expression indicates application or engagement (sbyor ba) directed toward virtuous phenomena. It emphasizes active effort in, or joining oneself to, virtuous qualities and practices.

Rendering Sanskrit kuśala-dharmābhāsa, the phrase indicates that something appears, or shines forth, as virtuous phenomena. The element snang ba corresponds to ābhāsa, the mode of appearance or semblance.

A phrase-level rendering designating sleep (gnyid) that is qualified as virtuous, i.e., of a virtuous rather than nonvirtuous or neutral character. The comparanda supply only this literal English gloss, with no Sanskrit equivalent.

dge ba'i me tog rgyas shing gsal ba.gloss: broad and bright flower of virtue

senses.gloss: broad and bright flower of virtue
senses.context: A descriptive phrase in which virtue (dge ba) is figured as a flower that is full-blown (rgyas pa) and radiant (gsal ba). Lokesh Chandra gives Sanskrit śubha-puṣpita-śuddhi, and Conze's rendering 'sweetly blooming purity' reflects the elements śubha (virtue, beauty), puṣpita (blossomed), and śuddhi (purity, brightness).

dge ba'i rtsa ba kun tu chad pa.gloss: one whose roots of virtue are thoroughly cut off

senses.gloss: one whose roots of virtue are thoroughly cut off
senses.context: Renders Sanskrit samucchinna-kuśala-mūla, describing a state (or person) in which the roots of virtue — the wholesome bases from which good qualities grow — have been completely severed or annihilated. The force of kun tu (samud-/sam-) is 'thoroughly, entirely', indicating total rather than partial destruction.

Renders kuśala-mūla-audāryatva, the abstract quality (-tva, nyid) of the roots of virtue being extensive, magnificent, or vast. Used of practitioners whose accumulated wholesome bases are of great scope.

Renders kuśala-mūla-samucchedana, the act of severing or cutting the roots of virtue, i.e. destroying the wholesome bases from which virtuous qualities arise. The nominal form names the process or agency of severing, as distinct from the resulting state.
Renders kuśala-mūla-daurbalya, the feebleness or frailty of one's roots of virtue. Describes wholesome bases that are present but insufficiently strong.

dge ba'i rtsa ba dpag tu med pa'i gnas.gloss: basis/source of immeasurable roots of virtue

senses.gloss: basis/source of immeasurable roots of virtue
senses.context: Renders aprameya-kuśala-mūla-āśraya, a support or foundation (gnas, āśraya) from which roots of virtue beyond measure arise. The qualifier aprameya (dpag tu med pa) marks the roots of virtue as incalculable in extent.

dge ba'i rtsa ba dman pa.gloss: inferior roots of virtue, low/lesser roots of virtue

senses.gloss: inferior roots of virtue, low/lesser roots of virtue
senses.context: Describes a person's stock of virtuous roots as being weak, small, or of inferior quality (Sanskrit hīna-kuśala-mūla). Used to characterize beings whose accumulated virtue is insufficient or of a lower order.
Roots of virtue that have not yet been fully matured or brought to fruition (Sanskrit aparipakva-kuśala-mūla). The negation of the state in which virtuous roots have reached full ripening.
Roots of virtue that have been completely matured or brought to fruition (Sanskrit paripakva-kuśala-mūla). Also rendered as a statement, 'the roots of virtue are mature.'

dge ba'i rtsa ba yongs su smin par byed.gloss: thoroughly ripening the roots of virtue

senses.gloss: thoroughly ripening the roots of virtue
senses.context: The act or process of bringing roots of virtue to full maturity (Sanskrit paripācanā kuśale). The active, causative counterpart of the state of virtuous roots being thoroughly ripened.
Roots of virtue that have been amassed or built up (Sanskrit upacita-kuśala-mūla); the corresponding nominal form kuśala-mūlopacaya denotes the accumulation itself.

A good quality (guṇa) that is virtuous or auspicious in nature, rendered in the Sanskrit comparanda by guṇa and śubha. Used of the excellences that accrue to or characterize a virtuous person or practice.
Corresponds to śubha-karma-kārin, 'one who performs virtuous (śubha) deeds'. Describes the agent or the activity of engaging in virtuous karma.

Agricultural metaphor rendering kuśala-sasya / kuśala-mūla-sasya, the 'crop' or 'harvest' grown from virtue or from roots of virtue (kuśala-mūla). The image treats accumulated virtue as a ripening yield.

dge ba'i lo tog skyes pa 'joms pa.gloss: destroying the harvest of virtue that has been produced

senses.gloss: destroying the harvest of virtue that has been produced
senses.context: Renders utpanna-kuśala-mūla-sasya-dhvaṃsana, the ruining (dhvaṃsana) of a crop of roots of virtue that has already arisen (utpanna). Extends the agricultural metaphor: virtue already grown can still be laid waste.

dge ba'i lo tog rgyu mtshan.gloss: cause/sign of the harvest of virtue

senses.gloss: cause/sign of the harvest of virtue
senses.context: Corresponds to śubha-sasya-nimittatva, the state of being the sign or occasioning cause (nimitta) of the crop of virtue (śubha-sasya). Glossed by Hopkins as 'signs of harvest of virtue'.

klag par bya ba.gloss: to be written, to be copied out

senses.gloss: to be written, to be copied out
senses.context: Future/gerundive verbal form corresponding to Sanskrit likhati, glossed 'write; copy out' in Conze's materials; hence 'that which is to be written down' or 'should be copied out'. Typically used of setting a text down in writing.

senses.gloss: to be read, to be recited
senses.context: As the future form of klag pa (cf. klog pa), the phrase can also mark what is to be read or recited aloud. The comparanda here support only the writing/copying sense explicitly, so this reading rests on the verbal base.

klan ka 'jug rung.gloss: suitable for the assessment of censure; open to objection

senses.gloss: suitable for the assessment of censure; open to objection
senses.context: Said of a position, statement, or thesis that provides valid grounds for censure (klan ka) to be applied to it. Hopkins glosses 'suitable for the assessment of censure', i.e. fault-finding or objection can legitimately be brought to bear.

klan ka yongs su spang bar bya ba'i phyi.gloss: in order to thoroughly overcome objections

senses.gloss: in order to thoroughly overcome objections
senses.context: Rendering Sanskrit codyasya parihāra-arthaṃ: a purpose clause stating that something is said or done so as to dispel or completely set aside censure/objection (klan ka, codya). Used of explanations framed to forestall criticism.

klan ka'i skabs mchis pa.gloss: provides an occasion for censure; leaves room for fault-finding

senses.gloss: provides an occasion for censure; leaves room for fault-finding
senses.context: Said of a statement or position that gives an opening (skabs) for objection or fault-finding to be raised against it. Hopkins glosses 'provides an opportunity for assessment of censure; provides an opportunity for finding fault'.

klan ka'i rtsod pa.gloss: critical dispute; debate by way of objection

senses.gloss: critical dispute; debate by way of objection
senses.context: A dispute (rtsod pa) conducted through censure or objection (klan ka), i.e. contentious argument aimed at finding fault with an opponent's position.
Rendered in Sanskrit as nāgendra-rutā, the cry or roar (sgra) of the lord/king of nāgas. Used as an image of a powerful, resounding sound.

klu'i rtsa she rab.gloss: Nāgārjuna's Fundamental Treatise on the Middle Way, Called "Wisdom"

senses.gloss: Nāgārjuna's Fundamental Treatise on the Middle Way, Called "Wisdom"
senses.context: An abbreviated Tibetan title for Nāgārjuna's (klu sgrub) root text of the Middle Way, known by the short name "Wisdom" (she rab). The element klu'i marks the authorship by Nāgārjuna.

klu'i rtsa she rab byed.gloss: chapter of Nāgārjuna's Fundamental Treatise on the Middle Way, Called "Wisdom"

senses.gloss: chapter of Nāgārjuna's Fundamental Treatise on the Middle Way, Called "Wisdom"
senses.context: A citation form used in referring to a particular chapter (byed) of Nāgārjuna's root Madhyamaka text known as "Wisdom." Ordinarily followed by the chapter number.

klog tu gzhug par.gloss: cause to read out, have recited

senses.gloss: cause to read out, have recited
senses.context: Corresponds to Sanskrit vācayanti, the causative of reading/reciting aloud; in Perfection of Wisdom contexts it is glossed as preaching or speaking, i.e. causing a text to be recited or proclaimed to others.
A text or system setting out how to read and pronounce (klog) a scripture or language. Formed from klog (reading) plus thabs (method, means).
Corresponds to Sanskrit durlabha, 'difficult to obtain'. Used of what occurs seldom or is hard to come by; also nominally as 'rarity'.
By extension from scarcity, what is rare is valued as precious; compare the element dkon in dkon mchog ('rare and supreme', i.e. jewel).
Renders Sanskrit madhya, the central part or midpoint of something.
Renders tala, as in gaganatala, the expanse or surface of the sky.
Renders maṇḍala and maṇḍa; in this value it is the base of the compound dkyil 'khor and related ritual terms.

dkyil 'khor gyi khyams na.gloss: in the circular hall (with peaked roof)

senses.gloss: in the circular hall (with peaked roof)
senses.context: Locative form of a term rendering Sanskrit maṇḍala-māḍa, glossed as a circular hall with a peaked roof. It designates the round pavilion or hall in which an assembly or rite takes place.

dkyil 'khor gyi cho ga.gloss: maṇḍala rite, ritual of the maṇḍala

senses.gloss: maṇḍala rite, ritual of the maṇḍala
senses.context: Renders Sanskrit maṇḍalavidhi, the prescribed procedure or ritual manual for constructing and employing a maṇḍala.
An honorific designation for a maṇḍala held to be foremost among maṇḍalas.

Glossed as "hidden," but in a sense distinct from lkog gyur: it refers to the manner in which aspects are produced rather than to what is hidden from ordinary perception. The comparanda give no further specification of usage.

Rendered by Sanskrit kaṇṭha, gala (throat) and kandharā (neck), and glossed in English as "throat." The anatomical region of the throat/neck; the more specific identification as "adam's apple" is offered only tentatively in the comparanda.
Glossed in English simply as "astringent," i.e. the astringent quality or flavor.
Corresponds to Sanskrit sthūṇa (post, pillar) and stamba (clump, tuft, stalk). The comparanda supply only these equivalents, without indication of context.

Corresponds to Sanskrit eka-kṣaṇa-avabodha, an understanding or realization (rtogs pa) occurring in a single moment (skad cig gcig). Paired in the comparanda with the related term for single instantaneous full understanding.

see_also: skad cig gcig mngon rdzogs byang chub

senses.context: Corresponds to Sanskrit eka-kṣaṇa-abhisaṃbodha, a complete, manifest awakening or full understanding (mngon rdzogs byang chub) accomplished in one single moment (skad cig gcig). Distinguished in the comparanda from the simple single-instantaneous understanding (skad cig gcig gi rtogs pa).

see_also: skad cig gcig gi rtogs pa

senses.context: Verbal phrase built on skyo ba with 'gyur ba, expressing the onset of weariness, fatigue, or discouragement; the Sanskrit khedam āpadyate is glossed 'to feel fatigue'.

senses.gloss: become disenchanted, turn away in weariness
senses.context: Rendering nirvidyante, the sense is that of growing weary of and turning away from something, i.e. becoming disenchanted with it.

Instrumental phrase corresponding to nirvit-saṃjñin, 'having the perception of disenchantment', rendered by Hopkins as 'with disgust'. The Sanskrit gloss connects it to understanding phenomena and nirvāṇa as illusion-like, so the weariness is a discernment-based turning away rather than mere emotional revulsion.
Active verbal form of skyo ba, used for coming to feel discouragement or weariness with respect to something.
In some contexts the form expresses being averse to or turned away from an object.

skyo bar byed pa.gloss: develop weariness toward; develop disregard for

senses.gloss: develop weariness toward; develop disregard for
senses.context: Active form of skyo ba corresponding to saṃvegam āpadyate, the arising of weariness or disregard with respect to something.
Per the Conze-based comparandum, the phrase may be rendered 'it is a source of anxiety', i.e. it produces the disquiet that accompanies weariness with an object.
Conditional form of skyo bar byed pa (saṃvegam āpadyate), 'if/when one has become weary' or disregarding toward something; in Conze's rendering, 'it is a source of anxiety'.

skrag pa'i gzhi'i gnas ma yin pa nyid.gloss: not being a basis that is a ground of fear

senses.gloss: not being a basis that is a ground of fear
senses.context: Abstract noun (-nyid, Skt. -tva) formed on 'a place/state that is not a foundation of fear' (atrāsa-pada-sthānatva). It characterizes something as affording no ground or occasion for fear, fright, or dread.
Instrumental phrase rendering trasta-manasā, 'with a mind that is terrified'. It describes the manner in which one acts or reacts, i.e. trembling or alarmed in mind.

Corresponds to saṃjñin, 'one who has a notion/perception (of something)', here specified as a notion of fright. The instrumental indicates that the ensuing state or action arises from apprehending an object as fearful.

skrag par bya.gloss: to be feared; should be frightened

senses.gloss: to be feared; should be frightened
senses.context: Future/gerundive verbal form answering to uttrastavya and trāsya, expressing that fear or dread is to be felt (or is warranted) with respect to something.

skrag par bya ba.gloss: that which is to be feared; object of fear

senses.gloss: that which is to be feared; object of fear
senses.context: Nominalized gerundive (trasitavya) used for what warrants dread; the same Tibetan also renders uttrāsa, 'fright, terror' itself.
In the sense of uttrāsa, the phrase names the state of fear or dread rather than its object; context determines whether the objective (what is to be feared) or the affective (fear) reading applies.
In the tantric anatomy of subtle channels, the term renders Sanskrit lalanā, the channel located on the left side. Hopkins accordingly glosses it as the 'left channel'.
As a verbal form related to brkyang / brkyang ba ('extend, stretch'), it can carry the sense 'extended'. Hopkins records 'extend' alongside the channel meaning.
Renders Sanskrit kaṣāya (also spelled kasāya, kasava) as a quality of taste; Hopkins gives 'astringent'. Conze's material also allows the rendering 'bitter' for the same Sanskrit.
The equivalents ghana and sāndra given by Lokesh Chandra point to a sense of thickness or density, i.e. a concentrated astringent brew rather than a taste-quality alone.
Corresponds to Sanskrit pūraṇa and bharita, terms of filling or being filled. Hopkins gives 'fill' as the primary sense.
By extension of the sense of filling, the term means to bring something to completion or to fulfil it, as Hopkins' glosses 'fulfill; complete' indicate.
Renders forms of Sanskrit śuṣ (śuṣka, śuṣyanti, śoṣa, śoṣayāmi, śoṣita) and upaśuṣyati. It functions within the paradigm bskam / skam / bskams / skams.
Used of what dries out and shrinks; Hopkins gives 'wither', and Conze's material yields 'shrivel up' for upaśuṣyati.
Renders Sanskrit uttama-kalpa, i.e. a kalpa or eon qualified as highest or supreme. Hopkins gives 'supreme eon'.

A grammatical designation for the imperative — the verbal form or expression that urges, commands, or exhorts. Formed from bskul (to urge, incite, exhort) plus tshig (word, expression), i.e. a "word of urging."

bskor mgo.gloss: computational sequence; head of a cycle

senses.gloss: computational sequence; head of a cycle
senses.context: Glossed as a computational sequence, i.e. the ordered series in which a round of calculation proceeds. The elements bskor (revolution, cycle, round) and mgo (head, beginning) suggest the starting-point or heading of such a round.

Continuative form (byas nas, "having done") of bskor ba: having gone around, circled, or surrounded something, as in circumambulating an object of veneration. Corresponds to Sanskrit vartitva in the sense of having turned or revolved.
Used of turning or setting something in motion; the Sanskrit vartitva is rendered "having turned."
A liquid preparation produced by boiling (bskol) ingredients, thang designating the resulting broth or infusion. Corresponds to Sanskrit kvātha, a decoction.
Literally "broth of what has been boiled"; a preparation obtained by boiling ingredients down into a liquid. Corresponds to Sanskrit kaṣāya, a decoction or astringent brew.

Recorded by Hopkins only as a provisional gloss, "clay-floor," i.e. a floor of packed earth or clay. No Sanskrit equivalent is attested in the comparanda, so the term's range beyond this rendering cannot be determined.

bskyab par bya ba'i sems can yal bar bor.gloss: neglecting sentient beings who are to be protected

senses.gloss: neglecting sentient beings who are to be protected
senses.context: Renders Sanskrit trātavya-sattvopekṣā (MSA): indifference toward, or abandonment of, the very beings one is obliged to protect. The phrase names a fault — leaving aside (yal bar bor) those sentient beings (sems can) who are objects of protection (bskyab par bya ba).
Given by Hopkins as a provisional gloss for both the act of repeating and the quality of being repeated. Formed on bskyar, "again, repeat."
A verbal phrase pairing bskyed (generate, produce, engender) with yongs su bsngo ba (thoroughly dedicate). Hopkins offers "generate/produce/engender and thoroughly dedicate" as equivalent renderings.
Corresponds to Sanskrit avaropaṇatā, glossed by Conze as "planting," i.e. the sowing or implanting of what is then dedicated. On this reading the generating is understood as a planting.

bskyed dang rdzogs pa zung 'jug.gloss: union of the generation and completion stages

senses.gloss: union of the generation and completion stages
senses.context: Provisional gloss in Hopkins for the joining (zung 'jug) of bskyed (generation) and rdzogs pa (completion), the two stages being taken together as a unity. No Sanskrit equivalent is supplied in the comparanda.
Verbal form of bskyed pa in the continuative/connective construction (-par byed de), corresponding to Sanskrit vardhayati. Conveys causing something to increase, grow, or become strengthened.
Agentive nominal form of bskyed pa, rendering Sanskrit janetrī, 'genetrix, begettor, creator.' Designates that which produces or gives rise to something.
Used verbally in the sense of engendering or bringing into existence.
Honorific agentive form (mdzad pa) of bskyed pa, corresponding to Sanskrit janaka. Refers to the agent that engenders or brings something into being.
Conditional form of bskyod pa, 'to move, stir, shake.' The comparandum veṣṭate (adhimātram), glossed 'is (all) twisted,' suggests a context of extreme writhing or contortion.

Polite/humble verbal form of bskyod pa corresponding to Sanskrit uccālayati, 'to move up, lift away'; Hopkins glosses the attested usage as 'free oneself from,' i.e., shifting or removing oneself from something.

Rendering Sanskrit dhātu-kauśalya, this names expertise regarding the khams — the constituents or elements — i.e. proficiency in discerning them. Where khams is enumerated as the eighteen constituents, such skill concerns that set.

khams gsum gyi sa.gloss: the levels of the three realms

senses.gloss: the levels of the three realms
senses.context: A phrase-level rendering: the sa (levels, grounds, stages) belonging to the three khams or realms. It designates the graded levels comprised within the threefold division of existence, including its higher levels.
Corresponds to Sanskrit sarva-traidhātuka-adhipati, 'sovereign of all that belongs to the three realms.' It is attested as the name of a Buddha.
A locative phrase built on traidhātuka, the triple world, i.e. that which is in or belongs to the three realms. Used to locate something within the threefold division of existence.

khams gsum 'dus byas.gloss: compounded phenomena of the three realms

senses.gloss: compounded phenomena of the three realms
senses.context: Rendering traidhātuka-ātma-saṃskāra: the conditioned, compounded ('dus byas) factors that constitute or belong to the three realms. The expression pairs the threefold division of existence with the composite phenomena occurring within it.

khams gsum pa po.gloss: belonging to the three realms; of the triple world

senses.gloss: belonging to the three realms; of the triple world
senses.context: Rendering Sanskrit traidhātuka, formed from khams gsum ("three realms/triple world") with the possessive/agentive suffix -pa po. Used of that which is included in or pertains to the triple world.
In some attestations the term is glossed simply as "the triple world" itself, i.e. the whole of the three realms taken together.

khams gsum pa'i nyon mongs pa spong ba.gloss: abandoning the afflictions of the three realms

senses.gloss: abandoning the afflictions of the three realms
senses.context: Rendering tridhātu-kleśa-prahāṇa: the relinquishing (spong ba) of the afflictive emotions (nyon mongs pa) that belong to the three realms (khams gsum). The compound names a soteriological accomplishment defined by the scope of the afflictions eliminated.

khams gsum ma lus pa las.gloss: from the entirety of the three realms

senses.gloss: from the entirety of the three realms
senses.context: Corresponds to traidhātukānta, where khams gsum ma lus pa ("the three realms without remainder") is taken with the ablative las. It indicates the full extent of the triple world, with nothing of it left out.
Rendering traidhātuka-bandhana-gata: having come to be fettered (bcings par gyur pa) by the bonds of the triple world. Comparanda also give the more vivid "imprisoned in the triple world."

khams gsum sa dgu.gloss: the three realms and nine levels

senses.gloss: the three realms and nine levels
senses.context: An enumerative compound pairing khams gsum, the three realms, with sa dgu, the nine levels or grounds into which they are subdivided. The comparanda supply only this enumeration, without further specification of the nine.

A listed set of three faults, corresponding to Sanskrit pratigha-upekṣā-māna: hostility or anger (khong khro), neglecting or casting aside/indifference (yal bar 'dor), and pride (nga rgyal). The compound appears as an enumeration rather than a single technical term.
Negation of khong khro ba, i.e., free from hostility or aversion; used both attributively (not angry, not hostile) and as a noun (non-anger).

Rendering Sanskrit apratihata in Conze's usage, where the root prati-han is taken in the sense of striking against or obstructing; hence non-obstruction. Compare the Lokesh Chandra form apratihata-vijñāna-avirahita, 'not lacking unobstructed consciousness'.
Verbal form of khong khro ba, corresponding to Sanskrit pratihanyate: to become hostile, upset, or angered.
In Conze's renderings of pratihanyate the passive of prati-han is taken in the sense of being struck back, obstructed, or frustrated; also 'beat back'.

Negation of khong du chud pa ('to take inside', to understand or internalize), corresponding to Sanskrit ananubuddha, 'not understood'. Used of something not fully comprehended, penetrated, or internalized.

Corresponding to Sanskrit duranubodha / duravabodha, difficult to comprehend. Given the sense of khong du chud pa as taking something inside, it also renders 'hard to penetrate, realize, or internalize'.

khyab pa khas blangs pa red.gloss: the pervasion/entailment has been asserted; [you] have asserted the entailment

senses.gloss: the pervasion/entailment has been asserted; [you] have asserted the entailment
senses.context: A debate formula acknowledging or charging that the pervasion (khyab pa) of a syllogism has already been accepted by the opponent. Hopkins renders it both as an accusation addressed to the opponent ('[you] have asserted entailment/pervasion') and impersonally ('the entailment/pervasion has been asserted').

The pervasion or entailment in its proper, unmistaken form, as opposed to defective or distorted formulations of it. Hopkins glosses khyab pa rnal ma as 'normative entailment/pervasion,' 'natural entailment/pervasion,' and 'correct entailment/pervasion.'

A pervasion or entailment stated in inverted or erroneous form, hence faulty. Hopkins gives 'perverse forward pervasion,' 'perverse entailment/pervasion,' and 'mistaken entailment/pervasion'; it stands opposed to a correct or normative pervasion.

Sanskrit vyāpyālambana: an object of observation (dmigs pa, ālambana) characterized as pervading, i.e., one that extends over or encompasses what it takes as its objects. Hopkins renders it 'pervasive object of observation.'
Said of something whose very nature (rang bzhin) is to pervade, hence rendered by Hopkins simply as 'all-pervasive.' The comparanda do not specify what is pervaded or the doctrinal context.
Locative form of mkha' 'space, sky', corresponding to Sanskrit divi 'in the sky/heaven'. Used to state where something is located or occurs, i.e. in the open sky or in space.

senses.gloss: through the sky, through the air
senses.context: Rendering Sanskrit vihāyasā (= ākāśena), an instrumental sense: by way of the sky, through the air. Typically of motion or travel that proceeds through space rather than on the ground.

mkhar gyi rgyal po.gloss: king of a fort; commander of a fort

senses.gloss: king of a fort; commander of a fort
senses.context: Equivalent to Sanskrit koṭṭa-rājan, formed from mkhar 'fort, fortress' with rgyal po 'king'. Denotes the ruler or garrison commander in charge of a stronghold, as distinct from a king of a whole realm.

see_also: mkhar dang gnas la sogs pa'i ming

senses.context: Renders Sanskrit kauśalya-yukta, 'joined with/possessed of skillfulness'. Said of one who has the quality of mkhas pa — skill, expertise, or wisdom in a domain.

mkhas pa dang 'dzangs pas rig par bgyi b.gloss: to be known only by the learned and discerning

senses.gloss: to be known only by the learned and discerning
senses.context: Renders Sanskrit paṇḍita-vijñā-vedanīya, 'to be experienced/known by the learned and the discerning'. Marks a subject matter that can only be apprehended (felt, understood) by those who are both scholarly (mkhas pa) and sharp-witted ('dzangs pa).

see_also: mkhas pa rnams kyis tshul bzhin brtags na

senses.context: Renders Sanskrit daśavidhaṃ kauśalyam, 'skillfulness of ten kinds'. An enumerated set presenting skill or expertise (mkhas pa) under ten headings or aspects.

see_also: mkhas pa rnams kyi las rnam gsum po

senses.context: Rendered by Sanskrit vidu and glossed 'wise, experienced', the term combines mkhas ('skilled, learned') with rig pa ('knowing'). It designates a person possessed of expert knowledge or experience.

A verbal phrase corresponding to Sanskrit vicakṣaṇaś ca bhavati upāya-jñaḥ, predicating of someone that he is expert (mkhas = vicakṣaṇa) and at the same time knows techniques or means (thabs shes pa = upāya-jña).
Equated with Sanskrit kaṭa, kapola, and gaṇḍa, all terms for the cheek or side of the face; the Tibetan is glossed 'cheeks'. It belongs with mkhur ba, the simple term for cheek.

A phrase composed of mkho ba ('needed, required') with yo byad ('articles, requisites') and phran tshegs ('minor, petty'), glossed 'minor articles of necessity'. It refers to small items required for use, as distinguished from major requisites.

see_also: mkho yo byad mkho dgu sna tshogs su

senses.context: A metaphorical phrase, mkhyen pa ('exalted knowing/knowledge', honorific) with gter ('treasure, treasury'), glossed 'treasure of exalted knowledge'. It presents such knowledge as a rich store or repository.

gang gā'i klung mnyam.gloss: equal to (the sands of) the Ganges river

senses.gloss: equal to (the sands of) the Ganges river
senses.context: Renders Sanskrit gaṅgā-nadī-vālī-sama, literally "equal to the sands of the river Ganges." Hopkins gives both "equal with the Ganges" and, for the Conze-style usage, "like the sands of the Ganges."

senses.gloss: as numerous as the Ganges' sands
senses.context: Used as a figure of an incalculably large number, the sands of the Ganges serving as the standard of comparison; cf. the related phrases counting buddhas by that measure.

see_also: gang gā'i klung gi bye ma snyed
gang gā'i klung gi bye ma 'di snyed dang mnyam pa'i sangs rgyas

senses.context: A correlative construction rendering Sanskrit yadā ... tadā, in which gang gi tshe introduces the temporal clause and de'i tshe the correlate. Hopkins classes it simply as the correlative construction "when."

gang gi slad du.gloss: for what reason?; for the sake of what?

senses.gloss: for what reason?; for the sake of what?
senses.context: In interrogative use, corresponding to Sanskrit yannimittam or yena, asking after the reason or purpose of something.

senses.gloss: for the sake of which; because of which
senses.context: In relative use, corresponding to Sanskrit yena / yasmāt, introducing the reason or purpose to which a following correlate answers.
A relative construction (gang gis ... de) glossed by Hopkins as "one who knows emptiness," i.e. whoever cognizes emptiness, that person. No Sanskrit equivalent is supplied.
Renders Sanskrit yena ca pratipadyante yatra ca, a double relative specifying the agent who accomplishes (or practices) something and the place or basis in which it is accomplished.

gang ci'ang rung.gloss: whatever it may be; any and all

senses.gloss: whatever it may be; any and all
senses.context: Indefinite expression built on gang ("what, which") with the concessive rung, corresponding to Sanskrit yat kiñcid / yatkiñcit. Used to include indiscriminately anything that falls under the category at issue, hence Hopkins's rendering "any and all."

gang ltar khas len pa ni dpyad par bya'o.gloss: it should be analyzed what sort of assertion is to be made

senses.gloss: it should be analyzed what sort of assertion is to be made
senses.context: A full sentence-formula of scholastic exposition, combining gang ltar ("in what way, what sort of"), khas len pa ("assertion, to assert"), and dpyad par bya'o ("is to be analyzed/examined"). It defers a position, indicating that the manner of the assertion to be adopted requires further investigation.

gang du 'dod pa'i zhing du 'gro ba.gloss: going to whatever field one wishes

senses.gloss: going to whatever field one wishes
senses.context: Renders Sanskrit yatrecchā-kṣetra-gamanatā, the capacity of going to the field (kṣetra, zhing) to which one wishes to go. Hopkins glosses it both as "going to the pure land to which one wishes/wants" and, following Conze, as "going to the field one wishes to go to."

gang du dbang bskur pa'i dkyil 'khor.gloss: the maṇḍala in which initiation is bestowed

senses.gloss: the maṇḍala in which initiation is bestowed
senses.context: A tantric term designating the particular maṇḍala (dkyil 'khor) serving as the locus in which initiation (dbang bskur ba) is conferred upon the disciple.
Negative expression corresponding to Sanskrit na kaṃcid-gata (from kim), i.e., having gone nowhere at all. The gang du yang ... ma element supplies the universal negation of any destination.
Transliteration of the Sanskrit name Guṇaśrī, used as a personal (proper) name. The Tibetan retains the Sanskrit form rather than translating it.
A name combining gu ru (guru, teacher) with yid bzhin nor bu, the wish-fulfilling jewel (cintāmaṇi). It is attested as the designation of a particular form of Padmākara.
An orthographic variant of gug skyed / gug skyes, glossed as the vocalic ornaments (vowel marks) of the syllabary. It corresponds to Sanskrit mātrā, a vowel sign or measure.
In one tantric attestation the equivalent given is Sanskrit mudrā, in the spelling gug skyes.
Glossed as the vocalic ornaments, i.e. the vowel marks attached to consonants, rendering Sanskrit mātrā. The forms gug kyed and gug skyes are recorded as variants of the same term.
In tantric contexts the variant spelling gug skyes is attested for Sanskrit mudrā.
Attested in tantric literature as an equivalent of Sanskrit mudrā. The spellings gug skyed and gug kyed are recorded as variants.
In the spelling gug skyed the term corresponds to Sanskrit mātrā, the vowel signs or vocalic ornaments of the syllabary.
Renders Sanskrit sudṛśa/sudarśana, "of good/handsome appearance," glossed in English as "excellent appearance." Used of what is fair or splendid to look upon.

The plural Sanskrit form sudṛśāḥ given among the equivalents indicates use as the designation of a class of beings (gods) so named. In such contexts the term functions as a proper name rather than as a simple descriptive adjective.
Corresponds to Sanskrit praṇīta, "presented, choice, excellent," said of what is of the finest quality. The English comparandum "auspiciousness" points to the sense of something fine and favorable.
Where the term is taken substantivally it is glossed "auspiciousness," i.e. the quality of being excellent or of good augury.

Adverbial form corresponding to Sanskrit sahasā, "suddenly, forcibly, precipitately"; the English comparandum renders it with "hurries." It characterizes an action done abruptly or in haste rather than deliberately.

Equivalent to Sanskrit Dravya Mallaputra, identified in the English comparandum as the name of an arhat. The Tibetan reflects the components of the name element by element: gyad bu for mallaputra ("son of a wrestler/strong man") and nor for dravya.

Idiomatic construction corresponding to Sanskrit bhūtvā ... bhavati, i.e. "having become ... it becomes (again)." The gyur la clause gives the completed becoming and yang 'gyur the renewed becoming, expressing repeated or recurrent transformation.
Verbal expression for the act of putting on or wearing something, glossed by Hopkins as "put on, dress, wear." Formed from gyon (to wear) plus byed (to do, make).
The Sanskrit comparanda saṃnahantī (from saṃnāha, girding on/armor) indicate the sense of strapping or girding something on, as in donning armor.
A place name identified in the comparanda only as a cave associated with Guru Rinpoche (Padmasambhava). The comparanda supply no further descriptive information.
A college or constituent division of a monastery, where monks (grwa pa) are gathered for study. This is the unit counted in enumerations such as grwa sa gsum and grwa sa bzhi.

An enumeration of four Ge-luk-pa monastic seats: Se-ra (se rwa), Dre-pung ('bras spungs), Gan-den (dga' ldan), and Tra-shi-hlün-po (bkra shis lhun po). It extends the more common list of three (grwa sa gsum) by the addition of Tra-shi-hlün-po.

An enumeration of the three principal Ge-luk-pa monastic seats: Se-ra (se rwa), Dre-pung ('bras spungs), and Gan-den (dga' ldan). When Tra-shi-hlün-po (bkra shis lhun po) is added, the list becomes grwa sa bzhi, the four monastic colleges.
Renders Sanskrit ṛṣi, a sage or seer. Used of the ancient inspired sages of Indian tradition, glossed in English as "sage" or "seer".
Literally "not cut off by number," i.e. not delimited or bounded in number. Rendered as innumerable, uncountable, countless, measureless, incalculable, or infinite.

grangs 'gro.gloss: be reckoned among, go in the count of

senses.gloss: be reckoned among, go in the count of
senses.context: For Sanskrit saṃkhyāṃ gacchati, literally "goes into the number/count." Used of something counted or included within a given class or category.

senses.gloss: come to be called, derive one's name from
senses.context: In the sense equated with vyapadeśaṃ gacchati, it means to be styled or designated as something, to derive one's name from it, or (of an expression) that it makes sense to say so.
Renders Sanskrit sāṃkhya, denoting the Sāṃkhya system and, with the personal suffix pa, its adherents, translated as "Enumerators."

grangs snyed.gloss: as many as, equal in number to

senses.gloss: as many as, equal in number to
senses.context: A correlative expression of quantity: however many there are, that same number. Used to indicate that one set equals another in number.

gral gsham.gloss: lower rank; lower end of a row

senses.gloss: lower rank; lower end of a row
senses.context: Designates the inferior position within a seating order or hierarchy of ranks, as opposed to the upper portion (gral stod). Hopkins glosses it as 'lower rank'.

gras mtshungs pa.gloss: of the same class; matching in order

senses.gloss: of the same class; matching in order
senses.context: Formed on gras (class, category, set) with mtshungs pa (equal, alike), i.e. belonging to a like category or standing in like sequence. Hopkins renders it 'order; orderly fashion', suggesting the sense of items arranged in matching series.
Renders Sanskrit chāyā, the shade or shadow cast by an object. In this sense it overlaps with grib ma.
Extended sense of a covering or taint that obscures; compare grib pa med par (anāvaraṇa) 'without obscuration, undefiled' and grib pa rnam sel 'clearing away obscurations'.
Tibetan rendering of Sanskrit sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhī, the name of a bodhisattva, literally 'one who dispels (rnam sel) obscurations (grib pa)'.
Adverbial/qualifying form corresponding to Sanskrit anāvaraṇa, 'without covering or obstruction'. Negates grib pa in its sense of a screening or obscuring factor.
Hopkins also glosses it as 'undefiled; not filthy; without stain; uncontaminated', taking grib pa as taint or pollution rather than as a physical covering.

gru zhig.gloss: shipwrecked; one whose boat is wrecked

senses.gloss: shipwrecked; one whose boat is wrecked
senses.context: Literally a broken or ruined vessel; used of a person who suffers shipwreck, i.e., whose ship has come apart. The Sanskrit comparandum bhinna-bhāva points to the state of being broken up or shattered.

An awareness or mind that engages its object in a complete, total manner, as reflected in the reconstructed Sanskrit *viddhi-pravṛtti-buddhi. The term classifies a consciousness by the mode in which it takes up its object.

grub mtha' kun shes nas mtha' bral sgrub.gloss: title: Ocean of Good Explanations, commentary on Establishment of Freedom from Extremes through Understanding All Tenets

senses.gloss: title: Ocean of Good Explanations, commentary on Establishment of Freedom from Extremes through Understanding All Tenets
senses.context: The title of an explanatory treatise (rnam par bshad pa) on the work called 'Establishment of Freedom from Extremes through Understanding All Tenets,' composed by the translator Tagtsang Lotsāwa Sherab Rinchen (stag tshang lo tsā ba shes rab rin chen; b. 1405). It belongs to the genre of tenet-system (grub mtha') literature.

Said of abandoning or giving up a tenet of one's own system, specifically by asserting something contrary to it. The phrase describes an inconsistency in which a proponent's assertion undermines a position he holds.
A standard enumeration of four Buddhist tenet systems (grub mtha'). The term is used to group the philosophical schools treated in tenet-system literature.

Verbal phrase corresponding to Sanskrit forms of sidh- (siddhyanti, siddhyeta), i.e. coming to be established, accomplished, achieved, or perfected. Used where something turns out to be the case or is brought to completion.
In Prajñāpāramitā contexts (C) rendered 'will succeed', with the sense of arising, becoming, or coming to be.

grub par bya ba.gloss: that which is to be established/proved

senses.gloss: that which is to be established/proved
senses.context: Corresponds to Sanskrit sādhya, the object or thesis to be established, achieved, mastered, or perfected.
Also given for prasiddhi and siddhi, the state of being established or accomplished.
Honorific causative phrase indicating that something has been accomplished or achieved, or is taken/treated as established.
Given by Hopkins as the name of the animal, the badger.
Lokesh Chandra gives Sanskrit phulla, i.e. opened out or in full bloom; on this equivalence the term belongs with words for expansion and flowering rather than with the animal name.
Corresponds to Sanskrit khañja and paṃgu, denoting one who is lame or crippled in the legs; rendered 'lame' in Prajñāpāramitā contexts (C).

grur zhugs pa la brten nas.gloss: in dependence on being seated in a boat

senses.gloss: in dependence on being seated in a boat
senses.context: Adverbial phrase used in illustrations of mistaken sense perception: because one is riding in a boat, other things appear otherwise than they are. It regularly introduces the example of trees seeming to move for a passenger on a boat.

see_also: grur zhugs la brten nas ljon shing 'gro bar snang ba'i dbang shes

grur zhugs la brten nas ljon shing 'gro.gloss: sense consciousness to which trees appear to move because one is in a boat

senses.gloss: sense consciousness to which trees appear to move because one is in a boat
senses.context: A stock example of a mistaken (though sensory) consciousness: for someone who has boarded a boat, the trees on the shore appear to be moving. The appearance is caused by the observer's own motion, hence the consciousness is erroneous with respect to its appearing object.

see_also: grur zhugs pa la brten nas

senses.context: Name of a class of harmful spirit or ghost, glossed as mischievous. Apparently a compound of gre (see gre mo, 'ghost spirit') with gnyan, indicating its dangerous or troublesome character.
A type of ghost or spirit being. Compare gre po gnyan, identified as a mischievous ghost spirit of the same class.

Haribhadra's shorter commentary on Maitreya's Ornament for Clear Realization (Abhisamayālaṃkāra), Sanskrit Sphuṭārthā, also written 'grel pa don gsal. Its fuller title is given as Commentary on (Maitreya's) 'Ornament for Clear Realization, Treatise of Quintessential Instructions on the Perfection of Wisdom.'

see_also: shes rab kyi pha rol tu phyin pa'i man ngag gi bstan bcos mngon par rtogs pa'i rgyan ces bya'i 'grel pa

grol ba nyid.gloss: liberatedness, the state of being free

senses.gloss: liberatedness, the state of being free
senses.context: Abstract noun formed from grol ba ('to be freed, released'), corresponding to Sanskrit muktatā. It denotes release, freedom or liberation itself — the very fact or condition of being loosened and set free.
Agentive form of grol ba, rendering Sanskrit moktṛ. It designates the one who releases, frees or loosens — the agent of liberation.
Corresponds to Sanskrit kastūrīmṛga, the deer from which musk is obtained.
Also given for Sanskrit kastūrī, the musk substance itself; compare gla ba'i lte ba, the musk-pod (lit. 'navel') of the animal.
Corresponds to Sanskrit avatāru labhiṣyati, 'will find/obtain an entrance.' Used of gaining an opportunity or foothold — finding a chance or vulnerable opening (glags).

see_also: glags rnyed gyur nas dge 'phrog cing

glags rnyed par 'gyur.gloss: find an opportunity, get a chance

senses.gloss: find an opportunity, get a chance
senses.context: Corresponds to Sanskrit avakāśaṃ labhate, 'obtains an opening/scope.' Denotes gaining an opportunity or occasion with respect to something, i.e., finding a chance or opening (glags).
Personal name of a Ka-dam-pa Ge-shay, said to have been renowned for never laughing. Attested only as a proper name; the elements do not function here as a common noun.

Rendering Sanskrit bhrānta-hastin, an elephant that is mistaken or illusory rather than real. Used as an example of an appearance that is deceptive, glang po che being "elephant" and 'khrul pa indicating error or illusion.

see_also: glang po che la sogs par med pa

glang po che dang rta'i tshogs la sogs p.gloss: similar to herds of elephants and horses, etc.

senses.gloss: similar to herds of elephants and horses, etc.
senses.context: Corresponds to Sanskrit hasty-aśva-kāyādi-bhūtatva, i.e., being like a mass or troop of elephants, horses, and so forth. A comparative phrase built on glang po che (elephant) with rta (horse) and tshogs (herd, multitude).

see_also: glang po che la sogs pa

senses.context: Renders Sanskrit hastyādi, a listing phrase citing elephants as the first item of a series. The suffix la sogs pa indicates "and so forth," leaving the remaining members implicit.

see_also: glang po che la sogs par med pa

senses.context: Corresponds to Sanskrit hastitvādy-abhāva, the absence or nonexistence of elephants and the like. The negative counterpart of glang po che la sogs pa.

see_also: glang po che la sogs pa

senses.context: Rendering Sanskrit prīti-sahagata, literally accompanied by joy (prīti); said of a state or mental factor that goes together with joy. Hopkins glosses it as 'joyous; possessing joy; endowed with joy; happy.'

A negated compound: not being separated (bral ba med pa) from joy or happiness. Corresponds to Sanskrit avirati, which the Conze-based comparanda render as 'no discontent,' i.e. an unbroken state of delight or non-cessation of pleasure.

For Sanskrit rati-saṃprayukta, 'conjoined/associated with joy (rati).' The Tibetan mtshungs par ldan pa renders saṃprayukta, the technical term for a mental factor accompanying and concordant with another, hence Hopkins' 'having similar association with joy.'

Rendering prīti-saumanasya-jāta, in which joy (prīti, dga' ba) and gladness of mind (saumanasya, yid bde) have arisen or been produced. The comparanda offer both a causative-sounding English rendering ('generate/produce/engender joy and mental bliss') and descriptive ones ('exultant and glad,' 'full of zest and gladness,' 'overjoyed and enchanted').

For Sanskrit ratisaṃgrāhaka-manaskāra: a manaskāra (yid byed, mental contemplation or mental engagement) characterized as saṃgrāhaka, 'gathering/comprising,' with respect to joy (rati, dga' ba). Hopkins renders it 'mental contemplation of joy-withdrawal,' taking sdud pa in the sense of drawing in or collecting; the comparanda do not specify further the meditative context in which such a manaskāra

Verbal form built on dga' ba 'joy, delight', rendering Sanskrit ramate — to take pleasure or delight in something, with the gloss (=bhaktiṃ karoti) suggesting devoted attachment. Hopkins accordingly gives 'become joyful, enjoy oneself, delights in, have joy'.
Corresponding to Sanskrit spṛhaṇīya, the phrase can describe something that is an object of delight, hence 'desirable, to be envied, enviable'.

dga' bar mi bya ba.gloss: not to take joy, not to delight in

senses.gloss: not to take joy, not to delight in
senses.context: Negated form of dga' bar bya ba, corresponding to Sanskrit anabhirati, the absence of delight or pleasure. Hopkins glosses simply 'not take joy'.

dga' bar mi byed.gloss: does not take joy, does not delight

senses.gloss: does not take joy, does not delight
senses.context: Negated verbal phrase corresponding to Sanskrit ratir na kāryaṃ and na ramante — not to take pleasure or delight (in something). Hopkins gives 'not take joy, not take delight'; the equivalent apayāti points to turning away from an object of pleasure.

Renders Sanskrit prīṇayati (√prī), to gladden or satisfy. The Tibetan combines dga' ba (joy) with tshim pa (satisfaction), hence Hopkins's 'satisfy, joyously satisfy' — to satisfy someone in a way that produces delight.

dga' bar mdzad pa'i tshul gyis.gloss: in the manner of making joyous

senses.gloss: in the manner of making joyous
senses.context: Adverbial phrase (tshul gyis, 'by way of, in the manner of') on dga' bar mdzad pa, 'making (someone) joyful', rendering Sanskrit saṃharṣayamāṇa-rūpa. Hopkins also gives the Conze-style rendering 'with a thrill', i.e. displaying or arousing gladness.

Causal phrase (…phyir, "because of, due to") built on gnas pa "to abide, dwell" qualified by dga' ba "joy, delight" in the instrumental/comitative (dga' bas), rendering Sanskrit ratyā viharaṇāt. Used to give the reason that someone dwells or remains in a joyous state.

Causative formation on dga' "joy, delight," corresponding to Sanskrit pramodayāti, prītikara, priyaṃkara, priyakāra: that which causes joy or affection in others. Also used for ārādhana, gratifying or propitiating.
As a nominal, it renders Sanskrit nandaka, nandana, nandika, priya, mudira — "the one who gladdens, the delightful one" — and can function as a proper name or epithet.
Verbal form meaning to cause delight in another; the negated form mi dga' byed pa corresponds to udvejana, causing dismay or agitation.
Also used intransitively for Sanskrit āmodate (ā √mud) "rejoices," mādyanti "they delight," and for nirata "delighting in, devoted to"; vinodin suggests one who diverts or takes pleasure.
Honorific expression for a person's age, literally the count (grangs) of years (dgung), used of respected persons.
Term for the open sky or the expanse of space, including the intermediate space between earth and heaven.

dge ba'i bshes gnyen dang ldan.gloss: having a spiritual guide; accompanied by a virtuous friend

senses.gloss: having a spiritual guide; accompanied by a virtuous friend
senses.context: Renders Sanskrit kalyāṇa-mitra-sahita, 'accompanied by a good/virtuous friend'. Describes a person who is in possession of, or in the company of, a spiritual teacher or virtuous friend (dge ba'i bshes gnyen).

Corresponds to Sanskrit kalyāṇa-mitra-vaidhurya, the absence or deprivation of a virtuous friend. Used of one who does not have a spiritual teacher; the negative counterpart of dge ba'i bshes gnyen dang ldan.

Glossed as depending closely upon (nye bar brten) a virtuous friend or spiritual teacher, the Sanskrit comparandum having the sense of resorting to a true friend (mitram upāśritaḥ). Denotes the attitude of taking a spiritual guide as one's support.

dge ba'i sems.gloss: virtuous mind, virtuous state of mind

senses.gloss: virtuous mind, virtuous state of mind
senses.context: Equivalent to Sanskrit kuśala-citta or sucetas, a mind or mental state that is wholesome/virtuous. Refers to the mind itself as qualified by virtue, in contrast to non-virtuous states of mind.
The mental factors (sems byung) that are virtuous in nature, as distinguished from non-virtuous or neutral ones. Used in enumerations of mental factors accompanying a virtuous mind (dge ba'i sems).
An enumerative term for a set of eleven mental factors (sems byung) classed as virtuous (dge ba). The comparanda give only the count and the classification, without listing the members.
Renders Sanskrit kalyāṇāśaya, a thought or attitude (bsam pa) that is virtuous or good. Hopkins also allows the reading 'thought of virtue', i.e. a mental attitude directed toward virtue.

dge bar bya ba.gloss: acting virtuously; doing what is virtuous

senses.gloss: acting virtuously; doing what is virtuous
senses.context: A verbal-noun form of dge ba, glossed by Hopkins as 'acting virtuously' — the performance of virtue.
Corresponding to Sanskrit kalyāṇa, the term also carries the general senses 'good', 'lovely', and 'helpful(ness)' recorded in Conze's vocabulary.

dge bas 'phel bar byed pa.gloss: increase through virtue; cause to grow by virtues

senses.gloss: increase through virtue; cause to grow by virtues
senses.context: Translates Sanskrit kuśalair vardhayanti, 'they increase (something) by means of virtues/wholesome factors'. The Tibetan expresses causing growth or augmentation by means of virtue.

dge byed pa.gloss: making virtue; producing what is virtuous

senses.gloss: making virtue; producing what is virtuous
senses.context: Renders Sanskrit śubha-kara, literally 'virtue-maker', one who or that which produces virtue or the auspicious/good (śubha).

dge tshul gyi phyir bcos.gloss: novice's monastic discipline; corrective training for a novice (dge tshul)

senses.gloss: novice's monastic discipline; corrective training for a novice (dge tshul)
senses.context: Refers to the regime of Buddhist monastic discipline as it applies to a novice (dge tshul), i.e., the code by which a novice's conduct is trained and rectified. Attested only through the English gloss 'Buddhist monastic discipline for a novice'.

dge tshul gyi slob dpon.gloss: novice preceptor; master of a novice

senses.gloss: novice preceptor; master of a novice
senses.context: The slob dpon (teacher/master) who serves as preceptor for a dge tshul (novice), in the context of monastic ordination and training. Supported only by the gloss 'novice preceptor'.

dge tshul gyi bslab pa'i gzhi'i mdo.gloss: Śikṣāpada-sūtra; Sūtra of the Basic Points of Novice Monastic Training

senses.gloss: Śikṣāpada-sūtra; Sūtra of the Basic Points of Novice Monastic Training
senses.context: Title of a text, Sanskrit śikṣāpada-sūtra / śrāmaṇera-śikṣāpada-sūtra, setting out the bslab pa'i gzhi ('basic points of training', śikṣāpada) undertaken by a novice (dge tshul, śrāmaṇera). A variant form of the same title appears as dge tshul bslab pa'i gzhi mdo.

dge tshul bslab pa'i gzhi mdo.gloss: Śikṣāpada-sūtra; Sūtra of the Basic Points of Novice Monastic Training

senses.gloss: Śikṣāpada-sūtra; Sūtra of the Basic Points of Novice Monastic Training
senses.context: Variant title form of the same work as dge tshul gyi bslab pa'i gzhi'i mdo, Sanskrit śikṣāpada-sūtra / śrāmaṇera-śikṣāpada-sūtra. It presents the śikṣāpada, the basic points of training taken on by a novice (dge tshul, śrāmaṇera).

Rendering Sanskrit kuśalāpramatta: attentive and non-negligent (bag yod, apramatta) in relation to what is virtuous (dge ba, kuśala). Describes the quality of care exercised toward virtuous states and actions.

dge la yang dag par spro ba.gloss: enthusiasm for virtue, delighting in virtue

senses.gloss: enthusiasm for virtue, delighting in virtue
senses.context: Rendering Sanskrit utsāha kuśale samyak, the term denotes correct or thoroughgoing enthusiasm (spro ba) directed toward what is virtuous (dge ba). Attested in Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra-type contexts describing the mental vigor with which a practitioner takes up wholesome activity.
A mind or mental state (sems) qualified as virtuous (dge) in a distinguished or superior degree (khyad par can). The comparanda supply only this general descriptive sense.

Glossed by Sanskrit śrāmaṇyatā and rendered in the Conze materials as 'honoring recluses', i.e., recognizing or acknowledging someone as a monk or renunciate. The Tibetan literally has the sense of knowing or apprehending (shes pa) a person as a dge slong.
Negation of dge slong (bhikṣu), corresponding to Sanskrit abhikṣu. Used both for one who is not a monk at all and, in the Conze materials, for one who ceases to be a monk.
The precepts or points of training (bslab bya) prescribed for fully ordained nuns (dge slong ma). The comparanda support only this general disciplinary sense, without specifying the enumeration.

see_also: dge bsnyen dang dge bsnyen ma gnyis

senses.context: Rendered by Sanskrit eṇa, a kind of antelope or deer; used as the name of the animal.

A compound of dgongs (thought, intention, view) and nyams (experience), glossed as the perspective or outlook arising from experience. Only the English gloss is attested here, so the range of usage cannot be specified further.

dgongs pa can gyi don.gloss: meaning with a thought behind it; intentional meaning

senses.gloss: meaning with a thought behind it; intentional meaning
senses.context: Corresponds to Sanskrit abhiprāyikārtha, the sense (artha) that is intended (abhiprāyika) rather than stated literally. Used of statements whose real import lies in the speaker's underlying intention.

see_also: dgongs pa nges par 'grel pa'i mdo

dgongs pa der 'bab pa.gloss: the thought comes down to that

senses.gloss: the thought comes down to that
senses.context: Idiomatic phrase indicating that the underlying intention (dgongs pa) of a statement resolves into or amounts to the point just specified.

Continuative form (…de) of dgongs pa mdzad pa, honorific for thinking or considering; corresponds to Sanskrit samanvāharati. Used of a venerable subject who bears something in mind or turns his attention to it.

senses.gloss: his mind being impressed by; bringing to mind
senses.context: In the readings recorded from Conze, samanvāharati is glossed as 'his mind is impressed by,' 'bring to mind,' 'bear in mind,' and even 'thinks to himself' or 'behaves towards' — nuances of directing attention toward an object.

A set of four abhiprāya — modes of the Buddha's underlying thought or intention behind a statement — enumerated as a group (Skt. catvāro 'bhiprāyāḥ). Used where scriptural statements are classified according to the intention with which they were spoken.

Renders Sanskrit bhāvātigahana (Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra), describing an intention or meaning that is exceedingly deep and hard to fathom. Applied to the Buddha's underlying thought when it is not accessible on the surface of the words.

Skt. saṃdhyābhāṣā (also given as sandhyā-bhāṣa): utterance whose stated words carry an implied or intended meaning distinct from their literal sense. Corresponds to statements made with an underlying thought (dgongs pa) requiring interpretation.
Phrase used when a text's or author's underlying intention seems, on examination, to be such-and-such. Marks a tentative ascription of intent rather than an explicit statement.

dgongs gzhi dang dngos la gnod byed.gloss: the basis in [the Buddha's] thought and the damage to what is explicitly taught

senses.gloss: the basis in [the Buddha's] thought and the damage to what is explicitly taught
senses.context: A paired phrase naming two factors invoked in assessing a scriptural statement: the basis intended in the Buddha's thought (dgongs gzhi) and the invalidation of the literal, explicit sense (dngos la gnod byed). Occurs in discussions of which statements are to be taken literally and which require interpretation.

see_also: dgongs pa nges par 'grel pa'i mdo

senses.context: A compound of dgon (monastery, hermitage) with rnying (old, former). Attested only as a phrasal gloss, 'ancient monastery', i.e. a monastic establishment of long standing.

Renders araṇya-vanaprastha, a paired expression joining dgon pa (wilderness, secluded place) and nags 'dab (woodland, forest tract). Glossed simply as 'jungle', i.e. the uninhabited wooded country in which ascetics dwell.

see_also: dgon pa nags khrod chen po

senses.context: Renders araṇyamahāvanaprastha, combining dgon pa (wilderness) with nags khrod chen po (great forest thicket). Denotes an expanse of deep forest remote from settlement.
Taken with dgon pa in its sense of a secluded dwelling place, the term designates a hermitage or retreat situated within a great forest.

dgon pa pa.gloss: forest dweller, one living in the wilderness

senses.gloss: forest dweller, one living in the wilderness
senses.context: Renders āraṇyaka and āṭavika: one who dwells in the wilderness or forest, i.e. a practitioner keeping to remote hermitages rather than to villages. Also used adjectivally, 'belonging to the forest'.

dgon pa lhur byed cing.gloss: devoted to dwelling in the wilderness

senses.gloss: devoted to dwelling in the wilderness
senses.context: Renders araṇya-parama, 'having the forest as one's highest concern'. The verbal phrase dgon pa lhur byed describes one who applies himself wholeheartedly to life in the remote wilderness or forest.

dgon pa'i thig le.gloss: "drop of the wilderness," name of a tree

senses.gloss: "drop of the wilderness," name of a tree
senses.context: Rendering Sanskrit araṇye-tilaka, understood as the designation of a particular tree. The Tibetan compounds dgon pa (wilderness, remote place) with thig le (drop, mark), matching tilaka.

dgon pa'i lam.gloss: wilderness road, path through the wilds

senses.gloss: wilderness road, path through the wilds
senses.context: Corresponds to Sanskrit kāntāra-mārga (also attested as kāntāra-mārgi), the road across a wilderness or desert tract. Glossed simply as "wilderness" in the Conze-based materials.

see_also: dgon pa nags khrod chen po

senses.context: Renders Sanskrit araṇya-viveka-cārin, "one who courses in the detachment (viveka) of the remote forest (araṇya)." The term describes a practitioner whose conduct consists in dwelling apart in wilderness solitude.

see_also: dgon pa nags khrod chen po

senses.context: A grammatical designation for the word or particle expressing purpose or benefit, i.e. the dative case. Formed from dgos (need, requirement) plus ched (sake, purpose) and sgra (word, term).

dgos pa ltos pa'i grangs nges.gloss: definite enumeration in terms of purpose

senses.gloss: definite enumeration in terms of purpose
senses.context: A type of definite enumeration (grangs nges) established relative to a purpose (dgos pa ltos pa) rather than by other criteria. Also rendered "definite enumeration relative to purpose."

dgos pa thams cad byed pa.gloss: effecting all purposes; accomplishing every aim

senses.gloss: effecting all purposes; accomplishing every aim
senses.context: Renders Sanskrit sarva-kārya-karaṇa, 'the doing of all tasks/purposes.' Used of what brings about or fulfills every needed aim or function.

dgos pa byed do.gloss: performs its purpose; does its work

senses.gloss: performs its purpose; does its work
senses.context: Corresponds to kāryaṃ karoti, 'does the task.' Said of something that actually carries out the function or purpose proper to it.

see_also: dgos pa thams cad byed pa

dgos pa byed nus pa.gloss: able to perform its purpose; capable of functioning

senses.gloss: able to perform its purpose; capable of functioning
senses.context: Renders kārya-samartha, 'competent for the task.' Indicates capacity or fitness to carry out the work or purpose in question, as distinct from actually doing so.

see_also: dgos pa thams cad byed pa

senses.context: Corresponds to niṣprayojana, 'having no purpose or motive.' Used of what serves no aim or of what is not needed.
A second Sanskrit comparandum, nirupalepa ('free of smearing/adherence'), is also attested for this Tibetan phrase.

see_also: dgos pa thams cad byed pa

dgos pa shin tu yongs su rnyed pa.gloss: one who has thoroughly accomplished his task

senses.gloss: one who has thoroughly accomplished his task
senses.context: Renders supariprāpta-kārya, 'whose work has been well and fully attained.' Describes a person whose purpose or business has been completely achieved.

see_also: dgos pa thams cad byed pa

senses.context: A designation for a Foe Destroyer (dgra bcom pa) qualified as "unadorned" (rgyan med), i.e., lacking some further ornament or attainment attributed to other arhats. The comparanda supply only the rendering "Unadorned Foe Destroyer" and do not specify what the adornment consists of.

A dvandva phrase joining dgra bcom (arhat, Foe Destroyer) and rang rgyal (pratyekabuddha, Solitary Victor/Solitary Realizer), naming the two types of Hearer-vehicle and Solitary-vehicle adepts together. The Sanskrit comparandum is recorded as raha-pratyaya (rahapratyaya), reflecting the same pairing.

dgra bcom pa'i mkhyen pa.gloss: exalted knower of a Foe Destroyer

senses.gloss: exalted knower of a Foe Destroyer
senses.context: The wisdom or exalted knowledge (mkhyen pa) possessed by a Foe Destroyer (dgra bcom pa). The comparanda give only this rendering, without further specification of its objects or divisions.

dgra bcom zhugs pa.gloss: approacher to Foe Destroyer; one entered upon arhatship

senses.gloss: approacher to Foe Destroyer; one entered upon arhatship
senses.context: One who has entered upon (zhugs pa) but not yet attained the fruit of Foe Destroyer, corresponding to Sanskrit arhattva-pratipanna(ka). It contrasts with the abider in the fruit (dgra bcom 'bras gnas).

A compressed compound pairing arhats (dgra bcom) with pratyekabuddhas (rang rgyal), equivalent in sense to dgra bcom dang rang rgyal. The Sanskrit comparanda are given as arhata-pratyaya / raha-pratyaya.

dgra bcom rang rgyal theg pa.gloss: the vehicle(s) of Foe Destroyers (arhats) and Solitary Realizers

senses.gloss: the vehicle(s) of Foe Destroyers (arhats) and Solitary Realizers
senses.context: Compound term for the two non-Mahāyāna vehicles taken together, rendered in Sanskrit as raha-pratyaya-yāna (arhat- and pratyekabuddha-vehicle). Hopkins glosses it as the 'vehicles of Hearers and Solitary Realizers', i.e. the paths whose fruits are arhatship and solitary enlightenment respectively.

dgra bo'i 'du shes.gloss: the discrimination/notion of [someone as] an enemy

senses.gloss: the discrimination/notion of [someone as] an enemy
senses.context: Sanskrit amitra-saṃjñā: the apprehension or conceptual identification of another person as a foe. Here dgra bo is the enemy and 'du shes the discriminating notion applied to him.

dgra bo'i 'du shes su byed pa.gloss: discriminating [someone] as an enemy; forming the notion of a foe

senses.gloss: discriminating [someone] as an enemy; forming the notion of a foe
senses.context: Verbal form of dgra bo'i 'du shes, corresponding to Sanskrit śatru-saṃjñā-karaṇa, the act of making or entertaining the discrimination that someone is an enemy.

dgra byed mang ba.gloss: having many enemies; full of hostile forces

senses.gloss: having many enemies; full of hostile forces
senses.context: Renders bahū-āmatro (many foes/adversaries). Hopkins gives 'having many enemies/foes', with Conze's 'full of many hostile forces'.

dgra mang ba yin te.gloss: there are many enemies; provokes/is surrounded by much hostility

senses.gloss: there are many enemies; provokes/is surrounded by much hostility
senses.context: Finite verbal phrase corresponding to bahu-pratyarthikāni bhavanti, 'many adversaries arise'. Hopkins renders it as provoking much hostility or being surrounded by much hostility.
Rendered by Sanskrit abakīrṇa (scattered about) and prasārita (stretched/spread out), the term denotes spreading or strewing something over an area. Hopkins gives 'spread out' and 'set out'.
With vistīrṇa (extended, broad) the emphasis falls on the resulting wide extension of what has been laid out; hence Hopkins' 'arrange; set out'.
Sanskrit śatru-vaśa-ga, literally 'gone into the power (vaśa) of an enemy (śatru)'. It describes falling under the control or sway of a foe.
Corresponds to Sanskrit pramocana, parimocayati, pramokṣaṇa and mukti, all expressing release or liberation. Hopkins glosses 'release; free; set free; liberation'.
In a more concrete application the term covers loosening or untying what is bound, as reflected in Hopkins' 'loosen'.

dgrol ba'i phyir.gloss: in order to release, for the sake of freeing

senses.gloss: in order to release, for the sake of freeing
senses.context: The Sanskrit parimocitum and parimocayati indicate purpose, 'in order to set free'; the Tibetan phrase adds phyir to dgrol ba to express this aim.

senses.gloss: because of releasing, on account of liberation
senses.context: Sanskrit mokṣa-kāraṇāt ('from the cause of liberation') shows that phyir here can also mark reason rather than purpose, hence Hopkins' 'because of releasing'.
Given for Sanskrit hasita, 'laughed, laughter, smile'. Hopkins glosses 'laugh; smile', and also causatively 'make laugh or smile'.

bgo gzhi.gloss: basis of infusion; substratum that is infused

senses.gloss: basis of infusion; substratum that is infused
senses.context: Rendered as "basis of infusion," i.e. the gzhi (base, substratum) upon or into which something is spread, applied, or infused. The element bgo relates to the verb bgo ba, of spreading/apportioning something over a base.

senses.gloss: basis for apportionment, basis of a share
senses.context: Given the related terms bgo skal (share, portion) and bgo bsha' (division, apportionment), bgo gzhi can also be read as the base or ground on which a division into shares is made. The comparanda supply only the sense "basis of infusion," so this reading is secondary.

bgyi ba ma mchis pa.gloss: not something to be done; nothing to be done

senses.gloss: not something to be done; nothing to be done
senses.context: Corresponds to Sanskrit akaraṇīya, "not to be done, not fit to be done." The form is honorific: bgyi ba (to do, honorific) negated by the honorific existential ma mchis pa, hence "there is nothing to be done" or "that which is not to be done."

bgyis par 'gyur.gloss: comes to do, performs, makes, acts

senses.gloss: comes to do, performs, makes, acts
senses.context: Honorific verb bgyi ba in the form bgyis par 'gyur, "comes to do / will have done," covering do, perform, make, act, manufacture.
Equated with Sanskrit satkaroti, "to honor, treat with respect," a sense that in Tibetan usually appears with the object bkur sti, as in bkur stir bgyis par 'gyur.

bgrang ba las yang dag par 'das pa.gloss: thoroughly transcending enumeration; beyond all counting

senses.gloss: thoroughly transcending enumeration; beyond all counting
senses.context: Corresponds to Sanskrit gaṇanā-samatikramatā, the state of having completely passed beyond counting. Used of things so many that they cannot be reckoned: "they have transcended all counting."

bgrang bar 'dod pas.gloss: by one wishing to count; since one wishes to enumerate

senses.gloss: by one wishing to count; since one wishes to enumerate
senses.context: Instrumental/agentive form of bgrang ba (to count, enumerate) with 'dod pa (to wish): "by [someone] wishing to count," or causally, "because one wishes to enumerate."

A three-membered phrase rendering gaṇita-tulita-mīmāṃsita, listing successive operations: enumerating (bgrangs pa), weighing or measuring (gzhal ba), and examining or investigating (brtags pa). Used of thoroughgoing assessment, whether by counting and measuring or by comprehending and analyzing.
Corresponds to saṃvid in the sense of mutual understanding or agreement reached in common. The term names the joint deliberation of several parties rather than the pronouncement of one.
Rendering saṃgīti, singing or reciting together. Hopkins gives 'chorus'.

bgro bar byed pa.gloss: chanting together; discussing to settle a meaning

senses.gloss: chanting together; discussing to settle a meaning
senses.context: Renders saṃgāyamāna, glossed as determining the meaning of a text with one another (parasparaṃ grantha-artha-nirṇayāt). Hopkins gives 'chanting'; the Sanskrit gloss shows the activity is a joint recitation/discussion aimed at fixing the sense of a text.

bgrod dka' ba'i lam la kun tu zhugs pa.gloss: entering upon a path hard to travel

senses.gloss: entering upon a path hard to travel
senses.context: Renders durga-mārga-samārūḍha, having fully set out on (mounted, embarked upon) a road that is difficult to traverse. The phrase combines bgrod dka' ba, 'hard to travel', with full entry into the path.

bgrod thub pa.gloss: able to travel, traversable; able to advance

senses.gloss: able to travel, traversable; able to advance
senses.context: The verb bgrod ('go, travel, traverse, progress') with thub pa, 'to be able'. Hopkins glosses it as being able to progress, get along, advance, proceed, or traverse.

Past/perfect form of the verb 'to please, gladden', corresponding to Sanskrit ārādhayati, often with 'mind' (cittam) as object: to have gladdened someone's mind. Used of one who has been made happy or satisfied.
Present/agentive form of the verb corresponding to Sanskrit ārādhayati, 'to gladden, satisfy'; the compound yang dag mgu bar byed pa is equated with saṃ-√rādh.
In Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra usage it renders āvarjana, the act of drawing someone toward oneself by pleasing or gratifying them.
The neck or throat region of the body; the base for terms designating things worn at or associated with the neck.
A protective amulet or charm, literally a 'neck-guard', worn about the throat; formed from mgul (neck) and srung (to protect, guard).
Adverbial phrase corresponding to Sanskrit ekāṃśika, indicating that something holds in a single, unqualified way—hence 'definitely, for certain'.

mgo gcod pa.gloss: to cut off the head, decapitate

senses.gloss: to cut off the head, decapitate
senses.context: Verbal expression rendering Sanskrit śiraś-cheda / śīrṣa-ccheda, literally the severing (gcod pa) of the head (mgo). Used of beheading, and in contexts where someone's head is about to be cut off.
In nominal usage the same phrase names the act itself, corresponding to Sanskrit śiraścheda, 'decapitation'.

mgo mjug pa.gloss: beginning and end; the two ends

senses.gloss: beginning and end; the two ends
senses.context: Formed from mgo (head, beginning) and mjug (tail, end), the compound designates the opening and closing portions of something — e.g. all the beginnings and endings (mgo mjug thams cad) of a sādhana (sgrub thabs). By extension it can simply mean 'the two ends' of a sequence or text.

mgo mjug pa.sanskrit: sgrub thabs kyi mgo mjug thams cad

senses.context: Literally 'black-head(ed)', i.e. one whose hair is uncut, in contrast to the shaven ordained; used for lay people as opposed to monastics.

mgo smos pas go ba/ mgo smos pas go ba m.gloss: one who understands as soon as the main points are mentioned

senses.gloss: one who understands as soon as the main points are mentioned
senses.context: Renders Sanskrit udghaṭita-jña: a person who grasps the matter merely from the mention of the opening or chief points (mgo smos pa), without needing full elaboration. Rendered also as 'acquainted with the main points'.

senses.gloss: (negated form) one who does not understand from mere mention of the main points
senses.context: The paired negative phrase, mgo smos pas go ba ma yin pa, designates those who are not able to understand through the mere mention of the beginning or main points, i.e. 'unacquainted with the main points'.
Verbal idiom built on mgo, 'head, beginning': to set something going, make a start.
